description: Tequila sharpened with lime and orange liqueur behind a crust of salt. A perennial contender for the most-ordered cocktail in the United States.
funFact: 'Margarita' is Spanish for 'daisy,' and the drink is structurally a tequila Daisy — a 19th-century sour template of spirit, citrus, and liqueur.

ingredients.amount: 1 shaker full, plus fresh cubes for the glass

steps: Rub a lime wedge around the outer rim of a chilled margarita or rocks glass, then roll the outside edge in kosher salt. Set aside.
Add the tequila, orange liqueur, and lime juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds, until the tin is frosty.
Strain over fresh ice into the salt-rimmed glass (or fine-strain it straight up).
Garnish with a lime wheel on the rim and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel and a kosher-salt rim

name: Paper Plane
description: Equal parts bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, and lemon folded into perfect bittersweet symmetry. One of the few 21st-century drinks already treated as canon.
funFact: Sam Ross devised it in 2008 for Chicago's The Violet Hour and named it after M.I.A.'s song 'Paper Planes,' which was playing on repeat at the time.

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, and lemon juice to a shaker filled with ice — the drink lives or dies on the equal-parts measure, so jigger carefully.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds.
Double-strain (Hawthorne plus fine strainer) into the chilled coupe, no ice.
Serve as-is; optionally perch a tiny folded paper plane on the rim as a nod to the name.
recipe.garnish: None traditional; optionally a tiny folded paper plane clipped to the rim

name: Penicillin
description: Blended Scotch with lemon and honey-ginger syrup under a smoky float of Islay malt. Medicine-cabinet branding, world-class execution.
funFact: Sam Ross created it at New York's Milk & Honey in 2005, and it spread to bar menus worldwide purely by word of mouth — the definitive modern classic.

ingredients.item: Peaty Islay Scotch (e.g. Laphroaig), to float

ingredients.amount: 1 shaker full, plus 1 large cube for the glass

steps: Make honey-ginger syrup ahead: simmer 1 cup honey, 1 cup water, and a 6-inch knob of thinly sliced ginger for 5 minutes, steep off heat, then strain and chill.
Add the blended Scotch, lemon juice, and honey-ginger syrup to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds and strain into a rocks glass over one large ice cube.
Float the Islay Scotch by pouring it slowly over the back of a bar spoon so it rests on the surface — do not stir it in.
Garnish with a piece of candied ginger on a pick and serve.
recipe.garnish: Candied ginger on a cocktail pick

name: Pisco Sour
description: Grape brandy, lime, and sugar under a snowdrift of egg-white foam dotted with bitters. The subject of a genial but eternal custody dispute between Peru and Chile.
funFact: Credited to American expat bartender Victor Morris in 1920s Lima, it is honored in Peru with a national Pisco Sour Day on the first Saturday of February.

steps: Add the pisco, lime juice, simple syrup, and egg white to a shaker WITHOUT ice and dry-shake hard for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Open the shaker, fill it with ice, and shake again for 12-15 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled old fashioned glass, holding back the ice so the foam settles into a smooth white cap.
Let the foam set for a few seconds, then dot 3 drops of Angostura bitters on top.
Optionally drag a toothpick through the drops to marble them, and serve straight away.
recipe.garnish: 3 drops of Angostura bitters dotted (or swirled) on the egg-white foam

name: Sidecar
description: Cognac, orange liqueur, and lemon balanced on a sugared rim — the sour family in evening wear. A relic of 1920s Paris that never went out of style.
funFact: It is supposedly named for an army captain who was chauffeured to his Paris bar of choice in a motorcycle sidecar.

steps: If using the classic sugar rim, rub a lemon wedge around the outer rim of a chilled coupe and roll the edge in superfine sugar; let it dry while you mix.
Add the cognac, Cointreau, and lemon juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds, until the tin frosts over.
Double-strain into the chilled, sugar-rimmed coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface, drop it in or rest it on the rim, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist, with an optional sugared rim

name: Ward 8
description: A rye sour rounded with orange and grenadine — Boston machine politics rendered in liquid form, right down to the premature victory lap.
funFact: Legend says it was mixed at Boston's Locke-Ober in 1898 to toast Martin Lomasney's election win in the Eighth Ward — the night before the votes were actually counted.

steps: Chill a cocktail glass in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the rye, lemon juice, orange juice, and grenadine to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 12-15 seconds.
Double-strain into the chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with an orange slice and cherry flag on a pick and serve.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and maraschino cherry on a pick (a 'flag')

name: Whiskey Sour
description: The archetype of the sour family: whiskey, lemon, and sugar in perfect three-point balance, optionally cushioned with a cloud of egg-white foam.
funFact: Its best-known variations earned names of their own: shaken with egg white it is often called a Boston Sour, and a float of dry red wine on top turns it into a New York Sour.

ingredients.item: Egg white (optional, for a silky foam)

ingredients.amount: 1 shaker full, plus fresh cubes for the glass

steps: If using egg white, add all ingredients to a shaker WITHOUT ice and dry-shake hard for 15 seconds to build the foam; otherwise skip to step 2.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for 12-15 seconds, until well chilled.
Strain over fresh ice into a rocks glass (or serve it up in a chilled coupe if you prefer).
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry; if you used egg white, a few dashes of Angostura on the foam look and taste great.
Serve immediately, while the foam is still tall.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and maraschino cherry; Angostura dashes on the foam if made with egg white

name: Aperol Spritz
description: A sunset-orange aperitivo of Aperol, prosecco, and soda built for golden-hour piazzas. Bitterness with training wheels, in the best possible way.
funFact: The spritz traces back to 19th-century Austrian soldiers stationed in the Veneto, who asked for local wine 'gespritzt' — splashed — with water to tame it.

ingredients.amount: Enough large cubes to fill a wine glass

steps: Fill a large wine glass generously with ice — more ice keeps it colder and less watery.
Pour in the chilled prosecco first (this keeps the Aperol from sinking into a syrupy layer).
Add the Aperol, then top with a splash of soda water.
Give one gentle stir with a bar spoon to marry the layers without killing the bubbles.
Slide in the orange half-wheel and serve with a straw or spoon-side stir.

name: Bellini
description: White peach puree lifted by prosecco into a pale-pink Venetian daydream. Insists on white peaches; yellow ones are considered a diplomatic incident.
funFact: Giuseppe Cipriani of Harry's Bar named it in 1948 because its pink glow reminded him of robes in paintings by the Renaissance master Giovanni Bellini.

steps: Make the puree: blend ripe peeled white peaches until smooth (a teaspoon of lemon juice keeps the color bright) and chill thoroughly — no ice goes in this drink, so everything must be cold.
Pour the white peach puree into a chilled champagne flute.
Slowly add the prosecco in stages, pausing as the foam rises.
Stir gently once with a bar spoon, lifting from the bottom, to blend the puree evenly.
Serve immediately, ungarnished, while the fizz is lively.
recipe.garnish: None traditional; a thin white peach slice on the rim if you like

name: Champagne Cocktail
description: A bitters-soaked sugar cube dissolving at the bottom of a flute of champagne, releasing a slow ribbon of spiced bubbles. Victorian glamour, still operational.
funFact: It appears in Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide and later earned Hollywood immortality — Victor Laszlo pointedly orders champagne cocktails in 'Casablanca.'

steps: Chill a champagne flute and open a well-chilled bottle of champagne.
Set the sugar cube on a napkin and saturate it with 3-4 dashes of Angostura bitters.
Drop the soaked cube into the bottom of the flute.
Slowly top with champagne — pour gently down the side, as the cube makes it foam aggressively.
Express the lemon twist over the surface, drop it in, and serve while the cube is still streaming bubbles.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist, expressed and dropped in

name: Death in the Afternoon
description: Absinthe clouding into iced champagne like slow opaline weather. Named after a book about bullfighting by the man who invented it, which explains a lot.
funFact: Ernest Hemingway contributed the recipe to a 1935 celebrity cocktail book with the instruction to 'drink three to five of these slowly.'

steps: Chill a champagne flute in the freezer and make sure the champagne is thoroughly iced — the louche depends on cold.
Pour the absinthe into the chilled flute.
Slowly top with champagne, pouring down the side of the glass, and watch the drink cloud into its milky opalescence.
Stop when it reaches, in Hemingway's words, the proper opalescent milkiness — about 4 oz of champagne.
Serve ungarnished, and pace yourself; this one is far stronger than it looks.
recipe.garnish: None — the opalescent louche is the show

name: French 75
description: Gin and lemon given a champagne afterburner. Elegant enough for a wedding, potent enough to be named after artillery.
funFact: It is named after the French 75mm field gun of World War I, whose recoil the drink's kick was said to resemble; Harry's New York Bar in Paris popularized it.

steps: Chill a champagne flute in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds and double-strain into the chilled flute.
Slowly top with champagne, pouring down the side so it does not foam over.
Garnish with a long lemon twist draped into the glass and serve immediately.

name: Mimosa
description: Champagne diluted with orange juice, or orange juice elevated by champagne, depending on your brunch philosophy. Named for a flower it happens to match in color.
funFact: It appeared at the Paris Ritz around 1925, four years after London's nearly identical Buck's Fizz — the main difference being that the Fizz pours more champagne.

ingredients.item: Champagne (or dry sparkling wine, well chilled)

steps: Chill both the champagne and the orange juice thoroughly — the drink takes no ice, so cold ingredients are everything.
Strain the fresh orange juice to remove heavy pulp for a cleaner texture (optional but nicer).
Pour the champagne into a chilled flute first, tilting the glass to preserve the bubbles.
Slowly add an equal measure of orange juice — pouring juice into wine keeps it from foaming over.
Give one very gentle stir and serve immediately; add an orange twist on the rim if you want a garnish.
recipe.garnish: Optional orange twist or small orange wedge on the rim

name: Negroni Sbagliato
description: A Negroni in which the gin was 'mistakenly' replaced with prosecco — a happy accident promoted to permanent menu status.
funFact: Sbagliato means 'mistaken' — Bar Basso's Mirko Stocchetto grabbed sparkling wine instead of gin mid-Negroni in 1972, and a viral 2022 interview clip made his error a worldwide order.

ingredients.amount: Enough cubes (or one large cube) to fill a rocks glass

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice — one large clear cube is ideal.
Pour the Campari and sweet vermouth over the ice.
Stir briefly with a bar spoon to chill and combine.
Top with chilled prosecco and give one gentle lift with the spoon to integrate without flattening the fizz.
Garnish with the orange half-wheel and serve.
recipe.garnish: Orange half-wheel (or an expressed orange twist)

name: Seelbach
description: Bourbon, Cointreau, a startling fourteen dashes of bitters, and champagne — a drink whose flavor is genuine even if its history was not.
funFact: Its celebrated 'lost 1917 recipe' was a hoax: in 2016 its true creator admitted he invented the drink at the Seelbach Hotel in 1995 and fabricated the vintage backstory.

steps: Chill a champagne flute in the freezer for at least 10 minutes.
Add the bourbon, Cointreau, and all fourteen dashes of bitters directly to the flute — the dash count sounds absurd, but it is the point of the drink.
Swirl or stir briefly with a bar spoon to combine the base.
Slowly top with chilled champagne, pouring down the side of the glass.
Express the orange twist over the surface, drop it in, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist, expressed and dropped in

name: Black Russian
description: The White Russian's darker, leaner elder: just vodka and coffee liqueur over ice. Two ingredients, zero small talk.
funFact: Bartender Gustave Tops created it at Brussels' Hotel Metropole in 1949 for Perle Mesta, the United States ambassador to Luxembourg.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice cubes (or one large cube) and let it chill for a moment.
Pour the vodka directly over the ice.
Add the coffee liqueur.
Stir gently with a barspoon for about 10 seconds to combine and lightly dilute.
Serve immediately in the rocks glass.

name: Boulevardier
description: A Negroni that traded gin for bourbon and moved somewhere with worse weather. Richer, rounder, and built for autumn.
funFact: It appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 book and is credited to Erskine Gwynne, an American expat who edited a Paris magazine called The Boulevardier.

ingredients.amount: For mixing, plus one large cube to serve

steps: Fill a mixing glass two-thirds full with ice.
Add the bourbon, Campari, and sweet vermouth.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until well chilled and slightly diluted.
Strain over a large ice cube in a chilled rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Hanky Panky
description: Gin and sweet vermouth given a dark herbal jolt of Fernet-Branca. Proof that a few drops of the right bitter can rename an entire drink.
funFact: Ada 'Coley' Coleman, the Savoy's legendary head bartender, mixed it for actor Charles Hawtrey, who sipped it and declared, 'By Jove! That is the real hanky-panky!'

steps: Chill a coupe in the freezer or with ice water while you mix.
Add the gin, sweet vermouth, and Fernet-Branca to a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until thoroughly chilled.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Express the oils from an orange twist over the drink and drop it in.

name: Manhattan
description: Rye and sweet vermouth in stately equilibrium, seasoned with aromatic bitters. The borough it is named for reinvents itself constantly; the drink refuses.
funFact: The famous tale that it debuted at a banquet hosted by Winston Churchill's mother is almost certainly false — she was in England, pregnant with Winston, at the time.

steps: Chill a cocktail glass in the freezer while you mix.
Add the rye, sweet vermouth, and Angostura bitters to a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until well chilled and silky.
Strain into the chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry dropped into the glass.

name: Martinez
description: Old Tom gin and sweet vermouth kissed with maraschino and bitters — the plush Victorian ancestor from which the Martini was ruthlessly streamlined.
funFact: Often called the missing link between the Manhattan and the Martini, it first appeared in print in 1884, and the town of Martinez, California claims it with a commemorative plaque.

steps: Chill a coupe before you begin.
Combine the Old Tom gin, sweet vermouth, maraschino liqueur, and bitters in a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until cold and lightly diluted.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Martini
description: An austere, glacial aperitif of gin and dry vermouth that rewards precision and punishes hesitation. Its ideal ratio has been argued about for over a century without resolution.
funFact: The Martini grew steadily drier through the 20th century — Winston Churchill reputedly said the only vermouth required was a glance at the bottle across the room.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer — the colder the better.
Add the gin and dry vermouth to a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir briskly for about 30 seconds until glacially cold.
Strain into the chilled martini glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist expressed over the surface, or 1-3 olives on a pick — never both.

name: Negroni
description: Equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth: bitter, scarlet, and entirely sure of itself. A slow sipper that gradually trains the palate to crave it.
funFact: Legend holds that in 1919 Count Camillo Negroni asked a Florence bartender to stiffen his usual Americano by swapping the soda water for gin.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice — one large cube melts slowest.
Pour in the gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth in equal measure.
Stir gently in the glass for 15-20 seconds until chilled.
Garnish with an orange slice (or an expressed orange twist) and serve.

name: Old Fashioned
description: The fossil record of American drinking: spirit, sugar, and bitters arranged much as they were two centuries ago. It has survived every fad by simply refusing to evolve.
funFact: In 2015 Louisville, Kentucky declared the Old Fashioned its official cocktail and now celebrates it every June with 'Old Fashioned Fortnight.'

ingredients.amount: 1 cube or 1 tsp (or 0.25 oz / 7.5 ml simple syrup)
1 tsp (if using cube or granulated sugar)

steps: Place the sugar in a rocks glass, saturate it with the bitters and a teaspoon of water, and muddle until dissolved (skip muddling if using simple syrup).
Add the whiskey and stir briefly to combine.
Add one large ice cube.
Stir for 15-20 seconds until chilled and lightly diluted.
Express an orange twist over the surface, rub it around the rim, and drop it in.

name: Sazerac
description: Rye, sugar, and Peychaud's bitters swirled in an absinthe-rinsed glass, served without ice and without hurry. New Orleans in liquid form.
funFact: In 2008 the Louisiana legislature proclaimed the Sazerac the official cocktail of New Orleans — one of very few drinks with a statutory hometown.

ingredients.amount: 1 cube or 1 tsp (or 0.25 oz / 7.5 ml simple syrup)
1 barspoon (~5 ml), to rinse the glass
For mixing only — served without ice

steps: Chill a rocks glass, then rinse it: pour in the absinthe, swirl to coat the inside, and discard the excess.
In a mixing glass, muddle the sugar with the Peychaud's bitters and a small splash of water until dissolved (or just add simple syrup).
Add the rye and fill the mixing glass two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed glass — no ice in the serving glass.
Express the lemon peel over the surface; traditionally it is discarded, but you may perch it on the rim.

name: Vesper
description: Gin and vodka sharing one glass with a measure of aromatized wine — a Martini with dual citizenship, invented on the page rather than behind a bar.
funFact: Ian Fleming invented it in 'Casino Royale' (1953), where Bond names it after Vesper Lynd; the original Kina Lillet was reformulated away in 1986, so a period-accurate Vesper is now impossible.

steps: Chill a martini glass in the freezer.
Add the gin, vodka, and Lillet Blanc to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake very well for 10-12 seconds until ice-cold — Fleming's spec calls for shaken, not stirred.
Double strain into the chilled martini glass.
Garnish with a large, thin strip of lemon peel expressed over the drink.

name: Vieux Carré
description: Rye, cognac, sweet vermouth, and Bénédictine with two kinds of bitters — a drink as layered as the French Quarter it is named for.
funFact: Walter Bergeron created it in the 1930s at what is now the Hotel Monteleone, whose Carousel Bar still slowly rotates its drinkers one full turn every fifteen minutes.

ingredients.amount: For mixing, plus one large cube to serve

steps: Add the rye, cognac, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine, and both bitters to a mixing glass filled two-thirds with ice.
Stir for 25-30 seconds until well chilled.
Strain over a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in (a brandied cherry also works).

name: Hugo Spritz
description: The Aperol Spritz's alpine cousin, pale green and smelling of elderflower meadows. Mint leaves drift through the bubbles like leaves on a mountain stream.
funFact: Bartender Roland Gruber invented it in South Tyrol in 2005 using lemon balm syrup — elderflower took over later — and says he picked the name Hugo almost at random.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice cubes.
Slap the mint leaves between your palms to release their aroma and add them to the glass.
Pour in the elderflower syrup or liqueur.
Add the chilled prosecco, then top with a splash of soda water.
Stir once or twice very gently to combine without killing the bubbles, and add a lime wheel if you like.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and a lime wheel

name: Kir Royale
description: Champagne blushing violet with a whisper of blackcurrant. An aperitif that dresses for the occasion even when there isn't one.
funFact: It is named for Félix Kir, the wine-loving priest, Resistance figure, and mayor of Dijon who served the still-wine version at civic receptions to promote local cassis.

ingredients.amount: Top with ~4 oz / 120 ml, well chilled

steps: Chill a champagne flute and make sure the Champagne is thoroughly cold — no ice goes in this drink.
Pour the crème de cassis into the bottom of the flute.
Slowly top with Champagne, tilting the glass slightly to preserve the mousse.
Serve without stirring — the cassis will rise and blend on its own.
recipe.garnish: None traditional; optionally a fresh blackcurrant or a lemon twist

name: Bahama Mama
description: A sunset-colored double-rum lounger that never wears a watch. Coconut and grenadine blur together like the last hour of a beach day.
funFact: Bahamian bartender Oswald "Slade" Greenslade claimed he invented it at the Nassau Beach Hotel in 1961, naming it after a calypso-era song.

ingredients.amount: For shaking, plus fresh cubes to serve

steps: Add the dark rum, coconut rum, pineapple juice, and orange juice to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until frothy and cold.
Strain into a hurricane glass filled with fresh ice.
Slowly pour the grenadine down the inside of the glass so it sinks and creates a sunset gradient.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry, add a straw, and serve.

name: Blue Hawaii
description: Swimming-pool blue and garnished like a parade float. Curaçao dyes a rum-and-pineapple sour the exact color of a Waikiki postcard.
funFact: Hilton Hawaiian Village bartender Harry Yee invented it in 1957 when a Bols sales rep challenged him to build a drink around blue curaçao — four years before the Elvis film.

ingredients.amount: For shaking, plus fresh cubes to serve

steps: Add the light rum, vodka, blue curaçao, pineapple juice, and sweet-and-sour to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until well chilled and lightly frothy.
Strain into a hurricane glass filled with fresh ice.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cocktail umbrella — Harry Yee's original flourish — and serve with a straw.

name: Fog Cutter
description: A long tiki haymaker that throws rum, gin, AND brandy behind orgeat and citrus, with a sherry float as the parting shot. Visibility drops fast.
funFact: Trader Vic wrote of his own creation: 'Fog Cutter, hell. After two of these, you won't even see the stuff.'

steps: Add the light rum, gin, brandy, lemon juice, orange juice, and orgeat to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a tall fog cutter mug or highball glass filled with fresh crushed or cubed ice.
Gently pour the amontillado sherry over the back of a bar spoon so it floats on top.
Garnish and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and an orange slice

name: Jungle Bird
description: The rare tiki species with a bitter streak. Campari's red plumage flashes through dark rum and pineapple, giving this bird its unmistakable call.
funFact: It was created in the 1970s as a welcome drink at the Kuala Lumpur Hilton's Aviary Bar, where it was originally served in a ceramic bird-shaped vessel.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker and fill with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds — the pineapple juice should get nicely frothy.
Strain into a double rocks glass over fresh ice (one large cube looks great).
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and pineapple fronds.

name: Navy Grog
description: A three-rum broadside rigged with honey and grapefruit, famously sipped through a cone of shaved ice. Built for sailors; adopted by presidents.
funFact: Richard Nixon was reportedly a devotee of the Navy Grog at the Trader Vic's in Washington, D.C.

ingredients.item: Honey syrup (1:1 honey and warm water)

steps: Add all three rums, the lime juice, grapefruit juice, and honey syrup to a shaker.
Add about 1 cup of crushed ice and shake hard for 8-10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a double rocks glass and top with more crushed ice.
For the classic Don the Beachcomber look, pack an ice cone around a straw (freeze snow-cone ice packed in a pilsner glass) and set it in the drink.
Garnish and serve immediately.
recipe.garnish: Traditional ice cone with a straw, or a lime wheel and mint sprig

name: Rum Runner
description: A Florida Keys fruit smuggle of banana, blackberry, and rum. Sweet enough to hide its cargo until well past the checkpoint.
funFact: Lore at the Holiday Isle Tiki Bar says it was invented to burn through overstocked liqueurs before inventory, and named for Prohibition-era smugglers.

steps: Add the light rum, banana liqueur, blackberry liqueur, and grenadine to a shaker with ice.
Shake for 10 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a hurricane or tall tiki glass packed with crushed ice.
Float the dark rum on top by pouring it slowly over the back of a bar spoon.
Garnish and serve with a straw. (For a frozen version, blend everything with 1.5 cups of ice instead.)
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a maraschino cherry

name: Saturn
description: The gin-powered outlier of the tiki solar system. Passion fruit and almond orbit a juniper core, ringed appropriately with a lemon spiral.
funFact: Filipino-American bartender J. "Popo" Galsini rode the Saturn to victory at the 1967 IBA World Cocktail Championship — a rare gin drink in a rum-dominated genre.

steps: Add the gin, passion fruit syrup, lemon juice, orgeat, and falernum to a blender.
Add about 1 cup of crushed ice and flash blend for just 3-5 seconds (or shake hard with crushed ice if you have no blender).
Pour unstrained into a chilled coupe or small tiki bowl, topping with a little extra crushed ice if needed.
Coil a long lemon peel ribbon around the drink like Saturn's ring, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Long lemon peel ribbon coiled into a ring (add a cherry 'moon' if you like)

name: Scorpion Bowl
description: A communal volcano of rum, brandy, and orgeat meant for a table of allies. Long straws converge; individual dignity does not survive contact.
funFact: Trader Vic adapted it from a potent punch he encountered in Honolulu, and the classic garnish is a floating gardenia.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with plenty of ice (this is a single serving — multiply by 4 for a true communal scorpion bowl).
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until well chilled and slightly frothy.
Strain into a scorpion bowl or large double rocks glass filled with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish, add long straws, and serve. For a party bowl, scale up, shake in batches, and serve over a mound of crushed ice.
recipe.garnish: Edible flower (gardenia is traditional) or an orange slice and mint sprig

name: Suffering Bastard
description: A wartime hangover cure that mixes gin and brandy under a ginger-beer flag of truce. Gruff name, surprisingly gentle bedside manner.
funFact: Joe Scialom invented it at Cairo's Shepheard's Hotel in 1942, and gallons were reportedly sent to the front to fortify troops at El Alamein.

steps: Add the gin, brandy, lime juice, and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake for 8-10 seconds until chilled.
Strain into a double rocks glass or tiki mug filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold ginger beer and give it one gentle stir to combine.
Garnish with a mint sprig and orange slice, and serve.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and an orange slice

name: Three Dots and a Dash
description: A wartime victory toast in liquid Morse code. Honey, allspice, and aged rum signal triumph, garnished with three cherries and a pineapple dash.
funFact: Don the Beachcomber named it during World War II for the Morse code spelling of "V" — dot dot dot dash — for victory.

ingredients.item: Aged rum blend (e.g. 1.5 oz aged rhum agricole + 0.5 oz demerara rum)
Honey syrup (1:1 honey and warm water)

steps: Add the rum blend, lime juice, orange juice, honey syrup, falernum, allspice dram, and bitters to a shaker.
Add about 1 cup of crushed ice and shake hard for 8-10 seconds (or flash blend for 5 seconds).
Pour unstrained into a tall tiki glass or pilsner glass and top with more crushed ice.
Skewer three cherries and a pineapple chunk on a pick — the 'three dots and a dash' (Morse code for V, victory).
Lay the pick across the rim and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Three maraschino cherries and a pineapple chunk on a pick (Morse code for 'V')

name: Hurricane
description: A crimson double-barrel of rum and passion fruit served in its namesake lamp-shaped glass. New Orleans' preferred method of losing an afternoon.
funFact: Pat O'Brien invented it in 1940s New Orleans to burn through surplus rum — distributors then forced bars to buy cases of it to obtain scarce whiskey — and named it for the hurricane-lamp glass.

steps: Add both rums, the passion fruit syrup, orange juice, lime juice, and grenadine to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a hurricane glass filled with fresh crushed or cubed ice.
Garnish with an orange slice and cherry, and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a maraschino cherry

name: Mai Tai
description: Aged rum, lime, orange curaçao, and almond-rich orgeat — tiki's crown jewel, endlessly imitated and routinely butchered with pineapple juice.
funFact: When Trader Vic served the first one to Tahitian friends in 1944, one reportedly exclaimed 'Maita'i roa a'e!' — roughly 'out of this world, the best' — naming the drink on the spot.

steps: Squeeze the lime and keep one spent half-shell for the garnish.
Add the rum, lime juice, curaçao, and orgeat to a shaker with about 1 cup of crushed ice.
Shake hard for 8-10 seconds.
Pour everything, ice and all, into a double rocks glass and top with more crushed ice.
Nestle the spent lime shell on top like a little island, tuck a mint sprig beside it, and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Spent lime shell and a fresh mint sprig

name: Painkiller
description: Dark rum, pineapple, orange, and coconut cream under a blizzard of fresh nutmeg. Prescription strength varies from two to four ounces of rum.
origin: Jost Van Dyke, British Virgin Islands
funFact: It was born at the Soggy Dollar Bar, which has no dock — patrons swim ashore and pay with wet bills — and Pusser's later trademarked the name for its own rum.

steps: Add the rum, pineapple juice, orange juice, and cream of coconut to a shaker with ice.
Shake very hard for 12-15 seconds — cream of coconut is thick and needs the extra work to fully blend.
Strain into a hurricane glass or large tumbler filled with crushed ice.
Grate fresh nutmeg generously over the top.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a pineapple wedge

name: Piña Colada
description: Rum, coconut cream, and pineapple blended into a beach vacation with an umbrella in it. Subtlety was never the assignment.
funFact: Credited to bartender Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero at San Juan's Caribe Hilton in 1954, it has been the official national drink of Puerto Rico since 1978.

steps: Add the rum, cream of coconut, and pineapple juice to a blender.
Add about 1.5 cups of ice and blend until smooth and slushy, 20-30 seconds.
Pour into a chilled hurricane glass or poco grande.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and cherry, and serve with a straw. (No blender? Shake hard with ice and strain over crushed ice instead.)
recipe.garnish: Pineapple wedge and a maraschino cherry

name: Sex on the Beach
description: Vodka, peach schnapps, orange, and cranberry — the 1980s distilled into a highball. Orders itself best when shouted over loud music.
funFact: For all its spring-break reputation, it holds an official place on the International Bartenders Association cocktail list.

steps: Fill a highball glass with fresh cubed ice.
Pour in the vodka and peach schnapps.
Add the orange juice, then the cranberry juice.
Stir gently with a bar spoon to combine — a little layering of color is part of the charm.
Garnish and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a maraschino cherry

name: Singapore Sling
description: A rosy gin sling elaborated with cherry liqueur, pineapple, and herbs until it became a national landmark. The recipe varies; the legend does not.
funFact: Ngiam Tong Boon created it around 1915 at the Raffles Hotel's Long Bar, where tossing peanut shells straight onto the floor is still encouraged.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker and fill with ice.
Shake hard for 10-12 seconds — the pineapple juice should build a nice foamy head.
Strain into a tall sling or highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Garnish with a pineapple slice and cherry, and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Pineapple slice and a maraschino cherry

name: Zombie
description: Three rums, citrus, falernum, and spice engineered into tiki's apex predator. Tastes like fruit punch, behaves like heavy machinery.
funFact: Its creator Donn Beach guarded the 1934 recipe with coded, unlabeled bottles his bartenders mixed blind, and he capped customers at two Zombies apiece.

steps: Add all three rums, the lime juice, falernum, grapefruit juice, cinnamon syrup, grenadine, absinthe, and bitters to a blender.
Add about 1 cup of crushed ice and flash blend for just 5 seconds (or shake hard with crushed ice).
Pour unstrained into a tall zombie glass or tiki mug and pack with more crushed ice.
Garnish with a big mint sprig and serve with a straw.
Respect Don the Beachcomber's house rule: this is a strong one — limit two per person.

name: Bacanora
description: Sonora's clandestine agave spirit, distilled from wild agave in mountain hideouts through nearly eight decades of prohibition. Smoky, mineral, and still carrying the swagger of the outlaw years.
funFact: Bacanora was outlawed in Sonora from 1915 until 1992, so generations of families kept the tradition alive with hidden stills in the sierra.

serve.how: Pour an ounce or two into a veladora and let it sit for a minute or two so the alcohol vapors lift off before you nose it. Sip neat in small draws, rolling the spirit across your tongue to catch the mineral edge and desert-herb notes beneath the light smoke. Skip ice entirely; dilution flattens the wild-agave character that makes bacanora worth hunting down.

composition.summary: Distilled from Sonoran agave, mostly the wild-harvested Agave angustifolia known locally as pacífico.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave angustifolia ('pacífico'), much of it still gathered wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, then run through small copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Almost always bottled unaged and clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–48% ABV

composition.process: Roasting the agave hearts in earth-and-stone pits is what lays down that mountain smoke.

name: Mezcal Añejo
description: Mezcal aged at least a year in oak, where smoke, caramel, and leather negotiate a rich truce. A rarity, since most mezcaleros prefer their spirit young and untamed.
funFact: Unlike tequila's single permitted species, mezcal may legally be produced from dozens of different agave varieties.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve neat in a snifter and give it one gentle swirl, then let it rest so the barrel notes open up. Nose it with your mouth slightly open to soften the smoke, and look for where the caramel and leather meet the char on the finish. If it runs hot, a single large cube tames the heat without erasing the oak.

composition.summary: Pit-roasted agave, pot-distilled, then left in oak for at least a year.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Espadín or other permitted agave species, pit-roasted

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills, usually twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum one year in oak, per the mezcal standard

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–46% ABV

composition.process: A full year in wood is the negotiation that lets caramel and leather meet the smoke.

name: Mezcal de Pechuga
description: Ceremonial mezcal given a final distillation with seasonal fruits, spices, and a raw poultry breast suspended in the still. Brewed for weddings and saints' days, encountered by mortals almost never.
funFact: 'Pechuga' means 'breast' — traditionally a whole chicken or turkey breast hangs inside the still during the final pass, subtly rounding the spirit.

serve.how: Treat this like the ceremonial spirit it is: pour a small measure into a veladora, no ice, no mixing, and share it slowly with people you like. Take tiny sips and hunt for the stone fruit and holiday spice riding under the smoke, with that faint savory roundness from the pechuga itself on the finish. Let the glass sit between sips; it keeps evolving as it breathes.
pair: roast turkey or chicken with mole

composition.summary: Mezcal given a final still run with seasonal fruit, spices, and raw poultry breast.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pit-roasted agave, plus fruit, nuts, spices and raw poultry

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: An extra pass with the breast suspended inside the still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged — bottled straight after the pechuga run

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–55% ABV

composition.process: That third distillation over hanging poultry strips harshness and rounds the spirit into ceremony.

name: Mezcal Joven
description: Unaged mezcal, where agave hearts roasted in earthen pits deliver their famous campfire smoke and wild fruit. Oaxaca's rawest, truest voice.
funFact: Mezcal's signature smokiness comes from roasting agave hearts for days in stone-lined pits dug into the earth.

serve.how: Pour a modest measure into a wide, shallow veladora and let it breathe for a minute before nosing. Kiss it rather than gulp it: small sips held on the palate reveal tropical fruit and wet-stone minerality behind the campfire smoke. Traditional accompaniments are orange slices dusted with sal de gusano, not lime and shot glasses.
pair: orange slices with sal de gusano

composition.summary: Unaged mezcal from agave hearts roasted in earthen pits and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave hearts, most often cultivated espadín

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper or clay pot stills, typically twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None — bottled clear and straight off the still

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–52% ABV

composition.process: Days of roasting in stone-lined earth pits is the single step that makes mezcal smoky.

name: Mezcal Reposado
description: Mezcal rested briefly in wood, letting vanilla and honey settle over the smoke like dusk over a cookfire. A gentler on-ramp to the smoky arts.
funFact: Around nine in every ten bottles of mezcal are made from a single cultivated agave, espadín, prized for its relatively quick maturation.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Sip it neat from a veladora to catch the honey and vanilla the barrel has draped over the smoke, taking your time between small pours. This is the friendliest on-ramp to mezcal, so if the smoke still reads strong, a single large cube softens it into something almost dessert-like. Notice how the roasted agave core stays intact under the oak polish.

composition.summary: Pit-roasted agave mezcal rested a few months in wood before bottling.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pit-roasted agave, usually espadín

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper or clay pot stills, generally twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak from two months up to a year

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: A short rest in wood lays vanilla and honey over the smoke without burying it.

name: Mezcal Tobalá
description: Mezcal from the small, wild tobalá agave that hides in high mountain canyons and yields only a fraction of what farmed espadín gives. Often crowned 'the king of mezcals.'
funFact: Tobalá agave produces no clones or offshoots — it reproduces only by seed in the wild, which is a big reason it stays scarce and expensive.

serve.how: Pour sparingly, this is scarce juice, and let the glass sit for several minutes; tobala's floral perfume needs air to bloom. Sip in small, slow draws and chase the wild fruit and wet-stone notes that float above the gentle smoke. No ice, no citrus, no mixing: at this rarity you are tasting a plant that took a decade to grow in a mountain canyon.

composition.summary: Mezcal from wild tobalá agave, a small canyon-dwelling species that yields very little.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wild Agave potatorum, harvested from high mountain canyons

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, then twice through small copper or clay stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, so the wild agave stays the loudest voice

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–50% ABV

composition.process: It takes several times more tobalá hearts than espadín to fill a bottle.

name: Raicilla
description: West Jalisco's backwoods agave spirit, long distilled off the books in the sierra and along the coast — funky, fruity, and less smoky than its Oaxacan cousins. Mezcal's mischievous mountain kin.
funFact: Raicilla — 'little root' — reputedly got its name as a colonial-era tax dodge, and it finally received its own denomination of origin in 2019.

serve.how: Serve neat at room temperature in a veladora and nose it first: raicilla leads with ripe fruit and wild funk rather than smoke, so expect something closer to a natural wine's aromatics. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate, watching for the green agave brightness underneath the fermented-fruit character. Keep it away from ice and mixers until you have met it on its own terms.
pair: tropical fruit with chile and lime

composition.summary: Western Jalisco agave spirit from mountain and coastal species, cooked without heavy smoke.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Local Jalisco agaves such as maximiliana and inaequidens

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or filipino-style stills, often clay or wood-fired

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged, bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: Many producers cook the agave in above-ground ovens, which is why it reads fruity, not smoky.

name: Sotol
description: The spirit of the Chihuahuan Desert, distilled from the wild desert spoon plant into something grassy, mineral, and quietly feral. Tastes like the high desert after rain.
funFact: Despite being shelved with agave spirits, sotol is not made from agave at all — the desert spoon is a different plant that can take around 15 years to mature.

serve.how: Pour a small measure neat and give it a minute of air, then nose gently: sotol smells like the high desert after rain, all grass, pine, and mineral. Sip slowly and let it sit on the mid-palate, where the earthy, vegetal side unfolds; it is drier and greener than mezcal, so do not go looking for sweetness. Room temperature keeps those delicate herbal notes alive.

composition.summary: Distilled from the wild desert spoon plant, not agave at all.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wild Dasylirion — desert spoon — harvested across the Chihuahuan Desert

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Roasted, crushed, then run through small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Most is unaged; some producers rest it briefly in oak

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–48% ABV

composition.process: The plants are gathered wild from desert hillsides, so the spirit changes with the terrain.

name: Tequila Añejo
description: Tequila aged one to three years, trading youthful bite for caramel, chocolate, and dried fruit. Proof that agave can play in whiskey's league.
funFact: By law, añejo must age in oak barrels no larger than 600 liters, which keeps the wood's influence concentrated.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Treat anejo like a fine whiskey: pour into a snifter, swirl once, and let it rest a few minutes before nosing for caramel, chocolate, and cooked agave. Sip neat and slow, noting how the oak frames the agave rather than burying it. A single large cube is fine on a warm night, but skip crushed ice and mixers, this earned its barrel time.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila aged one to three years in oak barrels.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, steam-cooked in ovens or autoclaves

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled at least twice, usually in copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: One to three years in oak casks no larger than 600 litres

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–40% ABV

composition.process: Small barrels concentrate wood contact, pushing agave toward caramel and chocolate.

name: Tequila Blanco
description: Tequila in its purest form, bottled fresh from the still so the roasted blue agave speaks without oak interrupting. Peppery, vegetal, and vividly alive.
funFact: A blue Weber agave typically grows for six to eight years before a jimador harvests its heart, called the piña for its resemblance to a pineapple.

serve.how: Pour a couple of ounces into a caballito and sip, do not shoot; blanco is the purest expression of roasted blue agave and rewards patience. Take small sips and look for white pepper, citrus, and green herbs riding over the sweet agave core. A slight chill crisps it up in summer, but avoid heavy icing, which mutes the vegetal brightness.

composition.summary: Unaged tequila distilled purely from cooked blue Weber agave.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave piñas, steam-cooked until sweet

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice through copper pot or column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None, or a brief rest in steel — bottled clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–46% ABV

composition.process: Skipping the barrel entirely leaves the cooked agave with nothing to hide behind.

name: Tequila Cristalino
description: Aged tequila filtered through charcoal until it runs crystal clear, keeping barrel softness while shedding barrel color. Alchemy for drinkers who want their añejo invisible.
funFact: The cristalino craze is usually traced to Don Julio 70, launched in 2011 as the first widely marketed clear añejo.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve in a rocks glass either neat or over one large, slow-melting cube; cristalino is built for smooth, easy sipping. Notice the trick of it: the vanilla and soft caramel of an aged tequila with none of the color, and a finish that snaps clean like a blanco. It also makes a luxurious base for an ultra-clear Margarita or Paloma if you tire of sipping.

composition.summary: Aged tequila filtered through charcoal until the barrel colour is stripped out.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, cooked and fermented as usual

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled twice, then aged before the filtration step

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Reposado, añejo or extra añejo stock, later stripped clear

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 35–40% ABV

composition.process: Activated-charcoal filtration pulls the colour out while leaving much of the barrel sweetness behind.

name: Tequila Extra Añejo
description: Ultra-aged tequila that slumbers in oak for at least three years, emerging dark, plush, and cognac-like. The category tequila invented once it started wearing suits.
funFact: Extra añejo is the newest official tequila classification, created only in 2006 as producers pushed into luxury territory.

serve.how: Pour a small measure into a snifter, cup the bowl in your palm to warm it slightly, and give it several minutes to open. Sip in tiny draws the way you would a cognac, tracking the dark caramel, dried fruit, and polished oak through a long finish. No ice and no mixing; at three-plus years in barrel, dilution only steals what you paid for.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila aged a minimum of three years in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, steam-cooked and fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: At least two passes, typically copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak barrels up to 600 litres

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually bottled at 40% ABV

composition.process: Years of oak push agave into cognac territory — dark, plush, and slow.

name: Tequila Joven
description: The 'young' or gold style, usually a blanco softened with a splash of aged tequila or a touch of color and sweetness. The tequila of a million spring-break stories.
funFact: Most inexpensive 'gold' tequila gets its color from added caramel coloring rather than from time spent in a barrel.

serve.how: Joven is the party style, so chill it down and serve in caballitos, ideally with sangrita or citrus on the side rather than the salt-and-lime slam. If sipping, look for the caramel sweetness layered over young agave and mild pepper. It is also happiest in a Margarita or tequila sunrise, where its softened edges are a feature, not a flaw.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila, usually blanco blended with aged tequila or colouring.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, cooked and fermented like any tequila

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Standard double distillation in pot or column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly unaged — colour often comes from additives, not barrels

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–40% ABV

composition.process: Blending or colouring a blanco gives the look of barrel time without the barrel.

name: Tequila Reposado
description: Tequila 'rested' in oak for two months to a year, just long enough to drape vanilla and soft spice over the agave without smothering it. The diplomatic middle ground.
funFact: Reposado literally means 'rested,' and much of the resting happens in used American bourbon barrels shipped south across the border.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour into a rocks glass neat or over a single large cube and give it a short rest; reposado's vanilla and baking spice bloom with a little air. Sip and notice the balance point, enough oak to round the edges, enough agave to remember where it came from. It is also the sweet spot for an elevated Margarita or Old Fashioned riff.

composition.summary: Blue Weber agave tequila rested in oak from two months to a year.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Blue Weber agave, steam-cooked and fermented

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Twice distilled in copper pot or column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Two to twelve months, frequently in used American whiskey barrels

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 38–40% ABV

composition.process: Just enough time in wood to drape vanilla over the agave without smothering it.

name: Aperol
description: Campari's sunnier, gentler sibling, glowing neon orange and only lightly bitter. In spritz form it has colonized patios across the entire planet.
funFact: Aperol was created in 1919 by brothers Luigi and Silvio Barbieri of Padua and carries roughly half the alcohol of its rival Campari.

serve.temp: well chilled (38-45°F), served over plenty of ice
serve.how: Keep the bottle in the fridge and build the classic Spritz in a big wine glass: fill with ice, pour 3 parts chilled prosecco, 2 parts Aperol, 1 part soda, and garnish with an orange slice. Stir once, gently, so the Aperol does not sink and sulk at the bottom. Sip it slowly outdoors before dinner; the gentle rhubarb-orange bitterness is designed to wake up your appetite, not test it.

composition.summary: A low-proof Italian bitter aperitif built on neutral spirit and botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, water and sugar carrying an orange-led infusion

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Not distilled as such — botanicals are infused, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; bottled bright and fresh

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 11% ABV, roughly half its scarlet rival

composition.process: Bitter and sweet orange, rhubarb and gentian are infused and sweetened into that neon glow.

name: Campari
description: The scarlet gatekeeper of the aperitivo hour, bitter as a grudge and bright as a sunset. It tests new trainers with grapefruit-pith bitterness before rewarding them for life.
funFact: Campari's famous red color came from carmine dye made from cochineal insects until the company switched to artificial coloring in 2006.

serve.how: Serve over a large cube with a fat orange peel, or lengthen with soda in a highball for the classic Campari e soda. Sip slowly and let your palate acclimate: the first taste is a grapefruit-pith wallop, but by the third sip the herbs and cherry underneath start rewarding you. Keep it as a pre-dinner ritual, its bitterness is engineered to sharpen the appetite.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit infused with bitter herbs and fruit peel, sweetened and bottled red.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, water and sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: An infusion, not a distillate — herbs and peels steep in spirit

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Varies by market, roughly 20.5–28.5% ABV

composition.process: A secret herb-and-peel infusion delivers that grapefruit-pith bitterness the whole aperitivo hour rests on.

name: Cynar
description: An amaro that proudly wears an artichoke on its label, yet tastes of caramelized herbs rather than vegetables. A gentle, vegetal riddle beloved in low-proof cocktails.
funFact: Launched in 1952, Cynar takes its name from Cynara scolymus, the artichoke, one of thirteen herbs and plants in its recipe.

serve.how: Pour over a big cube with an orange twist, or top with soda water and a pinch of salt for the Italian classic. Sip slowly and notice the riddle: cola and caramelized-herb sweetness up front, a gentle vegetal bitterness on the back, and no actual artichoke flavor anywhere. Its low proof makes it a perfect unhurried afternoon or after-dinner drink.

composition.summary: An Italian bitter liqueur infused with thirteen herbs and plants, artichoke included.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit infused with artichoke and twelve other botanicals

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Made by maceration and blending rather than redistillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Artichoke leaf does the bittering work, but caramel sweetness keeps it from tasting like a vegetable.

name: Fernet-Branca
description: A menthol-black Italian amaro of legendary intensity, brewed from 27 secret herbs. Feared by novices, worshipped by bartenders, and consumed by Argentina in heroic quantities.
funFact: Argentina drinks well over 70% of all Fernet-Branca produced, mostly mixed with cola in the beloved fernet con coca.

serve.glass: Shot glass or small chilled rocks glass
serve.how: Pour a small measure neat as a digestif after a heavy meal; the menthol-and-bitter-herb blast is the point, so take it in confident sips rather than nervous ones. A light chill softens the eucalyptus edge for newcomers, but true believers drink it room temperature. For the Argentine experience, pour an ounce or two over ice and top generously with cola for a fernet con coca.

composition.summary: A ferociously bitter Milanese amaro built from twenty-seven herbs and spices.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape spirit infused with twenty-seven herbs, roots and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals are macerated and infused, then blended to recipe

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak casks before bottling

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 39% ABV

composition.process: Myrrh, saffron and menthol-heavy botanicals are steeped until the result tastes like medicine that won.

name: American Single Malt
description: One hundred percent malted barley from a single American distillery — Scotland's blueprint rebuilt with New World swagger. The newest official branch of the whiskey family tree.
funFact: American single malt only became an officially recognized U.S. whiskey category when the TTB finalized its rule in December 2024.

serve.how: Pour a standard dram into a Glencairn, swirl gently, and nose in short sniffs with your mouth slightly open to catch malt, chocolate, and orchard fruit. Sip neat first, then add a few drops of water to unlock the toasted-oak depths; many American single malts run above 43% and open beautifully. Compare it mentally to Scotch, the malt DNA is the same but the New World oak speaks louder.

composition.summary: One hundred percent malted barley, distilled and matured at a single American distillery.

components.label: Base
components.detail: All malted barley, no other grain permitted

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled at one US distillery, pot stills most common

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak casks up to 700 litres; new charred oak not required

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 43–50% ABV

composition.process: Scotland's all-malt blueprint, but with American oak, climate and no regional rulebook.

name: Bottled-in-Bond Bourbon
description: Whiskey with a government-stamped pedigree: one distillery, one distilling season, at least four years in a bonded warehouse, and exactly 100 proof. No fudging allowed.
funFact: The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 was one of America's earliest consumer-protection laws, arriving nine years before the Pure Food and Drug Act.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat into a Glencairn and let the 100-proof pour sit a couple of minutes before nosing for toffee, leather, and baking spice. Sip slowly; bonded bourbon is built to a standard, not a price, so the extra proof carries flavor rather than just heat. A few drops of water or one large cube will unwrap the oak if the finish runs hot.

composition.summary: Bourbon from one distillery and one season, aged four years, bottled at 100 proof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 51% corn, like any bourbon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: One distillery, one distilling season, no blending across either

components.label: Aging
components.detail: At least four years in a federally bonded warehouse

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Exactly 50% ABV — 100 proof, no negotiation

composition.process: The 1897 Bond Act ties provenance, age and proof to a government stamp.

name: Bourbon
description: America's signature whiskey, born of a corn-heavy mash and new charred oak. Sweet, sturdy, and sociable — it appears anywhere Americans gather to argue about whiskey.
funFact: In 1964 the U.S. Congress declared bourbon a distinctive product of the United States, though it can legally be made in any state, not just Kentucky.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers into a rocks glass and try it neat first, nosing for caramel, vanilla, and charred oak before the first sip. Let each sip rest on the tongue a beat so the corn sweetness spreads before the oak spice arrives. One large cube slowly opens it up on a warm evening, and if you would rather go long, bourbon and ginger ale is a forgiving classic.

composition.summary: American whiskey from a mash of at least 51% corn, aged in new charred oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Minimum 51% corn, rounded out with rye, wheat or malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still and doubler, distilled to no more than 160 proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak containers; 'straight' bourbon needs two years

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: Fresh charred oak, used exactly once, is what gives bourbon its caramel and vanilla.

name: Cask Strength Bourbon
description: Bourbon bottled straight from the barrel with no dilution — whiskey with the volume knob snapped off. Approach with water, patience, or bravado.
funFact: Bourbon may legally enter the barrel at no more than 125 proof, but years of evaporation in hot rickhouses can push some barrel-proof releases above 70% ABV.

serve.temp: room temp, with water on standby
serve.how: Pour a smaller-than-usual measure into a Glencairn and approach in stages: nose gently from a distance first, since 60%-plus alcohol will singe an eager nostril. Take a tiny first sip to calibrate, then add water a few drops at a time, tasting between additions until the burnt sugar and dark cherry bloom out of the heat. Finding each barrel's ideal dilution point is the whole sport.

composition.summary: Corn-based bourbon bottled straight from the barrel with no water added.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 51% corn, standard bourbon mash

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled and barrelled conventionally, at no more than 125 proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak, often in the hottest warehouse floors

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Commonly 55–70% ABV, wherever the barrel lands

composition.process: Skipping the proofing water means the barrel, not the blender, sets the strength.

name: Flavored Whiskey
description: Whiskey infused with cinnamon, honey, apple, or peach, engineered to go down like dessert. Purists scowl; sales figures do not.
funFact: Flavored whiskeys are often bottled below the 40% ABV minimum required of straight whiskey, which is why the flavor designation must appear on the label.

serve.how: Keep it in the fridge or freezer and serve as a chilled shot, where the cinnamon-candy or honeyed sweetness plays best. Over ice in a rocks glass it drinks like a low-effort dessert; topped with lemonade, apple cider, or ginger beer it becomes an easy porch highball. Do not overthink it, this category is engineered for fun, not contemplation.

composition.summary: American whiskey sweetened and infused with cinnamon, honey, apple or peach.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Whiskey, usually bourbon, plus flavourings and sweetener

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled as whiskey, then flavoured after the fact

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Base whiskey sees oak; the flavouring is added afterward

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Often 30–35% ABV, below the straight-whiskey minimum

composition.process: Post-barrel flavouring and sugar do the heavy lifting, which is why the label must say so.

name: High-Rye Bourbon
description: Still legally bourbon, but with the rye content cranked toward the ceiling for extra snap and spice. The bridge species between bourbon and rye whiskey.
funFact: One of Four Roses' two mash bills contains 35% rye — among the highest rye content of any major bourbon on the market.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat into a rocks glass and taste for the tug-of-war that defines the style: bourbon's caramel sweetness up front, then a cinnamon-and-pepper rye snap on the back half. A single large cube softens the spice without erasing it. This is also the ideal Old Fashioned bourbon, since the rye kick stands up to sugar and bitters.

composition.summary: Bourbon whose corn mash carries an unusually large share of rye.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Still majority corn, with rye pushed toward the ceiling

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still and doubler, same as any Kentucky bourbon

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak, as bourbon law requires

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: Loading the mash with rye adds pepper and snap while corn keeps it legally bourbon.

name: Moonshine
description: Unaged white whiskey with an outlaw pedigree, once run through the hollows in mason jars ahead of the revenuers. Today's legal versions keep the jar and skip the felony.
funFact: The name comes from distilling illegally by the light of the moon to avoid detection by tax collectors.

serve.how: Serve it cold, straight from the freezer if you like, in the traditional mason jar; the chill tames the raw ethanol edge and lets the sweet corn flavor through. Sip in small pulls rather than gulps, and taste for the popcorn-like graininess that barrel aging would normally polish away. It also mixes cheerfully with lemonade, sweet tea, or apple cider for a backporch punch.

composition.summary: Unaged corn whiskey, historically distilled off the books in Appalachia.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Corn mash, sometimes stretched with plain sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot or thumper stills, run fast and clear

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None — that was always the point

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–60% ABV, historically much wilder

composition.process: Bottling straight off the still skips the barrel, the time and, once upon a time, the tax.

name: Rye Whiskey
description: Bourbon's spicier, drier sibling, distilled from a mash of at least 51% rye grain. It bites first and charms second, which is exactly why bartenders adore it.
funFact: Before Prohibition, rye — not bourbon — was the dominant American whiskey, with Pennsylvania's Monongahela Valley as its most famous producing region.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers neat and take a small first sip: rye bites first with black pepper and baking spice, then charms with mint and dried fruit as your palate adjusts. A large cube rounds the edges if the spice runs sharp. And if you make one cocktail with it, make a Manhattan, rye is what the drink was born with.

composition.summary: American whiskey from a mash of at least 51% rye grain.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Minimum 51% rye, balanced with corn and malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled to no more than 160 proof, column or pot

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak; 'straight' rye requires two years

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: Rye's own peppery, herbal grain character survives the barrel — that's the whole appeal.

name: Single Barrel Bourbon
description: Every bottle drawn from one lone barrel, so no two barrels taste quite alike. Catching a great one is half the sport.
funFact: Blanton's, created in 1984 by master distiller Elmer T. Lee, is widely credited as the first modern bourbon marketed as a single-barrel bottling.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat into a Glencairn and taste attentively, because this exact flavor exists only in this one barrel's run: note the dark caramel, cherry, and oak, and jot down the barrel number if the label carries one. Add a few drops of water on higher-proof picks to spread the fruit out. Comparing two different barrels of the same label side by side is one of bourbon's great home games.

composition.summary: Corn-based bourbon bottled from one individual barrel rather than a blend.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 51% corn, standard bourbon mash bill

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled conventionally; the selection happens later

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak, then one cask chosen and bottled alone

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Ranges widely, roughly 45–65% ABV

composition.process: No vatting means every barrel's own warehouse position and quirks land in the glass.

name: Small Batch Bourbon
description: A curated blend of a modest number of barrels, aiming for a house flavor with a handcrafted halo. The batch is small; the marketing rarely is.
funFact: The term 'small batch' has no legal definition in the United States — a batch can be any number of barrels the producer decides to call small.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour into a rocks glass neat or over one big cube; small batch is blended for balance, so it rarely needs taming. Nose for vanilla and toasted nuts, then sip for the caramel mid-palate and gentle oak-spice finish that the blender worked to make consistent. It is the reliable house pour: great neat, great in an Old Fashioned, never a wasted dram.

composition.summary: Bourbon blended from a limited, hand-picked selection of barrels.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 51% corn, as bourbon law demands

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled conventionally at a single distillery

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak, then a modest number of casks married

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 43–52% ABV

composition.process: Marrying a handful of chosen barrels builds a house style — but nobody defines 'small'.

name: Straight Corn Whiskey
description: Made from at least 80% corn and aged only in used or uncharred oak, keeping the grain's sweet, popcorn-like soul front and center. A living fossil of early American distilling.
funFact: Corn whiskey is the only major American whiskey style that is forbidden from using new charred oak barrels — the very thing that defines bourbon.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat and taste it as a history lesson: with no new charred oak allowed, the sweet corn and popcorn notes stay front and center the way early American whiskey would have tasted. Sip slowly and notice the honeyed softness and only a whisper of wood on the finish. A single cube is fine, but heavy dilution washes out its delicate grain character.

composition.summary: American whiskey from at least 80% corn, aged only in used or uncharred oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Minimum 80% corn in the mash

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled to no more than 160 proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Used or uncharred new oak only; 'straight' means two years

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–50% ABV

composition.process: Banning new charred oak keeps the wood quiet and the sweet corn out front.

name: Tennessee Whiskey
description: Essentially a bourbon that takes a detour through sugar-maple charcoal before barreling, emerging mellower for the trip. Tennessee guards this ritual jealously.
funFact: A 2013 Tennessee state law requires whiskey labeled 'Tennessee whiskey' to use the charcoal-mellowing Lincoln County Process, with a grandfathered exception for one small distillery.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers into a rocks glass and sip neat first, looking for the signature banana-and-caramel softness the charcoal mellowing leaves behind. One large cube stretches it into an easy evening drink, and it famously partners with cola in a tall glass when the mood is casual. Notice how the finish is gentler than a comparable bourbon; that is the Lincoln County Process at work.

composition.summary: Corn-based whiskey filtered through sugar-maple charcoal before it ever meets a barrel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 51% corn, meeting the bourbon standard

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column distilled, then dripped through sugar-maple charcoal

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak barrels, matured in Tennessee

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–45% ABV

composition.process: The Lincoln County Process — charcoal mellowing before barrelling — is what state law actually requires.

name: Wheat Whiskey
description: Not a wheated bourbon but a true wheat-majority whiskey, soft and bready with a gentle sweetness. A quiet rarity in a category built on corn.
funFact: Wheat whiskey must contain at least 51% wheat in the mash, making it a legally distinct category from wheated bourbon, which remains majority corn.

serve.how: Pour a generous ounce and a half into a Glencairn and let it sit for a minute or two so the alcohol vapors settle. Nose it gently with your mouth slightly open, then take a small sip and let it coat your tongue before swallowing. Look for the soft fresh-bread and honey sweetness that sets wheat whiskey apart from spicier rye-heavy pours; a few drops of water will open it up if the 45-50% proof reads hot.

composition.summary: American whiskey from a mash of at least 51% wheat.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Minimum 51% wheat, usually with malted barley and corn

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled to no more than 160 proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak, like its corn and rye cousins

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–50% ABV

composition.process: Making wheat the majority grain — not a supporting one — is what separates it from wheated bourbon.

name: Wheated Bourbon
description: A bourbon that swaps rye for wheat as its flavoring grain, trading spice for a soft, bakery-sweet roundness. Gentle in youth, glorious in old age.
funFact: The cult favorite Pappy Van Winkle is a wheated bourbon, and its scarcity helped turn the whole 'wheater' style into a collector obsession.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Serve neat in a Glencairn to appreciate the bakery-sweet softness, or over a single large cube in a rocks glass if you like it rounder and slightly chilled. Swirl once, nose in short sniffs, and sip slowly, noticing how the wheat trades rye's pepper for bread-dough and red-fruit roundness. Higher-proof bottles reward a teaspoon of water, which unlocks extra honey and vanilla.

composition.summary: Bourbon that uses wheat instead of rye as its secondary flavouring grain.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Majority corn, with wheat replacing rye in the mash

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled to no more than 160 proof, then barrelled

components.label: Aging
components.detail: New charred oak; rewards long maturation more than most

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 45–54% ABV

composition.process: Swapping rye for wheat trades spice for a soft, bakery-sweet roundness.

name: Absinthe
description: The infamous Green Fairy: a potent wormwood-and-anise spirit that louches to opalescent cloud with water. Long blamed for madness it never actually caused.
funFact: Absinthe was banned in the United States from 1912 until 2007; modern science showed its supposed hallucinogenic powers were a myth all along.

serve.how: Pour one ounce into an absinthe glass, rest a slotted spoon with a sugar cube across the rim, and slowly drip 3-5 parts ice-cold water over the cube. Watch the louche bloom into an opalescent cloud — that slow reveal is half the ritual. Sip leisurely and notice how dilution transforms fierce wormwood and anise into layered alpine herbs; skip the flaming-sugar theatrics, which scorch the botanicals.

composition.summary: A high-proof spirit distilled with grande wormwood, green anise and fennel.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral or grape spirit macerated with the holy trinity of botanicals

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled, then often coloured by steeping fresh herbs

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged; traditionally rested in glass or steel

components.label: Strength
components.detail: A wide 45–74% ABV

composition.process: Anethole from the anise falls out of solution with water, which is the louche.

name: Arak
description: The Levant's grape-and-anise spirit, triple-distilled and diluted at the table until it swirls milky white. It presides over mezze spreads like a benevolent elder.
funFact: The name arak comes from the Arabic word for 'sweat' or 'perspiration,' a nod to the drops of condensed spirit dripping from the still.

serve.temp: 38-45°F, well chilled with water and ice
serve.how: Mix roughly one part arak with two parts cool water in a small tumbler, then add ice — always in that order, since ice added first can crystallize the anise oils into a film. Watch it swirl milky white, the classic louche of the Levant. Sip it alongside food rather than alone, letting small sips reset your palate between bites of mezze; notice the grape sweetness underneath the licorice.

composition.summary: A Levantine grape spirit redistilled with aniseed until it clouds with water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fermented grapes, typically local varieties like obeideh

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled repeatedly, aniseed added on the final pass

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Traditionally rested in porous clay amphorae

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–53% ABV

composition.process: Adding aniseed only to the last distillation keeps the perfume clean rather than heavy.

name: Ouzo
description: Greece's crystal-clear anise spirit that turns ghostly white with water or ice. It appears wherever grilled octopus, sea breezes, and long afternoons are found.
funFact: Under EU law, ouzo can only be produced in Greece and Cyprus, making it a protected badge of Greek identity.

serve.how: Pour two fingers into a small tumbler and add cold water or an ice cube to taste, watching it cloud ghostly white as the anise oils louche.
