components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often minimal; tropical maturation is fast

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 42.8%

composition.process: India taxes and defines whisky domestically, which is why molasses-based spirit can carry the name there.

name: Coconut Feni
description: The other Goan feni, distilled from coconut palm toddy rather than cashew apples. Older than the cashew version, since cashews only arrived with the Portuguese, and now much the rarer of the two.
funFact: Toddy tappers climb the palms twice daily and are a vanishing profession in Goa, which is the main reason coconut feni is disappearing.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or with lime soda, which is the standard Goan serve. It is funkier and more savoury than cashew feni, and it takes acid well.

composition.summary: Coconut palm sap fermented and pot-distilled in stages.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Toddy tapped from coconut palm flower stalks

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional pot distillation, typically three runs

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; some rest in earthenware

composition.process: The sap ferments within hours of tapping, so distillation happens the same day.

name: Mahua
description: Distilled from the flowers of the mahua tree, which fall in spring and are gathered by Adivasi communities across central India. Long dismissed as country liquor, it was reclassified as heritage liquor in 2021.
funFact: Mahua flowers are also eaten and used as a sweetener, and the tree is treated as sacred in several Adivasi traditions.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass. The flavour is floral and strange, closer to a fortified honey than to anything grain-based. The new commercial bottlings are considerably cleaner than the village versions.

composition.summary: Dried mahua flowers fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Flowers of Madhuca longifolia, gathered as they fall

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional clay or pot stills; modern producers use copper

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The flowers are naturally high in sugar and need no addition to ferment.

name: Indian Rum
description: Dark, sweet and heavily molasses-driven, of which Old Monk is the icon: a vatted seven-year rum that built a cult following without ever advertising. India drinks an enormous amount of it.
funFact: Old Monk was famously never advertised, relying entirely on word of mouth, and for decades it was among the best-selling dark rums in the world.

serve.how: Neat, over ice, or with cola. Indian winters call for it hot with water and honey. It is sweet and vanilla-forward, so it does not need much help.

composition.summary: Sugarcane molasses fermented, distilled and aged in the Indian climate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Indian sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, tropically matured; Old Monk is vatted at seven years

composition.process: India grows more sugarcane than almost anywhere, so molasses has always been the obvious base.

name: Tharra
description: Sugarcane moonshine from the northern Indian plains, distilled from fermented cane juice or jaggery in village stills. Illegal, widespread, and the subject of periodic poisoning tragedies when batches are adulterated.
funFact: Mass poisonings from methanol-adulterated country liquor remain a recurring public health emergency across northern India.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and only from a source you trust absolutely. This is one of the entries on this list where the safety caveat is not a formality.

composition.summary: Cane juice or jaggery fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane juice or jaggery

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Village pot stills, single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: Adulteration with industrial methanol to boost strength is the cause of most tharra fatalities.

name: Indian Gin
description: A genuinely new category: gins built on Indian botanicals — Goan coriander, Himalayan juniper, gondhoraj lime, black pepper from Kerala. India had no craft gin at all before 2017 and now exports it.
funFact: India grows a large share of the world's spices, so the botanical supply chain that most gin producers import from was already domestic.

serve.how: With a light tonic and a wedge of lime or a few crushed pink peppercorns. The spice-forward botanicals are strong enough that a heavily flavoured tonic will bury them.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with Indian and Himalayan botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Himalayan juniper, gondhoraj lime, coriander, pepper, fennel, cardamom

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour infusion

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Sourcing juniper from the Himalayas rather than Europe is what several producers use to define the category.

name: Ceylon Arrack
description: Sri Lanka's national spirit, distilled from the fermented sap of coconut flowers and rested in halmilla wood. Light, faintly funky and closer to a soft rum than to anything else, and quite unlike Batavia arrack.
funFact: Toddy tappers move between palm crowns on ropes strung fifteen metres above the ground rather than climbing down between trees.

serve.how: With ginger beer and lime, which is the Sri Lankan standard, or over ice with soda. The premium aged bottlings are worth drinking neat, where the halmilla wood shows as a soft spice.

composition.summary: Coconut flower sap fermented and distilled, then aged in halmilla casks.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Toddy from coconut palm flower stalks

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Halmilla wood vats, six months to fifteen years

composition.process: The sap must be distilled within a day of tapping, since it ferments almost immediately in the heat.

name: Kasippu
description: Sri Lanka's illicit moonshine, distilled from sugar, cane or fermented fruit in the countryside, and by some estimates outselling every licensed spirit on the island combined.
funFact: Estimates of unlicensed alcohol in Sri Lanka regularly put it at over half of all consumption, most of it kasippu.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, from a source you know. It is produced entirely outside regulation and is frequently adulterated, which makes it a genuine risk rather than a novelty.

composition.summary: Sugar, cane or fruit fermented and distilled in hidden stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugar, cane juice or fermented fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised stills, usually single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–60%, unmeasured

composition.process: Production is deliberately mobile, since the stills have to be moved to avoid enforcement.

name: Raksi
description: Nepali millet or rice spirit, distilled at home in stacked clay or metal pots and served warm in the hills. Cloudy, sour and warming, and offered at every festival and family occasion.
funFact: The traditional still is a stack of pots with a cold-water bowl on top, and the condensate is caught in a vessel suspended inside.

serve.how: Served warm, often with a piece of fried egg or meat floated on top at festivals. Strength varies wildly between households, so the first cup is a reasonable guide to pacing.

composition.summary: Millet or rice fermented with a starter cake and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Millet, rice or maize

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Marcha, a wild-yeast starter cake

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Stacked pot still over an open fire

composition.process: Marcha carries both the yeast and the moulds that convert the grain's starch to sugar.

name: Aila
description: The Newar community's rice spirit, distilled in Kathmandu valley courtyards and central to Newari feasts. Traditionally poured from a clay jug into a leaf cup, and drunk as part of ritual as much as celebration.
funFact: At certain Newari festivals aila is poured directly into the mouth from a clay jug held above the head, without touching the lips.

serve.how: Room temperature or gently warmed, as part of a Newari feast rather than on its own. The first distillate, called thaha, is the strongest and is kept for elders and guests.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a yeast starter and distilled in traditional stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice, sometimes with millet

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Manapu, a Newari yeast starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Stacked clay or copper pot still

composition.process: Successive fractions are collected separately, and the first is prized well above the rest.

name: Ara
description: Bhutan's home-distilled spirit, made from rice, maize, millet or wheat and served hot with butter and a scrambled egg dropped in. That version, called hoentay ara, is a genuine winter staple.
funFact: Commercial production and sale is restricted in Bhutan, so nearly all ara is made at home for family and guests.

serve.how: Heated with butter and a beaten egg stirred through, which sounds alarming and is genuinely good at altitude in winter. Also drunk cold and plain, though far less often.

composition.summary: Grain fermented with a local starter and distilled at home.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice, maize, millet or wheat

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Phab, a Bhutanese yeast starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Simple pot still over a stove

composition.process: Butter and egg are added at serving rather than in production, and the fat carries the warmth.

name: Murree
description: Pakistan's only legal distillery, founded in 1860 to supply the British garrison and still operating in an Islamic republic where most citizens cannot legally buy its products.
funFact: Murree cannot export easily and cannot sell to Muslim Pakistanis, so it operates in one of the strangest commercial positions of any distillery on earth.

serve.how: Neat or with a splash of water. The older single malts are genuinely accomplished and comparable to mid-range Scotch, which surprises almost everyone who tries one.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in Pakistan.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, some locally grown

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and sherry oak, eight to twenty-one years

composition.process: The brewery and distillery survived partition, prohibition and nationalisation by continuing to operate under licence.

name: Bangla Mod
description: Bangladesh's licensed country liquor, distilled from molasses or rice and sold through a small number of permitted outlets. Cheap, strong, and a rare legal product in a country with very tight alcohol laws.
funFact: Bangladesh requires a permit to buy alcohol legally, and country liquor shops operate under a licensing system inherited from colonial administration.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures. It is a functional spirit rather than a refined one, and the licensed version is considerably safer than the unlicensed alternatives circulating alongside it.

composition.summary: Molasses or rice fermented and distilled under licence.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses or rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: The licensed trade exists partly to displace the far more dangerous informal one.

name: Uzbek Konyak
description: Central Asian brandy made in the Soviet style from grapes grown in the Ferghana valley and around Samarkand. Sweeter and softer than French brandy, and a legacy of Soviet-era winemaking on the Silk Road.
funFact: The Soviet Union built a substantial brandy industry across Central Asia and the Caucasus, and konyak remains the standard local word for it.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, usually with a meal rather than after it, as is the custom across the former Soviet republics. Frequently accompanied by more toasts than is strictly advisable.

composition.summary: Uzbek wine distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grapes from the Ferghana valley and Samarkand region

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, three to twenty years

composition.process: Hot continental summers give very ripe grapes, which is why the resulting brandy runs sweet.

name: Sauce-Aroma Baijiu
description: The jiangxiang style, from Guizhou, and the most expensive baijiu made. Fermented and distilled seven times over a year, it tastes of soy sauce, mushroom and dried meat rather than anything a Western palate calls a spirit.
funFact: The production cycle runs a full year with nine steamings, eight fermentations and seven distillations, and the spirit is then aged for at least three more.

serve.how: Room temperature in a very small cup, with food, and shared. Chinese banquet custom is to toast rather than sip. The umami depth needs food alongside it; drunk alone it can be overwhelming.

composition.summary: Sorghum solid-state fermented with wheat qu in stone pits, distilled seven times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Red sorghum and wheat qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Seven distillations across a year-long cycle

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware jars, then blended

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 53%

composition.process: 53% is considered the point where water and ethanol molecules bind most tightly, and the style is bottled there deliberately.

name: Strong-Aroma Baijiu
description: The nongxiang style from Sichuan, fermented in mud pits that have been in continuous use for centuries and are treated as the distillery's most valuable asset. Pungent, fruity and enormously popular.
funFact: Luzhou Laojiao's oldest fermentation pits date from 1573 and have been running without interruption since, with the microbial culture in the mud considered irreplaceable.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with food. The fruit-and-funk profile is intense on its own but cuts through rich, oily Sichuan food remarkably well. Toast rather than sip.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in aged mud pits, distilled and blended.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, often with rice, wheat, corn and glutinous rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation in steamer stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The older the mud pit, the more complex the microbial population, and the higher the value of the spirit.

name: Light-Aroma Baijiu
description: The qingxiang style from Shanxi, fermented in stone jars rather than earth pits, which keeps it clean and floral. The most approachable baijiu for anyone new to the category, and the historical ancestor of Korean soju.
funFact: Fenjiu from Xinghua village is documented as far back as the Northern and Southern dynasties, making it one of the oldest named spirits in China.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food, or lightly chilled if it is your first baijiu. Its cleaner profile also makes it the style most usable in cocktails, where it behaves a little like a funky gin.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in stone jars with barley and pea qu.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, with a barley and pea qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, two fermentations

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware, typically shorter than other styles

composition.process: Stone jars keep the ferment isolated from soil microbes, which is why the style stays clean.

name: Rice-Aroma Baijiu
description: The mixiang style from Guangxi and southern China, distilled from rice rather than sorghum. The lightest and most delicate of the four classic aromas, and the closest baijiu gets to a soft, sweet spirit.
funFact: Sanhua jiu from Guilin is the best-known example and is traditionally aged in caves cut into the karst hills around the city.

serve.how: Room temperature or lightly chilled, in small cups. It is gentle enough to drink without food, which is unusual for baijiu, and it works well alongside lighter southern Chinese cooking.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a small qu starter and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice, sometimes glutinous

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Semi-solid-state fermentation, then distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars, sometimes in karst caves

composition.process: A smaller qu starter than the northern styles means less funk and more of the rice.

name: Erguotou
description: Beijing's everyday baijiu, cheap, clean and sold in a small green bottle that costs less than a bowl of noodles. The name means second pot head, referring to the middle fraction of the distillation that goes into it.
glassware: Small cup or straight from the bottle
funFact: The little green bottle of Red Star erguotou is such a Beijing fixture that it has become a design shorthand for the city itself.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with street food. It is a working drink and treated as one; nobody in Beijing contemplates their erguotou. It also mixes surprisingly well with sour or citrus flavours.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented and distilled, with only the middle cut kept.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation, middle fraction only

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimal

composition.process: Discarding the head and tail of the run is exactly what the name describes, and why it is cleaner than its price suggests.

name: Mei Kuei Lu Chiew
description: Baijiu infused with rose petals and rock sugar, used at least as often in Chinese kitchens as in glasses. It flavours char siu and roast meats, and quietly does the work in a great many restaurant dishes.
funFact: It is a standard ingredient in Cantonese roast meat marinades, where the rose note is barely detectable in the finished dish but its absence is.

serve.how: Neat in a small cup, though most bottles go into cooking. In the glass it is intensely floral and strong; a very small measure is enough. It also makes an interesting cocktail modifier.

composition.summary: Sorghum baijiu infused with rose petals and rock sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Light-aroma sorghum baijiu

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dried rose petals and rock sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused after distillation

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Around 54%

composition.process: The high strength is what makes it useful in cooking, since it carries flavour into fat and burns off cleanly.

name: Yaojiu
description: Chinese medicinal liquor, made by steeping herbs, roots, ginseng, deer antler or whole snakes in baijiu. Prescribed rather than ordered, and drunk in small measures for specific complaints.
funFact: Snake wine, in which a whole venomous snake is submerged in spirit, relies on the alcohol denaturing the venom, which it does.

serve.how: A small measure, taken deliberately rather than socially. Traditional Chinese medicine assigns different preparations to different conditions, and it is drunk in that spirit rather than for pleasure.

composition.summary: Baijiu steeped with medicinal herbs, roots or animal ingredients.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Baijiu, usually high strength

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ginseng, goji, deer antler, snake, wolfberry, dozens of herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, often for months or years

composition.process: High-strength spirit is used because it extracts compounds that water cannot.

name: Kaoliang
description: Sorghum spirit from Kinmen, a Taiwanese island a few kilometres off the Chinese mainland, distilled in tunnels dug during the artillery bombardments of the 1950s. Bottled at 58% and drunk with real ceremony.
funFact: The distillery was founded in 1952 to give the garrison something to make from local sorghum, and it became Kinmen's principal industry.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. At 58% it is not a sipping spirit; Taiwanese custom is to drain the cup on a toast and refill.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented with wheat qu and solid-state distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum grown on Kinmen

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Stored in granite tunnels cut into the island

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 38–63%, with 58% the signature

composition.process: The granite tunnels hold a stable cool temperature year-round, which is why they are still used.

name: Imo Shochu
description: Sweet potato shochu from Kagoshima, earthy and unmistakable, with a heavy aroma that divides opinion even within Japan. Single-distilled at low pressure to keep the character rather than strip it.
funFact: Kagoshima's volcanic soil is poor for rice but ideal for sweet potato, which is why the region distils rather than brews.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%, sometimes 20%

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

name: Mugi Shochu
description: Barley shochu, most of it from Oita, and the gentlest of the styles. Clean and lightly nutty, and the usual recommendation for anyone meeting shochu for the first time.
funFact: Iki island in Nagasaki holds a geographical indication for barley shochu and claims to have originated the style in the sixteenth century.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with cold water
serve.how: On the rocks, or mizuwari with cold water at about one to one. Barrel-aged versions drink comfortably neat and are often mistaken for a light whisky in a blind pour.

composition.summary: Barley fermented with barley koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barley

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Barley or rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, often under vacuum for a lighter result

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point and produces a markedly cleaner, fruitier spirit.

name: Kome Shochu
description: Rice shochu, the closest the category comes to sake in flavour, and concentrated in Kumamoto's Hitoyoshi basin where it holds a geographical indication. Soft, floral and quietly excellent.
funFact: Kuma shochu from the Hitoyoshi basin is one of only a handful of Japanese spirits with a protected geographical indication.

serve.temp: room temp, warm or on the rocks
serve.glass: Wine glass, or warmed in a choku
serve.how: Warmed gently in winter, on the rocks in summer, or neat at room temperature. Kuma shochu is traditionally pre-mixed with water and warmed in a ceramic flask overnight before serving.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Both the base and the koji are rice, which is why it sits so close to sake on the palate.

name: Kokuto Shochu
description: Brown sugar shochu, made only on the Amami islands between Kyushu and Okinawa, where a post-war tax arrangement granted the exclusive right to produce it. Nowhere else in Japan may legally make it.
funFact: Amami's exclusive right dates from the islands' return to Japan in 1953, when the arrangement was made to protect the local sugar economy.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with water
serve.how: On the rocks, or with cold water. Despite the base it is not sweet, since the sugar ferments out entirely. It sits somewhere between a light rum and a shochu, which is exactly what it is.

composition.summary: Brown sugar fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Amami kokuto, unrefined brown sugar

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji, which is legally required

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

composition.process: The rice koji requirement is what keeps it classified as shochu rather than as rum.

name: Japanese Gin
description: Gin built on Japanese botanicals — yuzu, sansho pepper, sencha, hinoki cypress, shiso — and distilled with the precision the country brings to everything else. A category that did not meaningfully exist before 2016.
funFact: Ki No Bi separates its botanicals into six groups and distils each separately before blending, which is closer to perfumery than to conventional gin-making.

serve.how: A Japanese-style highball with soda and a twist of yuzu or lemon, built in a tall glass with hard clear ice. Tonic works but is heavy-handed against sencha and sansho, which are easily lost.

composition.summary: Rice or grain spirit redistilled with Japanese botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice spirit or neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, yuzu, sansho, sencha, gyokuro, hinoki, shiso, ginger

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Often distilled in separate botanical groups, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: A rice spirit base is softer and slightly sweeter than grain, which suits the delicate botanicals.

name: Andong Soju
description: Traditional distilled soju from Andong, made from rice and nuruk at around 45%, and a completely different drink from the diluted green-bottle soju that dominates Korean sales. Designated an intangible cultural property.
funFact: Distilled soju arrived in Korea with the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century, and Andong was one of the garrison towns where the technique took root.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with nuruk and distilled in a traditional soju gori.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nuruk, a Korean wild-culture starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in an earthenware soju gori

composition.process: Nuruk carries a wilder mix of moulds and yeasts than Japanese koji, which gives a more rustic result.

name: Insamju
description: Korean ginseng liquor, with whole roots visible in the bottle, made by steeping ginseng in distilled soju. Taken as a tonic as much as a drink, and given as a gift at least as often as it is opened.
funFact: Korean red ginseng is graded and priced by shape as well as age, and roots resembling a human figure command a substantial premium.

serve.how: A small measure, room temperature, usually with a meal. Koreans treat it as restorative rather than recreational, and it appears at gatherings for older relatives more than young ones.

composition.summary: Distilled soju steeped with whole ginseng root.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Distilled soju

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Korean ginseng, often with jujube and honey

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for months

composition.process: Six-year-old red ginseng is the prized grade, and it keeps infusing in the bottle.

name: Korean Whisky
description: Korea released its first domestic single malt in 2023, matured through summers that swing far hotter and winters far colder than Scotland's. The extreme range pushes the spirit through wood at speed.
funFact: Ki One, from a distillery outside Namyangju, released Korea's first single malt after fewer than three years of maturation, which the climate made possible.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. These are young whiskies matured fast, so the wood arrives early and water helps separate it from the spirit. Cask-strength releases benefit most.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in Korea's continental climate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, largely imported

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and sherry casks, three years and up

composition.process: Summers above 35°C and winters below freezing drive the spirit in and out of the wood each year.

name: Arkhi
description: Mongolian spirit distilled from fermented mare's or cow's milk, made on the steppe in a wooden column set over the stove. Cloudy, sour and low in strength, and utterly unlike anything else distilled anywhere.
funFact: It is distilled from airag, fermented mare's milk, and the distilling apparatus sits directly on the family stove inside the ger.

serve.how: Served warm in a small bowl, offered with the right hand, and accepted with both. Refusing outright is impolite; touching it to your lips and returning it is not. Strength is low, so several rounds are normal.

composition.summary: Fermented milk distilled in a stovetop wooden column.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Airag, fermented mare's milk, or cow's milk

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Wooden column still set over the ger stove

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; drunk fresh

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 10–20%, redistilled versions higher

composition.process: Milk sugar is what ferments here rather than starch or fruit sugar, which is why nothing else tastes like it.

name: Arak Bali
description: Balinese spirit distilled from palm sap or rice, made in village compounds across the island and used in Hindu offerings as well as in glasses. Legalised for licensed production in 2020 after decades in the grey market.
funFact: Arak is poured on the ground as part of Balinese Hindu offerings before ceremonies, which is one reason prohibition was never realistic.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or as arak madu with honey and lime, which is the standard Balinese long drink. Buy licensed bottles; methanol adulteration in the informal trade has killed tourists and locals alike.

composition.summary: Palm sap or fermented rice distilled in village stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Coconut or palmyra palm sap, or fermented rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional pot and bamboo stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none

composition.process: The 2020 governor's regulation created a licensed category specifically to displace unsafe production.

name: Cap Tikus
description: Sulawesi's palm spirit, distilled from tapped sugar-palm sap in the Minahasa highlands. The name means rat brand, which the makers have never bothered to explain or improve upon.
funFact: Minahasan tappers climb the sugar palms twice a day, and the sap is boiled down to palm sugar when it is not being distilled.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, which is how it is drunk in Minahasa. Some licensed producers now bottle a cleaner version; the village product is much stronger and considerably rougher.

composition.summary: Sugar-palm sap fermented and distilled repeatedly.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap of the aren sugar palm

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Bamboo and pot stills, multiple runs for higher grades

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Grades are counted by how many times the spirit has been run through the still.

name: Ciu
description: Javanese cane moonshine, centred on Bekonang near Solo, where a whole village economy is built around small stills. Legal to produce as raw alcohol, ambiguous to sell as a drink, and widely drunk regardless.
funFact: Bekonang's distillers have operated for generations, officially producing industrial and medical alcohol while everyone understands where much of it ends up.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. Adulteration with methanol has caused repeated mass poisonings in Java, so this is a spirit where source is the only thing that matters.

composition.summary: Molasses or cane juice fermented and distilled in village stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses or juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small pot and column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: The same stills supply both drinking alcohol and legitimate industrial spirit, which blurs the regulation.

name: Sopi
description: The palm spirit of eastern Indonesia — Maluku, Flores, Timor — distilled from lontar or aren sap. The name comes from the Dutch zoopje, a small drink, and the tradition is centuries old.
funFact: In parts of Flores and Timor, sopi is required for customary ceremonies including marriage negotiations and dispute settlements.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, often from a bamboo cup, and always in company. It carries genuine ceremonial weight in eastern Indonesia and is offered before it is asked for.

composition.summary: Lontar or aren palm sap fermented and distilled over fire.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lontar or aren palm sap

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Bamboo or pot stills over wood fire

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Wood-firing the still is what gives eastern sopi its distinct smoke.

name: Lambanog
description: Filipino coconut spirit distilled from tuba, the fermented sap of the coconut flower, and traditionally bottled at around 80 proof. Quezon province makes most of it, and every fiesta there runs on it.
funFact: A single tapper may work dozens of palms a day, moving between crowns on bamboo poles rather than descending each tree.

serve.how: Neat in a shot glass, passed around a single glass in the traditional tagayan style where everyone drinks from the same one in turn. Flavoured versions with mango or bubblegum are popular and considerably sweeter.

composition.summary: Coconut flower sap fermented into tuba and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Tuba, fermented coconut palm sap

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, traditionally single, now often double

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–45%, traditionally higher

composition.process: Sap ferments within hours of tapping, so distilling has to follow the same day.

name: Ginebra San Miguel
description: The best-selling gin on the planet by volume, and almost all of it is drunk in the Philippines. Made since 1834, sweeter and lighter on juniper than a London Dry, and sold in the flat bottle known as a bilog.
funFact: It sells more cases a year than any other gin brand in the world, and has done for decades, largely on domestic consumption alone.

serve.glass: Shot glass, or highball for a gin pomelo
serve.how: Traditionally drunk in a tagayan circle from one shared glass, often with powdered juice mixed in — gin bulag. More conventionally, over ice with pomelo or calamansi soda.

composition.summary: Cane neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane neutral spirit, not grain

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper and a light botanical blend

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

composition.process: A cane base rather than grain is what gives it a rounder, slightly sweeter body than European gin.

name: Philippine Rum
description: Rum distilled from Philippine molasses and aged in the tropics, of which Tanduay is the giant: a distillery running since 1854 that regularly out-sells nearly every rum brand in the world.
funFact: Tanduay has repeatedly ranked as one of the largest rum producers globally by volume, which surprises most people outside Southeast Asia.

serve.how: Over ice with cola or calamansi soda. The aged expressions take a single cube neat and carry more oak than the price suggests, given how fast tropical maturation moves.

composition.summary: Sugarcane molasses fermented, column-distilled and tropically aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Philippine sugarcane molasses, largely from Negros

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak in tropical conditions, five to sixteen years

composition.process: Negros island supplies most of the country's cane and is known domestically as the sugar bowl.

name: Lao Khao
description: Thailand's white spirit, distilled from sticky rice or molasses and sold in every provincial shop in the country. Cheap, strong and the base for the herbal infusions found in roadside ya dong stalls.
funFact: The name simply means white spirit, and it has been a state-licensed product since Thailand brought distilling under government monopoly in the nineteenth century.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, or with soda and lime. Most of it ends up steeped with roots and herbs as ya dong, sold by the shot from glass jars at roadside stalls.

composition.summary: Sticky rice or molasses fermented with a starter and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sticky rice, sometimes molasses

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Look pang, a Thai yeast and mould starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

composition.process: Look pang works like Chinese qu, converting starch and fermenting in a single step.

name: Mekhong
description: Thailand's first domestically produced branded spirit, launched in 1941 from rice and molasses with a blend of herbs and spice. Marketed as Thai whisky for decades, it is closer to a spiced rum than to anything else.
funFact: It is the base of the Thai Sabai Sabai, essentially a Mai Tai variant, and was for years the only spirit most Thais could legally buy domestically.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and lime, or in a Sabai Sabai with lime and sugar. The spice blend gives it more character than its low strength suggests, and it works well in tiki-style builds.

composition.summary: Rice and molasses spirit blended with herbs and spices.

components.label: Base
components.detail: 95% sugarcane molasses, 5% rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: A blend of Thai herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column-distilled, then blended and infused

composition.process: The spice blend is added after distillation, which is what separates it from a plain rum.

name: Ya Dong
description: Lao khao steeped with roots, bark and herbs in big glass jars, sold by the shot from roadside carts across Thailand. Every stall has its own recipes and every recipe claims a specific medicinal purpose.
funFact: Ya dong stalls typically serve each shot with a chaser of pickled fruit or a slice of guava with chilli salt, which is not optional.

serve.how: One shot, straight, with the pickled fruit chaser the vendor hands you. Different jars are sold for different complaints — aches, circulation, energy — and the vendor will steer you toward one.

composition.summary: Rice spirit macerated with medicinal roots, barks and herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lao khao rice spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dozens of roots, barks and herbs; recipes vary by stall

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks in glass jars

composition.process: The jars keep infusing on the cart, so the same recipe changes over the course of a month.

name: Thai Rum
description: Agricole-style rum from fresh Thai cane juice, made by a small group of producers since 2012. Chalong Bay on Phuket distils from cane cut within hours and produces something notably grassy and clean.
funFact: Thailand's alcohol licensing made small-scale distilling nearly impossible until reforms in the 2010s opened the door to craft producers.

serve.how: In a daiquiri or with soda and lime, where the cane-juice grassiness shows best. The infused versions with lemongrass, kaffir lime or ginger work well in long drinks.

composition.summary: Fresh Thai sugarcane juice fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed Thai sugarcane, no molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly unaged; some oak-rested

composition.process: Cane is crushed within hours of cutting, since the juice degrades fast in tropical heat.

name: Rượu Đế
description: Vietnamese sticky-rice spirit, distilled in villages throughout the Mekong delta and the north. The name refers to the tall grass distillers once hid their stills in during the French colonial monopoly.
funFact: The French colonial administration monopolised alcohol production, which drove Vietnamese distillers into the fields and gave the spirit its name.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, poured for others and drunk together on a toast. It appears at weddings, funerals and Tết, and refusing the first cup is difficult to do politely.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a yeast starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Glutinous sticky rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Men, a Vietnamese yeast and herb starter cake

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, usually single

composition.process: The men starter often contains herbs and spices as well as the culture, which carries into the spirit.

name: Rượu Thuốc
description: Vietnamese medicinal liquor: rice spirit steeped with ginseng, herbs, and frequently a snake, gecko or seahorse. Taken as a tonic, offered to guests, and photographed by every visitor who sees the jars.
funFact: Snake wine is made by submerging a live cobra in spirit, and the alcohol denatures the venom, which is protein-based and therefore neutralised.

serve.how: A small measure, taken for its supposed properties rather than its flavour. Vietnamese hosts offer it to guests as a mark of respect, and it is drunk in one rather than sipped.

composition.summary: Rice spirit steeped with herbs, roots or animal ingredients.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rượu đế rice spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ginseng, cordyceps, snake, gecko, seahorse, bark and roots

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for months to years

composition.process: High-proof spirit is used because it extracts and preserves in a way lower strengths cannot.

name: Vietnamese Gin
description: Gin built on foraged botanicals from Vietnam's northern highlands — mac mat leaf, Sichuan-style pepper, wild ginger, pomelo. Sông Cái opened the category in 2018 and buys from highland communities directly.
funFact: Sông Cái sources dozens of botanicals through highland farming communities in the northern mountains, several of which have no common English name.

serve.how: With a neutral tonic and a strip of pomelo peel, or in a Negroni where the wild-ginger note holds its own against Campari. Avoid heavily flavoured tonics; the foraged botanicals are subtle.

composition.summary: Rice or cane spirit redistilled with foraged highland botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice or cane neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus mac mat, wild ginger, pomelo, cardamom, forest herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, some botanicals vapour-infused

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, though rested expressions exist

composition.process: Botanicals are wild-harvested seasonally, so batches shift with what the mountains give.

name: Sraa Sar
description: Cambodian white rice spirit, distilled behind houses across the country in stills made from clay pots and salvaged metal. The everyday drink of rural Cambodia and the base of the infused versions sold to visitors.
funFact: Home distilling is widespread and largely unregulated in Cambodia, and most villages have at least one household producing for the neighbourhood.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, shared. It is rough on its own, which is why so much of it ends up infused with fruit and spice before it reaches anyone's glass.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a starter and distilled in simple stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice, sometimes with palm sugar

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: A local yeast starter cake

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Clay and metal pot stills

composition.process: Single distillation is the norm, which is why the base spirit is usually infused rather than drunk plain.

name: Sombai
description: Cambodian rice spirit infused with fruit and spice in decorated jars, made in Siem Reap. A modern product built on the traditional practice of steeping sraa sar, and the version most visitors actually enjoy.
funFact: The jars are hand-painted by local artists, and the decoration has become as much of the product as the liqueur inside.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice with soda. Banana-cinnamon, ginger-red chilli and anise-coffee are the signature infusions, and they lean sweet, so keep the measure short.

composition.summary: Rice spirit macerated with fruit, spice and palm sugar.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cambodian rice spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Banana, ginger, anise, coffee, chilli, mango, palm sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated after distillation

composition.process: Palm sugar rather than cane sugar is used for sweetening, which keeps it distinctly Cambodian.

name: Lao-Lao
description: Laos's sticky rice spirit, distilled in villages along the Mekong and sold in whatever bottle is available, sometimes with a snake or scorpion inside. Cheap, strong and completely central to Lao social life.
funFact: At a Lao baci ceremony the same small glass is passed around the whole gathering, refilled each time, and everyone drinks from it in turn.

serve.how: Poured into one glass that passes around the circle, each person drinking and returning it. Refusing is awkward; taking a small sip and passing it on is not. Village strength varies enormously.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Glutinous sticky rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: A local yeast and mould starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Village pot stills, single distillation

composition.process: The snake and scorpion bottles are a separate infused product rather than the everyday spirit.

name: Htan Yay A-Yet
description: Burmese toddy palm spirit from the dry zone around Bagan, distilled from the fermented sap of the toddy palm. Sold at roadside stands with palm sugar sweets, and made in the same villages for generations.
funFact: Toddy palm climbers in the dry zone ascend with a bamboo ladder lashed to the trunk, and the profession is passed down within families.

serve.how: Neat in a small cup, usually alongside the palm sugar jaggery made from the same sap. Roadside toddy stands serve both, and the sweet cuts the spirit's rough edges.

composition.summary: Toddy palm sap fermented and distilled over wood fire.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap of the toddy palm, tapped daily

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Clay or metal pot stills over wood fire

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: The same sap is either drunk fresh, fermented into toddy, boiled to jaggery, or distilled.

name: Myanmar Rum
description: Rum distilled from molasses of cane grown along the Irrawaddy, made commercially since the colonial period. Dark, sweet and rarely seen outside the country or its immediate neighbours.
funFact: Myanmar's distilling industry dates to British Burma, and several brands still in production trace their origins to that period.

serve.how: Over ice with soda or cola, which is how it is drunk locally. It is sweet and simple, and the aged expressions take a cube neat well enough given how fast tropical maturation works.

composition.summary: Molasses from Irrawaddy cane fermented, distilled and aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, tropically matured

composition.process: Central Myanmar's dry zone grows the cane, and the heat pushes maturation fast.

name: Samsu
description: A Malaysian and Singaporean cheap spirit distilled from cane or rice, often sold as a herbal or medicinal preparation to sidestep alcohol duty. Legal, unglamorous and drunk mostly by plantation workers.
funFact: Selling it as medicated samsu attracted a lower duty rate for years, which is why so many bottles carry herbal branding.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. Licensed samsu is safe; illicit versions have caused methanol poisoning outbreaks in Malaysia, so the distinction is worth paying attention to.

composition.summary: Cane or rice spirit, often infused with herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugarcane or rice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Herbs in the medicated versions

composition.process: The herbal designation is a tax classification at least as much as a recipe.

name: Singapore Gin
description: A young category built on Southeast Asian botanicals — pandan, torch ginger, chrysanthemum, calamansi. Singapore had no distillery at all until Brass Lion opened in 2018, which for the home of the Singapore Sling was overdue.
funFact: Singapore had been without a working distillery for decades before Brass Lion, despite lending its name to one of the world's most famous cocktails.

serve.how: With a light tonic and a wedge of calamansi, or in a Singapore Sling made properly with cherry brandy and Bénédictine. The pandan note is delicate, so avoid a heavy tonic.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with Southeast Asian botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, pandan, torch ginger, chrysanthemum, calamansi, lemongrass

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still with vapour infusion

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Vapour infusion is used for the most delicate botanicals, which would be cooked out by maceration.

name: Tua Sabu
description: Timor-Leste's palm spirit, distilled from the sap of lontar and coconut palms in villages across the country. Made informally, drunk at every ceremony, and central to Timorese social life.
funFact: Tua sabu is required at Timorese customary ceremonies, and efforts to formalise its production have focused on safety rather than restriction.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, shared. Quality varies widely between makers, and there have been poisoning incidents from adulterated batches, so a known source matters.

composition.summary: Lontar or coconut palm sap fermented and distilled over fire.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Lontar or coconut palm sap

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Bamboo and pot stills over wood fire

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Bamboo is used for both the still's condenser and the serving vessel in traditional production.

name: Australian Whisky
description: Tasmania leads a category barely thirty years old, using small casks, maritime air and a climate that matures spirit fast. Australian single malts have taken world titles against far older distilling nations.
funFact: Distilling was illegal in Tasmania from 1839 until Bill Lark had the law overturned in 1992, which is why the whole industry is so young.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. Small casks mean heavy wood extraction, so water pulls the spirit forward. Many are bottled at cask strength and non-chill-filtered, where dilution genuinely helps.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in small casks in Tasmania.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Australian malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 100 and 200 litre ex-fortified-wine casks, two years and up

composition.process: Ex-apera and ex-tokay casks from Australian fortified wine producers are the local signature.

name: Australian Rum
description: Queensland molasses rum, of which Bundaberg is the national icon and Beenleigh the oldest, running since 1884. Sweet, heavy and inseparable from Australian drinking culture, particularly north of Brisbane.
funFact: The 1808 Rum Rebellion, the only successful armed takeover of government in Australian history, was triggered partly by attempts to control the rum trade.

serve.how: With cola and ice, which is how the overwhelming majority is drunk. The aged and small-batch releases from Beenleigh and Bundaberg's Master Distillers series deserve a rocks glass and a single cube.

composition.summary: Queensland molasses fermented and distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses from Queensland sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column and pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and ex-fortified oak, two years and up

composition.process: Beenleigh has run since 1884, making it one of the oldest continuously operating distilleries in the southern hemisphere.

name: Australian Gin
description: Gin built on native botanicals that grow nowhere else — lemon myrtle, wattleseed, pepperberry, finger lime, strawberry gum. Australia went from almost no gin distilleries to hundreds in a decade.
funFact: Four Pillars' Bloody Shiraz gin is made by steeping whole shiraz grapes in gin for eight weeks, which turns it deep purple.

serve.glass: Large copa with plenty of ice
serve.how: With a dry tonic and a wedge of grapefruit or a few native pepperberries. Lemon myrtle is intensely citrusy on its own, so adding lime tends to be redundant rather than complementary.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and Australian native botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain or grape spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus lemon myrtle, wattleseed, pepperberry, finger lime, river mint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour baskets

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged, though barrel-aged versions exist

composition.process: Many native botanicals are harvested by Indigenous-owned enterprises, which several distilleries source from directly.

name: Bush Tucker Liqueur
description: Liqueurs made from Australian native fruits — Davidson plum, quandong, riberry, muntrie — most of which have no equivalent anywhere else and only entered commercial cultivation in the last few decades.
funFact: Davidson plum is intensely sour and almost inedible raw, which is exactly why it works so well steeped and sweetened.

serve.glass: Small cordial glass or over ice
serve.how: Cold and neat after dinner, or topped with sparkling wine. The tartness of Davidson plum and quandong makes them better in a spritz than most fruit liqueurs, which tend to cloy.

composition.summary: Native Australian fruit macerated in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Davidson plum, quandong, riberry, muntrie, finger lime

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and sweetened

composition.process: Most of these fruits are still wild-harvested or grown at very small scale, which keeps production tiny.

name: New Zealand Whisky
description: A category that died and came back: New Zealand's last big distillery closed in 1997, its stock was bought by a collector, and new distilleries have since started from scratch in Otago and beyond.
funFact: When the Willowbank distillery in Dunedin closed, its remaining casks were bought en masse and bottled over the following two decades as the country's only aged stock.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. The rescued Willowbank stock is now genuinely old and worth treating carefully; the new-make from the modern distilleries is younger and takes water more readily.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in New Zealand.

components.label: Base
components.detail: New Zealand malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and ex-wine casks; the old Willowbank stock ran past 20 years

composition.process: A cool maritime climate means slow maturation, closer to Scotland than to Tasmania.

name: Hokonui Moonshine
description: Southland's illicit whisky, distilled in the Hokonui hills by Scottish settlers through a local prohibition that ran from 1902 to 1954. Now legal, and made openly by the descendants of people who did not.
funFact: Invercargill and the surrounding district voted itself dry in 1902, and the Hokonui hills supplied the region illegally for over fifty years.

serve.how: Neat or with a splash of water. The peated versions carry real smoke, drawn from Southland peat rather than Islay. It is a young whisky and drinks like one, which is part of the appeal.

composition.summary: Malted barley, often peated with local peat, distilled in Southland.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some unaged in the moonshine style, some oak-matured

composition.process: Southland peat gives a different smoke profile from Scottish peat, being younger and more vegetal.

name: New Zealand Gin
description: Gin built on native flora — horopito, kawakawa, mānuka, kelp, and the citrus that grows well in the north. A small but unusually inventive scene, helped by a country where almost everything botanical is endemic.
funFact: Horopito is known as the pepper tree and carries a genuine chilli-like heat, which comes through clearly in a gin distilled with it.

serve.how: With a dry tonic and a slice of feijoa or grapefruit. Horopito's peppery heat builds, so a lighter tonic and a citrus garnish keep it in balance rather than letting it dominate.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and New Zealand natives.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain or whey spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, horopito, kawakawa, mānuka, kelp, citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Some producers use whey spirit from the dairy industry as their base, which is distinctly New Zealand.

name: Feijoa Liqueur
description: Made from a South American fruit that New Zealand adopted so completely that most New Zealanders assume it is native. Aromatic, tart and almost impossible to describe to anyone who has not eaten one.
funFact: Feijoas fall from the tree when ripe rather than being picked, which is why they barely travel and are almost unknown outside a few countries.

serve.glass: Small glass, or highball with soda
serve.how: Cold and neat, or with soda over ice, which suits the tartness better than tonic. It also works topped with sparkling wine. The vodka-based versions are cleaner than the cream ones.

composition.summary: Feijoa fruit macerated or distilled into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or vodka

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Feijoa (pineapple guava) fruit

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, sometimes distilled, then sweetened

composition.process: The fruit oxidises within minutes of being cut, so it has to be processed almost immediately.

name: Fijian Rum
description: Column-still rum from Lautoka cane, made with unusually long fermentations that build a fruity, ester-rich spirit. Fiji's sugar industry is over a century old, and the rum is finally getting attention abroad.
funFact: Fermentation at the Lautoka distillery can run several times longer than industry standard, which is where the pronounced fruit character comes from.

serve.how: Neat for the aged expressions, or in a daiquiri where the ester-driven fruit does most of the work. It has enough character to stand in for Jamaican rum in a tiki build.

composition.summary: Fijian molasses fermented long and column-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses from Lautoka sugarcane

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak, tropically matured

composition.process: Extended fermentation builds esters, which is the same principle Jamaican distillers use to make funk.

name: Rhum de Tahiti
description: Agricole rum from French Polynesia, distilled from cane grown on Taha'a and Tahiti. A tiny production in the middle of the Pacific, made in the French island tradition and almost never seen elsewhere.
funFact: Cane was reintroduced commercially to Taha'a specifically to supply the distillery, having largely disappeared from the islands.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or in a Ti' Punch with lime and cane syrup as the French islands drink it. The floral character is delicate and gets buried by anything heavier.

composition.summary: Fresh Polynesian cane juice fermented and column-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed cane from Taha'a and Tahiti

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Creole column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Mostly unaged; some oak-rested

composition.process: The volcanic soil and heavy rainfall of the Society Islands give a notably floral cane.

name: Hawaiian Rum
description: Rum from the last of Hawaii's sugar cane, an industry that dominated the islands for a century and closed its final mill in 2016. Small distilleries now grow their own cane to keep making it.
funFact: Hawaii's last commercial sugar plantation closed in 2016, so distilleries there now cultivate their own cane specifically for rum.

serve.how: In a Mai Tai made properly with lime, orgeat and curaçao, or neat for the aged bottlings. The cane-juice versions are grassy and bright and make an excellent daiquiri.

composition.summary: Hawaiian cane juice or molasses fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Hawaii-grown sugarcane, juice or molasses

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot and column stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak, tropically matured

composition.process: Several distilleries grow heirloom Hawaiian cane varieties that the plantations had abandoned.

name: Steamit
description: Papua New Guinean home-distilled spirit, made from whatever will ferment — sugar, fruit, cassava — in improvised stills. Illegal, widespread, and known by the pidgin word for what comes off the still.
funFact: Papua New Guinea has periodically debated regulating steamit rather than prosecuting it, on the same public health logic Kenya applied to chang'aa.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with real caution. It is entirely unregulated, frequently very strong, and adulteration is a genuine hazard rather than a theoretical one.

composition.summary: Sugar, fruit or cassava fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugar, fruit, cassava or sweet potato

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised stills from drums and pipe

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 40–70%, unmeasured

composition.process: Nothing about production is standardised, which is why strength and safety vary batch to batch.

name: Clarito
description: The Argentine Martini: gin and dry vermouth, stirred hard, served brutally cold with a lemon twist. Older than most people assume.
funFact: Buenos Aires had a serious cocktail culture by the 1920s, and the Clarito — 'the clear little one' — was its house drink, poured in the grand cafés of Avenida de Mayo.

steps: Chill a coupe thoroughly in the freezer.
Stir the gin, vermouth and bitters over plenty of ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into the frozen coupe.
Express a wide lemon twist over the surface and rest it on the rim.

name: Gancia Batido
description: Gancia, lemon and sugar shaken to a foam — the Argentine aperitivo that college towns adopted and never gave back.
funFact: Gancia is an Italian bitter aperitif that found a second life in Argentina; batido versions are so entrenched that the brand is now more associated with Rosario than with Piedmont.

steps: Add the Gancia, lemon juice and sugar to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds until foamy.
Pour unstrained into a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda and a lemon wheel.

name: Aruba Ariba
description: Aruba's signature pour: vodka, rum, crème de banana and the island's own Coecoei liqueur, layered orange and red over crushed ice.
funFact: Coecoei is made on Aruba from the fermented sap of the agave-like kukwisa plant, and it is what makes an authentic Aruba Ariba impossible to reproduce properly off the island.

steps: Shake the vodka, rum, crème de banana and the juices with ice.
Pour into a hurricane glass filled with crushed ice.
Float the Coecoei over the top so it streaks red through the orange.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Bundy and Coke
description: Bundaberg rum and Coke, poured heavy. Queensland's contribution to world drinking, and defended with real feeling.
funFact: Bundaberg Rum has been distilled in Queensland since 1888 from local sugarcane molasses, and its polar bear mascot was introduced in the 1960s to suggest it could ward off the cold.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the rum.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and squeeze in a lime wedge if you like.

name: Fluffy Duck
description: Advocaat, gin and lemonade with a float of cream. Pale, foamy and unapologetically 1970s — Australia never let it go.
funFact: Australian RSL clubs and country pubs kept the Fluffy Duck on the menu long after the rest of the world moved on, which is why it now reads as Australian rather than as generic seventies.

steps: Shake the advocaat, gin and orange juice with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled highball glass.
Top with lemonade and stir once.
Float the cream over the back of a spoon.
Garnish with a cherry and an orange slice.

name: Jagertee
description: Black tea and overproof rum with spice and citrus, served scalding in Alpine huts. Designed for people who have just come down a mountain.
funFact: Austrian law reserves the name 'Jagertee' for versions made with Inländerrum, an 80-proof Austrian rum; anywhere else in the EU it has to be sold as 'Jagatee' or 'hunter's tea'.

steps: Brew the black tea strong and keep it hot.
Warm the orange slice, cinnamon and cloves in the mug with the sugar.
Pour over the hot tea and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the rum last, off the heat.
Serve very hot with the spices left in.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a cinnamon stick

name: Weißer Spritzer
description: White wine and sparkling water, half and half. Vienna's most-poured drink, and proof that the simplest spritz is still a spritz.
funFact: Order a 'G'spritzter' anywhere in Austria and this is what arrives; a 'Sommerspritzer' has more water, a 'Winterspritzer' more wine, and the vocabulary is taken seriously.

steps: Chill both the wine and the mineral water.
Pour the wine into a wine glass.
Top with the sparkling water.
Do not add ice — Austrians consider it dilution twice over.

name: Goombay Smash
description: The Abacos' most guarded secret: coconut rum, dark rum, pineapple and apricot, in a recipe the original bar has never fully written down.
funFact: Miss Emily's Blue Bee Bar on Green Turtle Cay invented it in the 1960s and has kept the exact proportions in the family ever since; every other version in the Bahamas is a reconstruction.

steps: Add the coconut rum, apricot brandy, pineapple juice and lemon juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake for 10 seconds and strain into an ice-filled highball glass.
Float the dark rum over the top.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.

name: Sky Juice
description: Gin and coconut water with sweetened condensed milk and nutmeg — Bahamian breakfast, sold from roadside stalls before the sun is fully up.
funFact: Also called 'gully wash', it is traditional at Junkanoo — the Bahamian street parade that runs through the small hours of Boxing Day and New Year's Day.

steps: Whisk the condensed milk into the coconut water until fully dissolved.
Add the gin and stir.
Pour over ice into a cup or jar.
Grate fresh nutmeg generously over the top.

name: Yellow Bird
description: Rum, Galliano and banana liqueur over citrus — sunshine yellow, named for the calypso standard that plays on loop across the islands.
funFact: The song 'Yellow Bird' is an adaptation of an 1880s Haitian melody; the cocktail borrowed the name in the 1960s when Galliano was on every back bar in the Caribbean.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake for about 12 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe, or over fresh ice in a highball.
Garnish with an orange wheel.

name: Bajan Rum Punch
description: The rhyme, sung the Barbadian way: sour, sweet, strong, weak, with Angostura across the top and nutmeg over that.
funFact: Barbados claims the rhyme as its own national verse, and adds a fifth line most islands leave off: 'a dash of bitters and a sprinkle of spice'.

steps: Combine the lime juice, sugar syrup, rum and water in a jug in that order.
Stir well and chill thoroughly — punch should never be shaken to order.
Pour over ice into rocks glasses.
Dash Angostura generously over each glass.
Grate nutmeg over the top.

name: Corn 'n' Oil
description: Barbadian and barely diluted: dark rum, falernum and lime, stirred until it looks like crude oil in the glass. Clove, almond and molasses.
funFact: Falernum is a Barbadian invention — a low-proof syrup-liqueur of lime, clove, almond and ginger — and this is the drink it exists for. The name describes the drink's dark, slick appearance.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with crushed ice.
Add the falernum and lime juice.
Pour the rum over the top and stir briefly with a swizzle stick.
Dash the Angostura across the surface.
Garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Krambambula
description: Vodka and honey mulled with cinnamon, clove and nutmeg — a Belarusian recipe rescued from the eighteenth century and now a national symbol.
funFact: Krambambula was originally a Danzig cherry liqueur, but the Belarusian version — honey, spice and spirit, served hot — became a marker of national identity during the cultural revivals of the 1990s.

steps: Simmer the water, honey and all the spices together for 10 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for a few minutes.
Stir in the vodka off the heat.
Strain and serve hot in small mugs, or bottle it and reheat as needed.

name: Half en Half
description: Half still white wine, half Belgian sparkling, poured cold. Brussels' aperitif, and older than most of the city's cocktail bars.
funFact: It is the house pour at Brussels' oldest wine bars around the Grand-Place, where the sparkling half is traditionally a Belgian méthode traditionnelle rather than champagne.

steps: Chill both wines well.
Pour the still white wine into a wine glass.
Top with the sparkling wine, poured slowly down the side.
Serve immediately without ice or garnish.

name: Maitrank
description: White wine steeped with sweet woodruff, sugar and cognac, drunk in May with a strawberry in the glass. Arlon's own, and legally protected.
funFact: Arlon holds a Maitrank festival every May and the recipe carries a protected designation; woodruff must be picked before it flowers, or it turns bitter and mildly toxic.

steps: Wilt the woodruff for a few hours so its aroma develops, but do not let it flower.
Steep it in the white wine with the sugar and orange slices for about 24 hours in the fridge.
Strain out the herb and orange.
Stir in the cognac and chill thoroughly.
Serve in wine glasses with a strawberry in each.

name: Panty Ripper
description: Belize's unofficial national drink, with the least diplomatic name in the Caribbean: coconut rum and pineapple juice, over ice, on a beach.
funFact: Every bar from Caye Caulker to San Ignacio serves it, and every bartender tells a different story about the name — none of which they will repeat in front of your parents.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the coconut rum and the lime juice.
Top with cold pineapple juice.
Stir briefly to combine and garnish with a pineapple wedge.

name: Rum Swizzle
description: Bermuda's national drink and the reason swizzle sticks exist: black rum, falernum and juices churned over crushed ice until the glass frosts.
funFact: The Swizzle Inn near the airport has been serving it since 1932 under the slogan 'Swizzle Inn, Swagger Out'; the swizzle stick itself comes from the forked branch of the Caribbean Quararibea tree.

steps: Fill a tall glass or a small pitcher with crushed ice.
Add all the ingredients.
Spin a swizzle stick between your palms until the outside of the glass frosts over.
Top with more crushed ice to refill the glass.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Chuflay
description: Singani and ginger ale with a squeeze of lime — Bolivia's national highball, invented by homesick railway engineers.
funFact: The name is said to come from British railway workers asking for a 'short fly' — a quick drink — which Bolivian ears rendered as 'chuflay'. Singani is Bolivia's protected grape brandy.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the singani and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Yungueñito
description: Singani shaken with fresh orange juice — the Yungas valleys in a glass, where Bolivia's oranges and its grape brandy come from the same slopes.
funFact: Named for Los Yungas, the humid valleys northeast of La Paz; the full-size version, the Yungueño, is served in a jug for the table.

steps: Add the singani, orange juice and syrup to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe or over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with an orange wheel.

name: Batida de Coco
description: Cachaça blended with coconut milk and condensed milk until it drinks like a cold dessert. Brazil's beach cocktail when the Caipirinha feels too sharp.
funFact: 'Batida' simply means 'beaten' or 'shaken' — the family covers dozens of fruit versions (maracujá, morango, amendoim), of which coconut is the one that travelled.

steps: Add the cachaça, coconut milk and condensed milk to a blender.
Add the ice and blend until smooth and frothy.
Pour into a chilled rocks glass.
Grate a little fresh coconut or dust cinnamon over the top.

name: Caipiroska
description: The Caipirinha with vodka instead of cachaça — cleaner, less funky, and the version most of the world actually orders.
funFact: Brazilian bars will make it without comment but consider it a compromise; the same swap with white rum is a Caipirissima, and with sake a Sakerinha.

steps: Put the lime wedges and sugar in the bottom of a sturdy rocks glass.
Muddle firmly until the sugar dissolves into the lime juice and oil.
Fill the glass with ice.
Pour over the vodka and stir hard from the bottom up.
Serve with the spent lime wedges still in the glass.

name: Capeta
description: 'Little devil': cachaça, guaraná powder, condensed milk and cinnamon — a Brazilian student drink built to keep you upright until sunrise.
funFact: Guaraná seed carries roughly twice the caffeine of coffee by weight, which is exactly the point — the Capeta is northeastern Brazil's original energy cocktail, decades before Red Bull.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a blender with the ice.
Blend on high until completely smooth.
Pour into a rocks glass.
Dust with extra cinnamon and serve cold.

name: Leite de Onça
description: 'Jaguar's milk': cachaça, condensed milk, cocoa and crème de cacao, shaken cold. Minas Gerais' answer to a nightcap.
funFact: A Festa Junina staple in Minas Gerais alongside quentão, and one of the few Brazilian drinks that is genuinely better made the night before and left in the fridge.

steps: Whisk the cocoa powder into a little of the warm milk to make a smooth paste, then cool.
Add the paste, remaining milk, condensed milk, crème de cacao and cachaça to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled tumbler.
Dust with cocoa powder or cinnamon.

name: Quentão
description: Festa Junina in a mug: cachaça simmered with ginger, cinnamon and citrus peel until the whole street smells like winter, in the middle of a Brazilian June.
funFact: Quentão means 'big hot one' and belongs to Festa Junina, the June harvest festivals — held in the Brazilian winter, which is why a country famous for cold drinks has a national mulled one.

steps: Melt the sugar in a heavy pan over medium heat until it just turns amber.
