Add the ginger, cinnamon, cloves and orange peel and stir for a minute.
Pour in the water and simmer for 10 minutes to build the infusion.
Add the cachaça and heat gently — do not let it boil hard or you lose the alcohol.
Strain into mugs and serve steaming.
recipe.garnish: A cinnamon stick and a strip of orange peel

name: Rabo-de-Galo
description: 'Rooster's tail': cachaça and red vermouth, stirred and served short. Brazil's Manhattan, drunk standing up at a botequim counter.
funFact: The name is a literal translation of 'cocktail'; the traditional street version is a rough 50/50 of cachaça and Cynar, while the bar version leans on aged cachaça and good vermouth.

steps: Combine the cachaça, vermouth and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 seconds until chilled.
Strain into a small tumbler, over one large ice cube or straight up.
Express an orange twist over the top.

name: Maple Old Fashioned
description: An Old Fashioned sweetened with maple syrup instead of sugar. Quebec's obvious move, and it works better than obvious usually does.
funFact: Quebec produces roughly seventy percent of the world's maple syrup and keeps a strategic reserve of it — a genuine stockpile, held in a warehouse, against bad harvest years.

steps: Stir the maple syrup and both bitters together in a mixing glass.
Add the rye and plenty of ice.
Stir for 25 seconds until chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.

name: Toronto
description: Canadian rye stirred with Fernet-Branca, sugar and bitters. Bitter, minty and bracing — an Old Fashioned with a mean streak.
funFact: It appears in Robert Vermeire's 1922 'Cocktails: How to Mix Them' with the note that it is favoured 'by the people of Toronto' — one of the earliest cocktails ever named for a Canadian city.

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe, or over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Borgoña
description: Red wine and macerated strawberries, chilled and eaten as much as drunk. Chile's Fiestas Patrias in a jug.
funFact: Served at every September 18 fonda alongside its white-wine cousin, the chicha-based Clery; the strawberries at the bottom of the jug are the prize and go to whoever is quickest.

steps: Toss the strawberries with the sugar in a large jug and leave for an hour to macerate.
Pour over the red wine and stir.
Refrigerate for at least two hours — overnight is better.
Serve cold over ice, spooning strawberries into each glass.

name: Cola de Mono
description: 'Monkey's tail': coffee, milk, cloves and aguardiente, chilled and bottled for Christmas. Chile's answer to eggnog, and considerably more drinkable.
funFact: Chilean families bottle it in reused wine bottles in early December and keep it in the fridge until Christmas Eve; the name's origin is disputed, with the best story involving President Pedro Montt and a borrowed pistol.

steps: Warm the milk with the sugar, cloves and cinnamon until the sugar dissolves; do not boil.
Stir in the instant coffee and vanilla, then remove from the heat.
Cool completely and strain out the spices.
Stir in the aguardiente, bottle, and refrigerate for at least a day.
Serve very cold in small glasses.

name: Piscola
description: Pisco and cola, no ceremony. Chile's default drink at every party, poured with a heavy hand and measured by nobody.
funFact: Chile consumes so much of it that pisco producers bottle expressly for the mix; there is an annual National Piscola Day, and the drink is often blamed for Chile's reputation as South America's heaviest spirit drinkers.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the pisco.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once. Add a lime wedge only if you must — most Chileans do not.

name: Serena Libre
description: Pisco with papaya juice and a squeeze of lime — the northern Chilean coast's alternative to the Piscola, built on the fruit that grows there.
funFact: The papaya of La Serena is a small, aromatic variety grown in the Elqui Valley — the same valley that produces most of Chile's pisco, which is why the pairing is local rather than clever.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the pisco, papaya juice and lime juice.
Stir well to combine.
Top with a splash of soda and garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Guihua Jiu
description: Osmanthus blossom steeped in rice wine — intensely floral, apricot-scented, and traditionally opened at the Mid-Autumn Festival.
funFact: Guilin is named for its osmanthus forests — 'gui' is the flower, 'lin' the forest — and the wine is drunk at the Mid-Autumn Festival when the trees are in bloom.

steps: Rinse the dried osmanthus blossoms briefly and let them dry.
Layer them with rock sugar in a clean glass jar.
Pour over the rice wine and seal.
Store somewhere dark for at least one month, longer for a stronger infusion.
Strain and serve in small cups, lightly chilled or at room temperature.

name: Warm Huangjiu
description: Shaoxing rice wine warmed with ginger and dried plum. Nutty, savoury and closer to a dry sherry than to anything in the wine aisle.
glassware: Small ceramic cup and warming pot
funFact: Huangjiu has been brewed in Shaoxing for over two thousand years, and warming it is not just for comfort — heat volatilises the harsher notes and brings the amino-acid savouriness forward.

steps: Pour the huangjiu into a small ceramic warming pot.
Add the ginger slices, dried plum and rock sugar.
Stand the pot in a bowl of hot water — never over direct heat — until it reaches about 40°C.
Pour into small cups and drink while warm, alongside food.

name: Guaro Sour Colombiano
description: Aguardiente antioqueño — anise-forward and unapologetic — shaken with lime and sugar into something that tames it, slightly.
funFact: Colombian aguardiente is flavoured with anise, which makes it a completely different animal from Costa Rican guaro; the sin azúcar version now outsells the sweetened original.

steps: Dry-shake the aguardiente, lime, syrup and egg white without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime twist across the foam.

name: Refajo
description: Beer and Colombiana cream soda, poured half and half. Sweet, fizzy, faintly ridiculous, and served at every Colombian family lunch.
funFact: Colombiana is a red 'kola champagne' soda bottled since 1904; the mix has been formalised into a canned product, but Colombians still insist the fresh pour is better.

steps: Chill both the beer and the soda thoroughly.
Pour equal parts into a tall glass, soda first to control the foam.
Stir once, very gently.
For a 'refajo con aguardiente', add a shot of aguardiente before topping up.

name: Chiliguaro
description: A Costa Rican shot that behaves like a tiny Bloody Mary: guaro, tomato, lime and enough Salsa Lizano heat to wake the table up.
funFact: Salsa Lizano — a tangy Costa Rican condiment closer to brown sauce than hot sauce — is the ingredient that separates a real chiliguaro from a small Bloody Mary.

steps: Combine everything in a shaker with ice.
Shake briefly, about 8 seconds — you want it cold, not diluted.
Strain into chilled shot glasses.
Serve immediately with lime wedges on the side.

name: Guaro Sour
description: Costa Rica's national spirit taken the simplest possible way: guaro, lime, sugar, ice. Clean, sharp and dangerously easy in the heat.
funFact: Guaro — Cacique is the state-blessed brand — is a sugarcane spirit so central to Costa Rican life that its production was a government monopoly for most of the twentieth century.

steps: Rim a rocks glass with lime and salt.
Shake the guaro, lime juice and simple syrup hard with ice.
Strain into the rimmed glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel on a salted rim

name: Bevanda
description: Red wine cut with still water — the Dalmatian working drink, and a habit inherited more or less directly from the Romans.
funFact: Diluting wine with water was standard practice in the classical Mediterranean, where drinking it neat was considered barbaric; the Dalmatian coast simply never stopped.

steps: Pour the red wine into a plain tumbler.
Add still water to taste — roughly half and half for a working bevanda.
Stir once.
Serve at cellar temperature, with food.

name: Gemišt
description: White wine and sparkling mineral water. Croatia's default afternoon drink, and the reason Croatian mineral water brands are household names.
funFact: The ratio is regional and argued about — inland Croatia leans to half and half, while the coast pours a heavier wine measure and calls the weaker version an insult.

steps: Chill the wine and the mineral water.
Pour the wine into a tumbler.
Top with the sparkling mineral water.
Serve immediately; ice is a coastal habit and inland Croatia disapproves.

name: Canchánchara
description: The oldest Cuban drink of them all: raw cane spirit, honey and lime, served in a clay cup. Rougher than the Daiquiri and considerably older.
funFact: Cuban independence fighters, the mambises, drank it in the 1860s as a field ration and a cold remedy; the bar La Canchánchara in Trinidad still serves it in the traditional earthenware cups.

ingredients.item: Aguardiente de caña or white rum

steps: Stir the honey and cold water together in the bottom of a clay cup until the honey loosens.
Add the lime juice and stir again.
Pour in the cane spirit and add cracked ice.
Stir until the outside of the cup is cold, and serve with the spoon still in it.

name: El Presidente
description: Havana's aristocrat: aged rum stirred with blanc vermouth, curaçao and a whisper of grenadine. Silk where the Daiquiri is citrus.
funFact: Named for Cuban president Gerardo Machado and the drink of choice for the American upper class who fled Prohibition to Havana — Basil Woon called it 'the aristocrat of cocktails' in 1928.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until well chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Havana Special
description: A Daiquiri that took a detour through the pineapple fields: rum, pineapple juice and maraschino, shaken to a pale gold froth.
funFact: Recorded in Havana's Sloppy Joe's bar menu in the 1930s — a bar so central to American drinking tourism that its cocktail list was sold as a souvenir booklet.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a pineapple leaf or a cherry.

name: Mary Pickford
description: Pink, pineapple-bright and named for a silent film star: white rum, pineapple, maraschino and grenadine, invented while Hollywood was drinking out its Prohibition exile.
funFact: Created at the Hotel Sevilla-Biltmore in Havana in the 1920s for Mary Pickford, who was in Cuba filming with Douglas Fairbanks and Charlie Chaplin.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds — fresh pineapple juice needs the aeration.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.

name: Mulata
description: A Daiquiri built on aged rum and crème de cacao — chocolate and lime, which should not work and completely does.
funFact: Created at Havana's Floridita, the same bar that made the Daiquiri famous; 'mulata' refers to the drink's brown-gold colour once the cacao and aged rum combine.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with a scoop of crushed ice, or shake hard with cubed ice.
Blend or shake until frosty.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Grate a little dark chocolate over the top.

name: Saoco
description: Rum and coconut water, straight from the nut. The Piña Colada's lean, unsweetened ancestor — and far better on a genuinely hot day.
funFact: Traditionally the top is macheted off a green coconut, rum is poured straight in, and the whole thing is drunk from the shell — the coconut meat is scooped out afterwards.

steps: If using a coconut, cut a wide opening in the top and pour off a little water to make room.
Add the rum and lime juice directly to the coconut or to an ice-filled highball glass.
Top with coconut water.
Stir once and drink through a straw.
recipe.garnish: A lime wedge, or nothing at all

name: Beton
description: Becherovka and tonic — the Czech Republic's national mixed drink, named by acronym and tasting of cinnamon and gentian.
funFact: The name is an acronym of BEcherovka and TONic, and also happens to be the Czech word for concrete — a coincidence the marketing has always enjoyed.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Becherovka and the lemon juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wedge.

name: Sønderjysk Kaffepunch
description: The Danish version of the coin test, with schnapps instead of moonshine — and a firm local rule about how many you are allowed.
funFact: Southern Jutland tradition says you drink an odd number and never stop at one — the old joke is that stopping at two leaves you 'walking in circles', so you continue to three.

steps: Put the sugar cubes and a clean coin in the bottom of a coffee cup.
Pour in hot coffee until the coin is just hidden.
Top up with aquavit until the coin reappears.
Stir once and drink hot, while the sugar is still dissolving.

name: Santo Libre
description: The Cuba Libre's lighter neighbour: white rum, lime and lemon-lime soda instead of cola. Crisper, and easier in the afternoon.
funFact: Named in deliberate contrast to the Cuba Libre — the Dominican version swaps the cola for Sprite or 7-Up, which locals argue lets the rum actually taste like rum.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the rum and lime juice.
Top with cold lemon-lime soda.
Stir once gently and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Canelazo
description: Andean altitude medicine: cinnamon and naranjilla simmered with sugar, spiked with aguardiente and drunk hot at ten thousand feet.
funFact: Naranjilla — lulo in Colombia — is a small orange Andean fruit that tastes like rhubarb crossed with citrus, and it is what separates a real canelazo from hot cinnamon water with booze in it.

steps: Simmer the water with the cinnamon sticks and panela for 15 minutes.
Add the naranjilla pulp and lime juice and simmer for another 5 minutes.
Strain into mugs.
Add the aguardiente to each mug off the heat.
Serve immediately with a cinnamon stick.

name: Millimallikas
description: 'Jellyfish': a layered shot of sambuca and Irish cream that curdles into tendrils, finished with a dash of something bitter. Looks alive, briefly.
funFact: The curdling is the point: the acid and alcohol in the sambuca destabilise the cream's proteins, and the strands that form are what give the shot its name.

steps: Pour the sambuca into a shot glass.
Drop the Irish cream into the centre slowly so it sinks and spreads into tendrils.
Add two dashes of bitters over the top.
Serve immediately — it only looks right for about a minute.

name: Vana Tallinn Coffee
description: Estonia's rum liqueur stirred into hot coffee with cream on top — citrus, vanilla and cinnamon against a Baltic winter.
funFact: Vana Tallinn has been made since 1960 to a recipe the distillery still does not publish; Estonians add it to coffee, to hot chocolate, and — controversially — to milk.

steps: Pour the Vana Tallinn into a warmed glass mug.
Add the hot coffee and stir once.
Float lightly whipped cream over the back of a spoon.
Do not stir the cream in — drink the coffee through it.
recipe.garnish: Floated cream and a dusting of cinnamon

name: Tej
description: Honey wine fermented with gesho twigs, cloudy gold and served in a round-bottomed flask you cannot put down. Ethiopia's national drink.
funFact: Gesho — a native buckthorn — plays the role hops play in beer, adding bitterness and stopping the honey from tasting cloying. The berele flask has a round bottom precisely so you have to keep holding it.

steps: Dissolve the honey in warm water in a large fermentation vessel.
Add the gesho twigs and cover loosely with cloth.
Leave at room temperature for a week, stirring daily, until it ferments actively.
Strain out the gesho and let it settle for another one to two weeks.
Serve cool in a berele flask, cloudy and unfiltered.

name: Lonkero
description: Gin and grapefruit soda, invented by the state for the Helsinki Olympics and never given up since. Finland's national long drink.
glassware: Tall glass or straight from the can
funFact: Alko, Finland's alcohol monopoly, created it in 1952 to serve the flood of visitors to the Helsinki Olympics quickly; 'lonkero' means tentacle, from the original nickname 'octopus drink'.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the gin.
Top with cold grapefruit soda.
Stir once and garnish with a grapefruit wedge.

name: Salmiakki Shot
description: Salty liquorice dissolved into vodka until it turns tar-black. Finland's most divisive export, and it divides on the first sip.
funFact: Salmiakki is flavoured with ammonium chloride, which is why it tastes faintly of ammonia to anyone who did not grow up in the Nordics — Finns consider this a feature.

steps: Crush the salmiakki sweets roughly and put them in a sealable jar.
Pour over the vodka and seal.
Shake daily for three to five days until the sweets have fully dissolved and the liquid is black.
Strain if any grit remains, then keep in the freezer.
Serve ice cold in shot glasses.

name: Absinthe Drip
description: Absinthe, a slotted spoon, a sugar cube and iced water dripped over it until the glass clouds green-white. The ritual is most of the drink.
glassware: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
funFact: The louche — the cloud that forms as water hits — happens because the anise oils are soluble in alcohol but not water; if your absinthe does not louche, it is coloured spirit, not absinthe.

steps: Pour the absinthe into an absinthe glass or a small tumbler.
Rest a slotted spoon across the rim and set the sugar cube on it.
Drip iced water very slowly over the sugar cube so it dissolves into the absinthe.
Keep dripping until the drink turns opaque — roughly three to five parts water to one of absinthe.
Stir once and drink at room temperature.

name: Blue Lagoon
description: Vodka, blue curaçao and lemonade — electric blue, faintly ridiculous, and genuinely refreshing if you make it with real lemon.
funFact: Created at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in the 1960s — the same bar credited with the Bloody Mary, the Sidecar and the French 75, and responsible for a suspicious share of the twentieth century's drinking.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the vodka, blue curaçao and lemon juice.
Top with lemonade and stir once.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Champs-Élysées
description: Cognac, Chartreuse and lemon — a Sidecar that went to the monastery and came back with opinions about herbs.
funFact: It appears in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, and is one of the few classics where green Chartreuse plays a supporting role rather than dominating everything it touches.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.

name: Communard
description: The Kir's red half-brother: red Burgundy with cassis, named for the Paris Commune and considerably more serious about itself.
funFact: Also called a Cardinal, for the colour of a cardinal's robes — the two names carry opposite politics for exactly the same drink.

steps: Pour the crème de cassis into a wine glass.
Add the cold red wine.
Stir gently and serve.
Keep the wine light — a heavy red buries the cassis.

name: Kir
description: White Burgundy with a measure of blackcurrant liqueur. Invented to make thin wine drinkable and now ordered on its own merits.
funFact: Named for Canon Félix Kir, mayor of Dijon after the war, who served it at official receptions to promote two local products at once — the sharp Aligoté grape and Dijon's cassis.

steps: Pour the crème de cassis into the bottom of a wine glass.
Top with cold dry white wine.
Stir once, gently, to combine.
Serve without ice or garnish.

name: Mauresque
description: Pastis softened with orgeat until it turns milky and almond-sweet. The gentlest member of the Marseille colour family.
funFact: The name means 'Moorish', a nod to the almond-and-orange-flower orgeat that came into Provence through North African and Spanish trade.

steps: Pour the pastis and orgeat into a tumbler.
Top slowly with cold water until the drink turns opaque and pale.
Stir once to combine.
Add ice last if you want it colder.

name: Monaco
description: Lager, lemonade and grenadine — pink, low-proof and what half of France orders on a café terrace in July.
funFact: It sits in a French family of low-proof beer mixes: the Panaché is beer and lemonade, the Tango uses grenadine with more beer, and the Monaco is the one with all three.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of the glass.
Add the lemonade.
Top slowly with the lager, tilting the glass to control the head.
Stir once, very gently, to bring the pink through.

name: Monkey Gland
description: Gin, orange juice, grenadine and absinthe, named after a genuinely alarming 1920s medical procedure.
funFact: It is named for Serge Voronoff, a surgeon who grafted monkey testicle tissue onto human patients as a rejuvenation treatment; Harry MacElhone named the drink while the story was still in the papers.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

name: Perroquet
description: Pastis turned green with mint syrup — the 'parrot', one of a whole southern French family named for their colours.
funFact: The southern French colour code is fixed: mint makes a Perroquet, grenadine a Tomate, orgeat a Mauresque, and lemon syrup a Canari — order by colour and every bar from Nice to Sète understands you.

steps: Pour the pastis and mint syrup into a tall tumbler.
Add cold water slowly and watch the drink go cloudy and green.
Stir once.
Add ice only after the water — ice first will make the pastis seize.

name: Picon Bière
description: A shot of bitter orange Picon in the bottom of a beer glass. Eastern France's default order, and an acquired taste worth acquiring.
funFact: Amer Picon was created in Algeria in 1837 as a quinine tonic for French soldiers; its modern formulation is much weaker than the original, which is why old cocktail books calling for Picon rarely taste right today.

steps: Pour the Picon into the bottom of a beer glass.
Fill slowly with cold lager, letting the beer mix it as it goes.
Do not stir — the pour does the work.
Serve with no garnish.

name: Rose
description: Dry vermouth, kirsch and a whisper of raspberry, stirred pale pink. The Paris cocktail the Prohibition Americans took home with them.
funFact: Created around 1920 by Johnny Mitta at the Chatham Hotel bar in Paris, and one of the most-ordered cocktails in the city between the wars before it vanished almost entirely.

steps: Combine the vermouth, kirsch and raspberry syrup in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry.

name: Tomate
description: Pastis stained red with grenadine. No tomato involved — the name is purely about what it looks like in the glass.
funFact: In Provençal bars the pastis, the syrup and a jug of cold water arrive separately, and diluting it yourself is part of the ritual — roughly five parts water to one of pastis.

steps: Pour the pastis and grenadine into a tumbler.
Add cold water slowly until the drink louches to a cloudy pink-red.
Stir once.
Serve with a jug of extra water on the side.

name: Berliner Weisse mit Schuss
description: Berlin's sour wheat beer sweetened with raspberry or woodruff syrup, served bright red or alarming green in a wide bowl glass.
funFact: Napoleon's troops reportedly called it 'the champagne of the north'; the syrups were added in the twentieth century because the unadulterated beer was too sour for modern palates.

steps: Pour the syrup into the bottom of a wide bowl-shaped glass.
Pour the cold Berliner Weisse over it slowly — the beer foams aggressively.
Let the head settle, then top up.
Serve with a short fat straw, which is traditional and genuinely useful.

name: Feuerzangenbowle
description: A rum-soaked sugarloaf set on fire above a bowl of mulled wine, dripping caramel into it as it burns. German Christmas at its most theatrical.
funFact: The 1944 film 'Die Feuerzangenbowle' made it a national ritual; German students still hold screenings where the audience makes the drink along with the film.

steps: Heat the wine with the citrus slices and spices in a wide bowl — hot but never boiling.
Set the metal Feuerzange tongs across the bowl and place the sugarloaf on them.
Soak the sugarloaf with overproof rum and set it alight.
Keep ladling more rum over the loaf as it burns and drips caramelised sugar into the wine.
When the sugar has gone, stir the bowl and ladle into mugs.
recipe.garnish: An orange slice and a cinnamon stick

name: Glühwein
description: Red wine heated with cinnamon, clove and citrus. The smell of every Christmas market between Cologne and Vienna.
funFact: German law regulates it: Glühwein must be made from wine, cannot be watered down, and must not fall below 7% ABV — a rare case of a mulled drink with a legal definition.

ingredients.amount: 1 oz / 30 ml per mug, optional 'mit Schuss'

steps: Put the wine, orange slices, spices and sugar in a pan.
Heat gently to about 70°C — steaming but never simmering, or the alcohol goes.
Hold at that temperature for 20 minutes to let the spices infuse.
Strain into mugs, adding a shot of rum to each for 'mit Schuss'.
Serve hot with a cinnamon stick.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a cinnamon stick

name: Kalte Ente
description: 'Cold duck': white wine and sparkling wine over a spiral of lemon peel, chilled hard. A German garden-party punch that Americans misheard into their own version.
funFact: The name is probably a corruption of 'kalte Ende' — the cold end of the evening, when leftover wines were combined. American 'Cold Duck' took the name and made it a sweet red sparkling instead.

steps: Peel the lemons in one continuous spiral and hang the peel in a punch bowl.
Add the sugar and the juice of one lemon and stir.
Pour in the still white wine and chill for at least two hours.
Add the sparkling wine and a block of ice just before serving.
Ladle into wine glasses.

name: Lumumba
description: Hot chocolate with a shot of brandy or dark rum and a cap of whipped cream. Northern European winter, no further explanation offered.
funFact: Named — with no clear justification and a fair amount of later discomfort — after Congolese independence leader Patrice Lumumba, sometime after 1961. It is often now simply called a 'Tote Tante' in the north.

ingredients.item: Hot chocolate, made with whole milk

steps: Make a rich hot chocolate with whole milk and good dark chocolate.
Pour into a warmed mug, leaving room at the top.
Stir in the brandy or rum.
Cap with whipped cream and dust with cocoa or grated chocolate.

name: Rakomelo
description: Cretan raki warmed with honey, cinnamon and clove. Served in winter, and pressed on you whether or not you asked.
funFact: In Crete, raki arrives free at the end of a meal whether you ordered it or not; rakomelo is the winter version, and refusing it is harder than it sounds.

steps: Warm the raki gently in a small pan with the cinnamon and cloves.
Stir in the honey until it fully dissolves.
Do not let it boil — you want it hot, not evaporating.
Strain into small heatproof glasses and serve at once.

name: Ponche de Frutas
description: Christmas in a mug across Guatemala: tropical fruit simmered with cinnamon and panela, spiked with rum at the last minute.
funFact: The fruit is meant to be eaten, not strained out — a Guatemalan ponche is served with a spoon, and the pieces at the bottom of the mug have been quietly soaking in rum all evening.

steps: Bring the water, panela and cinnamon sticks to a simmer in a large pot.
Add the diced fruit and raisins and simmer gently for about 40 minutes, until the fruit is soft and the liquid is amber.
Ladle the hot punch and a generous spoonful of fruit into each mug.
Add the rum to each mug individually, off the heat, so the alcohol survives.
Serve hot with a spoon.
recipe.garnish: A cinnamon stick and the stewed fruit

name: Kremas
description: Haiti's Christmas in a bottle: rhum, coconut cream, condensed milk, lime zest and spice, thick enough to coat the glass.
funFact: Also spelled cremas or kremasi, it is the drink of Haitian holidays and diaspora gatherings — and every family insists their version is the correct one, usually over the amount of star anise.

steps: Warm the coconut cream gently with the spices and lime zest, then cool completely.
Blend the spiced coconut cream with the condensed milk, evaporated milk and vanilla until smooth.
Stir in the rhum — never blend it in hot, or the texture breaks.
Strain into bottles and refrigerate for at least 24 hours before drinking.
Serve very cold in small glasses; it keeps for weeks.

name: Guifiti
description: Garífuna herbal medicine that became a shot: raw rum steeped for weeks with roots, bark and spices until it turns dark, bitter and faintly medicinal.
funFact: Guifiti recipes are family property along the Honduran and Belizean Garífuna coast, traditionally prescribed for everything from stomach trouble to low spirits — the recipe is often only shared with an heir.

steps: Pack the roots, barks, cinnamon and cloves into a clean glass jar.
Cover completely with the overproof rum and seal.
Leave in a dark place for at least three weeks, shaking the jar every few days.
Strain out the solids, stir in the honey until dissolved, and rebottle.
Serve in small measures at room temperature.

name: Fröccs
description: Wine and soda, with an entire naming system attached: the ratio decides what you call it, and Hungarians know every name.
funFact: The vocabulary is exact: kisfröccs is 1 wine to 1 soda, nagyfröccs 2 to 1, hosszúlépés 1 to 2, and a házmester is 3 wine to 2 soda. There are at least a dozen more.

steps: Chill both the wine and the soda water thoroughly.
Pour the wine into a tumbler.
Add the soda water, adjusting the ratio to the fröccs you want.
Serve immediately, traditionally without ice.

name: Puszta Cocktail
description: Apricot brandy, Unicum and dry vermouth — bitter, stone-fruit and herbal, named for the Hungarian plain.
funFact: Unicum has been made by the Zwack family since 1790 from over forty herbs, and the family smuggled the recipe out of Hungary during the communist period, brewing a placebo version at home in the meantime.

steps: Combine all three in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.

name: Brennivín og Appelsín
description: Iceland's caraway schnapps lengthened with local orange soda — the mid-winter compromise for people who do not want it neat.
funFact: Brennivín is nicknamed 'svarti dauði' — black death — for its black label, a hangover from the temperance era when Iceland required spirits to be sold in deliberately unappealing packaging.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the very cold Brennivín.
Top with orange soda.
Stir once and serve with an orange wedge.

name: Old Monk and Cola
description: India's dark vanilla-heavy rum with cola and lime. Sold on nostalgia and almost no advertising, and ordered in every Indian bar regardless.
funFact: Old Monk has barely advertised since it launched in 1954 and still sells on word of mouth alone — for decades it was among the largest-selling dark rums in the world.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum and the lime juice.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Urrak with Limca
description: The first distillation of cashew feni, cut with lemon soda, salt and a green chilli. Goa's summer drink, available for about three months a year.
funFact: Urrak only exists during the cashew season from March to May — it is feni stopped after the first distillation, and it cannot be stored, so Goans drink the whole supply in a single summer.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice and add the pinch of salt.
Pour in the urrak and the lime juice.
Top with cold Limca.
Drop in a slit green chilli and stir once.
Drink cold, in the shade.

name: Arak Madu
description: Balinese palm arak with honey and lime, over ice. Simple, floral and everywhere on the island once the sun goes down.
funFact: Balinese arak is distilled from palm sap or rice and is used in Hindu ceremony as well as at the beach bar — the ritual pouring of arak onto the ground precedes many temple offerings.

steps: Loosen the honey with a splash of warm water so it will mix.
Shake the arak, honey syrup and lime juice hard with ice.
Strain into a tumbler over fresh ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Hot Whiskey
description: Irish whiskey, boiling water, sugar, a lemon studded with cloves. Prescribed for colds, drunk for weather, effective for both.
funFact: Irish pubs serve it in a glass with a metal spoon left in — not for stirring, but to conduct heat away from the glass so it does not crack when the boiling water hits.

steps: Stud the lemon slice with the cloves and drop it into a heatproof glass.
Add the sugar and the whiskey.
Put a metal spoon in the glass, then pour in the boiling water.
Stir until the sugar dissolves and leave for a minute before drinking.

name: Irish Flag
description: Green, white and orange, layered in that order: crème de menthe, Irish cream, orange liqueur. Structurally demanding, spiritually simple.
funFact: The layering only holds if you pour in descending sugar density — and the Irish cream will curdle if it touches anything acidic, which is why the orange liqueur goes on top and never underneath.

steps: Pour the crème de menthe into the bottom of a shot glass.
Float the Irish cream over the back of a barspoon held against the glass.
Float the Grand Marnier the same way to finish the flag.
Serve immediately and drink in one.

name: Arak Grapefruit
description: Arak and fresh grapefruit juice over crushed ice — the drink Tel Aviv's Carmel Market bars pour faster than anything else.
funFact: It became the signature of Tel Aviv's market bars in the 2000s, poured into whatever glassware was to hand — the jam jar service was originally not a style choice.

steps: Fill a tumbler with crushed ice.
Pour in the arak — it will turn cloudy as it hits the ice.
Top with fresh grapefruit juice.
Stir once and slap a mint sprig between your palms before dropping it in.

name: Barbajada
description: Milan's forgotten winter drink: hot chocolate, coffee and whipped cream beaten together until foamy, with a shot of liqueur if the weather warrants.
funFact: Named for Domenico Barbaja, a nineteenth-century Milanese waiter who became one of Europe's most powerful opera impresarios — he invented the drink before he discovered Rossini.

steps: Make a thick hot chocolate and keep it hot.
Combine it with the hot espresso in a jug.
Whisk in the whipped cream vigorously until the whole thing is foamy.
Add the liqueur if using, pour into a warmed mug and dust with cocoa.

name: Barracuda
description: Gold rum, Galliano and pineapple, topped with prosecco. Tropical and Italian at once, and an official IBA drink since 2011.
funFact: It is one of the newer additions to the IBA list, and one of the only official cocktails that combines a tiki structure with an Italian sparkling wine top.

steps: Shake the rum, Galliano, pineapple juice and lime juice with ice.
Strain into a large glass over fresh ice.
Top with cold prosecco.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a lime wheel.

name: Bicicletta
description: Campari, white wine and soda — the low-proof afternoon drink named for how its drinkers wobbled home.
funFact: Northern Italian lore says it is named for the elderly regulars who cycled home from the bar afterwards, taking a somewhat scenic route.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add the Campari and the white wine.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir gently and garnish with an orange or lemon slice.

name: Caffè Corretto
description: An espresso 'corrected' with a shot of grappa or sambuca. Ordered at the bar, drunk standing, over in ninety seconds.
funFact: In some northern Italian bars you can order it 'separato' — the spirit arrives in its own glass so you can decide how much correction the coffee actually needs.

steps: Pull a fresh espresso into a warmed cup.
Add sugar if you take it, and stir.
Pour the grappa straight into the coffee.
Drink standing at the bar, immediately.

name: Milano-Torino
description: Campari and red vermouth, equal parts, over ice. The two-ingredient ancestor of the Americano and the Negroni both.
funFact: The name is geographic: Campari from Milan, Vermouth di Torino from Turin. Add soda and it becomes an Americano; add gin instead and you have a Negroni.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Add the Campari and the vermouth.
Stir for 15 seconds to chill and lightly dilute.
Garnish with an orange slice.

name: Rossini
description: Prosecco over fresh strawberry purée — the Bellini's red sibling from the same bar, named for the same kind of artist.
funFact: Harry's Bar in Venice named a whole family after Venetian painters and composers: peach makes a Bellini, strawberry a Rossini, pomegranate a Tintoretto, and mandarin a Puccini.

ingredients.amount: 1 barspoon, if the strawberries are tart

steps: Blend fresh strawberries and pass through a fine sieve to make a smooth purée.
Chill the purée thoroughly — a warm purée will kill the bubbles.
Pour the purée into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco, stirring gently with a barspoon as you pour.

name: Ve.n.to
description: Grappa shaken with chamomile-infused honey and lemon. Italy's own entry into the modern IBA canon, built to make grappa approachable.
funFact: The name plays on 'vento' — wind — and on the initials of the Veneto region; it was added to the IBA list in 2011 as a deliberate showcase for grappa, which had almost no cocktail presence.

steps: Infuse honey syrup with chamomile flowers by steeping them in warm syrup for 20 minutes, then strain.
Add the grappa, chamomile honey, lemon juice and apple juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a chamomile flower or a lemon twist.

name: Bob Marley
description: Red, gold and green in a shot glass — grenadine, banana liqueur and melon, layered so the flag holds. More about the pour than the palate.
funFact: The layers work because of sugar density: grenadine is heaviest and sinks, melon liqueur is lightest and floats — pour in the wrong order and you get a muddy brown shot.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of a shot glass.
Float the banana liqueur over the back of a barspoon so it settles on top of the grenadine.
Float the melon liqueur the same way to make the top layer.
Serve immediately without stirring.

name: Dirty Banana
description: A frozen banana milkshake that went to Negril and came back with rum and coffee liqueur. Resort poolside, distilled.
funFact: It is the default poolside order across Jamaica's north coast, and the reason most Jamaican hotel bars keep a dedicated blender running from mid-morning.

steps: Put the banana, milk, rum, coffee liqueur and banana liqueur into a blender.
Add the ice and blend until completely smooth.
Pour into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with a banana slice and a dusting of grated chocolate.

name: Planter's Punch
description: One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak — the rhyme that built Caribbean punch, poured long over crushed ice with nutmeg on top.
funFact: The rhyme predates the cocktail glass: 'one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak' appears in Caribbean sources from the 1800s and still governs rum punch across the islands.

steps: Combine the rum, lime juice, sugar syrup and water in a shaker with ice.
Shake briefly, about 8 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tall glass and top with more crushed ice.
Dash the Angostura over the top so it bleeds down through the ice.
Grate fresh nutmeg over the surface.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and an orange slice

name: Ting with a Sting
description: Jamaica's whole cocktail culture in two words: Ting grapefruit soda, white overproof rum, ice. The sting is not a metaphor.
funFact: Ting has been bottled in Jamaica since 1976 and is deliberately bitter; the 'sting' is traditionally Wray & Nephew White Overproof, which runs at 63% ABV.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the overproof rum and the lime juice.
Top with cold Ting.
Stir once and garnish with a grapefruit or lime wedge.

name: Bamboo
description: Dry sherry and dry vermouth, stirred cold with bitters. Low-proof, saline and quietly elegant — and one of the first great cocktails invented in Asia.
funFact: Created by Louis Eppinger at the Grand Hotel in Yokohama in the 1890s — decades before Japan's cocktail culture became famous, and still the best argument for sherry in a mixing glass.

steps: Combine the sherry, vermouth and both bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds — this drink is low-proof, so watch the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Lemon Sour
description: Shochu, soda and a whole lemon's worth of juice. Japan's izakaya default — and in Tokyo you often squeeze it yourself, at the table.
funFact: Some Tokyo izakayas serve a 'denki bran' style tabletop version with a frozen lemon half and a hand press, and others install taps that dispense the shochu-soda base directly.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice — the colder the better.
Add the shochu and the fresh lemon juice.
Top with well-chilled soda water.
Stir once, vertically, to preserve the carbonation.
Garnish with a lemon wheel or a squeezed half.

name: Million Dollar
description: Gin, vermouth, pineapple and egg white shaken to a thick foam. Eppinger's other Yokohama invention, and the one Somerset Maugham wrote about.
funFact: Maugham name-checked it in his Malayan stories, and the Raffles Hotel in Singapore served it long enough that both cities now claim it.

steps: Dry-shake all the ingredients without ice for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate a little nutmeg over the foam.

name: Umeshu Soda
description: Japanese plum liqueur lengthened with soda over ice. Sweet-tart, almond-scented, and the easiest drink in any Japanese fridge.
funFact: Umeshu is made by steeping unripe ume — closer to an apricot than a plum — in shochu with rock sugar; families still make it each June and the stone gives it a faint marzipan note.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the umeshu.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once gently and drop in a preserved ume if you have one.

name: Kumys
description: Fermented mare's milk, faintly fizzy and sharply sour. The steppe's oldest drink, and still poured for guests before anything else.
funFact: Herodotus described the Scythians making it 2,500 years ago; the fermentation is both alcoholic and lactic, which is why it fizzes and sours at the same time.

steps: Warm the fresh mare's milk to about 25°C.
Stir in the starter culture from a previous batch.
Churn or agitate the mixture repeatedly over one to two days — traditionally thousands of strokes.
Ferment until it turns sharp, slightly fizzy and faintly alcoholic.
Serve cool in wide bowls, offering the first cup to the guest.

name: Dawa
description: 'Medicine' in Swahili: vodka, honey and lime crushed together with a honey-coated wooden stick you keep stirring as you drink.
glassware: Rocks glass with a dawa stick
funFact: The dawa stick is dipped in honey and left in the glass — the drinker controls the sweetness by how much they stir it, which makes every Dawa slightly different by the last sip.

ingredients.amount: 1 tbsp, plus more for the stick

steps: Muddle the lime quarters with the sugar in a rocks glass.
Fill the glass with crushed ice.
Pour over the vodka.
Dip a wooden stick in honey and stand it in the glass.
Serve with the stick still in — the drinker stirs the honey in to taste.

name: Black Balsam and Blackcurrant
description: Riga's tar-black herbal bitters stirred into hot blackcurrant juice. Medicinal, warming, and the standard Latvian answer to a cold.
funFact: Riga Black Balsam has been made since 1752 from 24 botanicals and is bottled in ceramic; Catherine the Great is said to have recovered from an illness in Riga after drinking it, which the distillery has never stopped mentioning.

steps: Heat the blackcurrant juice until steaming but not boiling.
Pour into a glass mug and stir in the honey if using.
Add the Black Balsam and stir once.
Serve hot with a lemon slice.

name: Riga Black Magic
description: Black Balsam shaken with citrus and apple juice — the modern Riga bar's way of making 24 botanicals approachable.
funFact: Latvia's bar scene spent the 2010s reverse-engineering Black Balsam into something that did not taste like medicine, and apple juice turned out to be the ingredient that finally rounded it off.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a thin apple slice.

name: Arak Lemonade
description: Levantine arak lengthened with lemonade and mint — the anise softened into something you can drink through a Beirut summer.
funFact: Lebanese arak is distilled three times and aged in clay amphorae, and the mountain villages that make it argue about grape variety the way Burgundy argues about vineyards.

steps: Gently press the mint leaves in the bottom of a tall glass — bruise, do not shred.
Add the arak and lemon juice.
Fill with ice and top with cold lemonade.
Stir once and garnish with a mint sprig and a lemon wheel.

name: Planteur
description: The French Antilles' planter's punch: rhum agricole with mango, guava and passionfruit, softer and more perfumed than its English-speaking cousin.
funFact: Rhum agricole is distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, which is why a Planteur tastes grassy and vegetal where a Jamaican punch tastes of treacle.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice.
Shake for 10 seconds.
Pour into an ice-filled highball glass.
Grate nutmeg over the top and garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Cazuela
description: A clay bowl the size of your head, packed with citrus, tequila and grapefruit soda, drunk through straws by everyone at the table. Sonora's answer to the punch bowl.
funFact: The bowl is the point: cazuelas are served in unglazed or glazed earthenware that keeps the drink cold, and in Hermosillo the bar brings it with the fruit still floating and scissors to cut more.

steps: Rim a large clay cazuela with lime and chilli salt.
Squeeze the orange, lime and grapefruit wedges into the bowl and drop the spent wedges in.
Fill with ice and pour over the tequila.
Top with grapefruit soda and stir once with a long spoon.
Serve in the middle of the table with straws for everyone.
recipe.garnish: The squeezed fruit wedges, left floating

name: Charro Negro
description: The Cuba Libre's tequila-drinking cousin: blanco, cola, lime, salt on the rim if you're doing it properly. Jalisco's default order when the Paloma feels like too much work.
funFact: Named for the charro — the Mexican horseman — and 'negro' for the cola; in Jalisco cantinas it is often built straight into the bottle-sized 'vitrolero' glass and shared.

steps: Run a lime wedge around the rim of a highball glass and roll it in salt.
Fill the glass with ice cubes.
Add the tequila and lime juice.
Top with cold cola and stir once, gently, to combine.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on a salted rim

name: Chelada
description: Beer, lime, salt, ice. That's it — no tomato, no sauces, no debate. The Michelada stripped back to the two things that actually matter on a hot afternoon.
funFact: Mexicans distinguish sharply between chelada (lime and salt only) and michelada (with tomato juice and sauces); ordering the wrong one in Monterrey will get you corrected, politely.

steps: Rim a chilled schooner or pint glass with lime and salt.
Fill the glass with ice cubes.
Add the lime juice.
Pour the cold lager down the side of the glass to keep the head under control.
Garnish with a lime wedge and top up from the bottle as you drink.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on a salted rim

name: La Bandera
description: Not one glass but three: lime, tequila, sangrita — green, white, red, the flag on the bar top. Sip across them in any order and argue about it afterwards.
funFact: The order is a national argument: most drinkers go lime, tequila, sangrita, but purists insist sangrita comes last only to cleanse, never to chase — the tequila is meant to be sipped, not shot.

steps: Pour the lime juice into the first caballito, the tequila into the second, and the sangrita into the third.
Line the three glasses up left to right so they read green, white, red.
Serve at cool room temperature — never over ice, and never mixed.
Sip the tequila slowly, alternating with small sips of lime and sangrita.
recipe.garnish: None — the three colours are the garnish

name: Mexican Firing Squad
description: A 1930s Mexico City sour that Charles H. Baker wrote down and the world then forgot for seventy years: tequila, lime, grenadine, a hard lash of Angostura.
funFact: Baker recorded it at La Cucaracha bar in 1937 in his 'Gentleman's Companion', calling it a drink of 'considerable authority' — one of the earliest tequila cocktails documented in English.

steps: Add the tequila, lime juice, grenadine and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice.
Add a small splash of soda if you want it longer.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Mezcalita
description: The Margarita rebuilt on mezcal, which changes everything: the smoke arrives first, the lime cuts through it, and the agave finishes earthy rather than bright.
funFact: The rim is the tell: real Oaxacan service uses sal de gusano — salt ground with toasted agave worm and chilli — which tastes far better than its description suggests.

ingredients.item: Sal de gusano or chilli salt

steps: Rim a rocks glass with lime and sal de gusano, then set it aside.
Shake the mezcal, lime juice, agave syrup and orange liqueur hard with ice.
Strain into the rimmed glass over a large ice cube.
Garnish with a lime wheel and, if you have one, a dried chilli.

name: Submarino
description: A shot of tequila dropped, glass and all, into a beer. It sinks, it fizzes, it disappears — and then so does your evening.
glassware: Beer stein with a caballito inside
funFact: The same trick appears worldwide — Boilermaker in the US, U-Boot in Germany, Jägerbomb everywhere — but the Mexican version insists the submarine be tequila and the ocean be a light lager.

steps: Pour the beer into a large stein, leaving room at the top.
Fill a caballito shot glass with tequila.
Lower the shot glass carefully into the beer so it sinks upright.
Drink immediately, before the tequila fully diffuses.

name: Torito
description: Veracruz in a bottle: cane liquor whipped with condensed milk and fruit — peanut, guanabana, mango — until it drinks like a boozy milkshake with a suntan.
funFact: Toritos are sold from coolers along the Veracruz malecón in a dozen flavours; the peanut ('de cacahuate') version is the benchmark, and every vendor claims their abuela's ratio.

ingredients.item: Aguardiente de caña or white rum

steps: Add the milks and the peanut butter or fruit purée to a blender.
Pour in the cane spirit and add the ice.
Blend on high for about 30 seconds until completely smooth and frothy.
Pour into a chilled tumbler and serve immediately, before it separates.
Dust the top with ground cinnamon or crushed peanut.

name: Vampiro
description: Tequila, grapefruit soda and sangrita in one blood-red glass. Sweet, salty, citric and quietly spicy — the Paloma after it learned to bite.
funFact: The name means 'vampire' — for the colour, not the bite. It is the house drink of the bars around Tlaquepaque, where sangrita is made fresh daily and never contains tomato juice from a can.

steps: Rim a highball glass with lime and chilli salt, then fill it with ice.
Pour in the tequila, sangrita and lime juice.
Top with grapefruit soda.
Stir gently from the bottom once to marble the colours without fully mixing them.
Garnish with a lime wheel and an extra dusting of chilli salt.

name: Airag
description: Fermented mare's milk, sour and lightly effervescent. The drink of the steppe, offered to every guest who enters a ger.
funFact: Refusing the bowl outright is a serious discourtesy in Mongolia; the accepted compromise is to touch it to your lips and return it, which satisfies the custom.

ingredients.item: A leather khokhuur bag or wooden churn

steps: Pour the fresh mare's milk into the khokhuur with a cup of the previous batch as starter.
Churn it repeatedly throughout the day — traditionally a thousand strokes or more.
Let it ferment for one to three days, continuing to churn.
Taste until it is sour, faintly fizzy and lightly alcoholic.
Serve cool in a wide bowl, offered with the right hand.

name: Tongba
description: Fermented millet in a wooden pot, topped with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. Refill the water and keep going until it stops tasting of anything.
glassware: Wooden tongba pot with a bamboo straw
funFact: It belongs to the Limbu people of eastern Nepal, and the etiquette is specific: you top up the same millet with hot water several times, and it is impolite to stop after one.

ingredients.item: A wooden tongba pot and bamboo straw (pipsing)

steps: Pack the fermented millet into the wooden tongba pot.
Pour in hot — not boiling — water to cover.
Let it steep for about five minutes.
Sip through the perforated bamboo straw, which filters out the grain.
Top up with more hot water two or three times as you drink.

name: Kopstootje
description: 'Little head-butt': a tulip glass of jenever filled to the brim and a beer beside it. First sip taken bent over, hands behind your back.
glassware: Tulip glass and a beer glass
funFact: The jenever is poured to a convex meniscus, so the only way to take the first sip without spilling is to lean down to the glass — hands behind the back is the traditional form.

steps: Chill the jenever thoroughly and fill the tulip glass right to the brim.
Pour a cold pilsner alongside it.
Bend down to the jenever glass, hands behind your back, and take the first sip without lifting it.
Then pick up the glass, finish the jenever, and chase it with the beer.

name: L&P and Vodka
description: Lemon & Paeroa — New Zealand's own lemony mineral soda — lengthening a shot of vodka. 'World famous in New Zealand', as the bottle says.
funFact: L&P was originally made by mixing lemon juice with mineral water from a spring at Paeroa; the town has a giant L&P bottle on the main road, which is the country's most photographed soft-drink monument.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the vodka and the lemon juice.
Top with cold L&P.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wedge.

name: Macuá
description: Nicaragua's official national cocktail, decided by public contest: white rum, guava, lemon and orange, tropical without tipping into syrup.
funFact: In 2006 Nicaragua's tourism board ran a nationwide competition to name a national drink; the winner was submitted by a paediatrician from Granada, and the Macuá is named after a local bird.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake for about 12 seconds until the outside of the tin frosts.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Palm Wine
description: Sap tapped straight from the palm, fermenting as you carry it. Sweet in the morning, sour and sharp by evening — the clock is part of the drink.
funFact: Fermentation begins within hours of tapping, with no yeast added — the wild yeasts are already on the tree. A morning tapping is mild and sweet; the same container by nightfall is sour and considerably stronger.

steps: Tap the sap from the palm into a clean container — traditionally at dawn.
Leave it to ferment naturally; wild yeasts start work within a couple of hours.
Taste as it goes: sweet and lightly fizzy early, dry and sour by the end of the day.
Strain through cloth to remove debris.
Serve at ambient temperature, the same day it was tapped.

name: Karsk
description: Coffee and moonshine, measured by a coin: drop it in the cup, add coffee until it vanishes, add spirit until you see it again.
funFact: The coin trick is a genuine Trøndelag tradition, and the coffee is deliberately brewed weak so that the coin disappears early and the spirit measure ends up generous.

steps: Drop a clean coin into the bottom of a coffee cup.
Pour in weak coffee until the coin just disappears from view.
Add the spirit slowly until the coin becomes visible again.
Stir in sugar if you take it, and drink hot.

name: Seco con Leche
description: Panama's national spirit cut with milk over ice — sounds wrong, drinks like a cold, boozy horchata with a sugarcane backbone.
funFact: Seco Herrerano is triple-distilled from sugarcane and is Panama's national spirit; the milk serve — 'seco con leche' — is standard at interior festivals, especially during Carnaval.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Pour in the seco.
Top with cold whole milk.
Stir gently until the glass frosts, and serve straight away.

name: Caña con Ruda
description: Cane spirit steeped with rue, drunk in one shot on the first of August. Bitter, herbal and, by tradition, obligatory.
funFact: Guaraní tradition holds that a shot of caña con ruda on an empty stomach on August 1 wards off the illnesses of the coming winter; the custom is shared with Argentina and Uruguay.

steps: Wash and dry the rue sprig thoroughly.
Push it into the bottle of caña and seal.
Leave to macerate for at least a week — traditionally from the previous winter.
On the morning of August 1, pour a single shot and drink it on an empty stomach.
Do not drink more than three: the tradition is specific about this.

name: Clericó
description: White wine and chopped summer fruit, chilled hard. Sangria's lighter South American cousin, and Christmas dinner across the Southern Cone.
funFact: Because Christmas falls in high summer in Paraguay, the festive drink is served ice cold with fruit — the name traces back to the English 'claret cup' by way of Spanish.

ingredients.item: Mixed fruit (peach, apple, orange, grape), diced

steps: Toss the diced fruit with the sugar and leave for an hour.
Pour over the white wine and refrigerate for at least four hours.
Top with soda water just before serving.
Serve very cold, spooning plenty of fruit into each glass.

name: Algarrobina
description: Pisco with carob syrup, condensed milk and egg — dark, sweet and faintly smoky, Peru's dessert cocktail and reputed aphrodisiac.
funFact: Algarrobina is boiled down from the pods of the Peruvian carob tree that grows in the northern deserts; Peruvians credit it, without much evidence and with great confidence, with restorative powers.

steps: Add the pisco, algarrobina, condensed milk and egg yolk to a blender.
Add the ice and blend until thick and uniform.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Drizzle a little extra algarrobina over the surface and dust with cinnamon.

name: Capitán
description: The Peruvian Manhattan: pisco and red vermouth, stirred cold. Sipped in the highlands where the nights get serious.
funFact: It belongs to Puno and the Peruvian Andes, where army officers — the 'capitanes' of the name — are credited with the habit of cutting pisco with vermouth against the cold.

steps: Add the pisco, vermouth and bitters to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 to 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry or a lemon twist.

name: Chilcano
description: Peru's everyday pisco drink: pisco, ginger ale, lime and bitters over ice. Lighter than a Pisco Sour and far easier to make ten of.
funFact: Peru holds a national Semana del Chilcano every January; the drink descends from the 'chilcano de pescado', a fish broth once drunk as a hangover cure in the port of Chilca.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the pisco and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Dash the Angostura over the surface.
Stir once gently and garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Machu Picchu
description: Green, yellow and red in one tall glass, layered to look like the mountain at sunrise. A tourist drink Cusco has fully embraced.
funFact: It exists almost entirely for the photograph — but Cusco's bars have made it well enough for long enough that it has become a genuine local order.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of a tall glass.
Fill the glass carefully with crushed ice to hold the layers apart.
Shake the pisco with the orange juice and pour slowly over the ice.
Float the crème de menthe on top over the back of a spoon.
Serve with a straw and let the drinker mix it themselves.

name: Gin Pom
description: Ginebra San Miguel with powdered pomelo juice and ice. Cheap, sharp and the most-drunk gin serve in the world's biggest gin market.
funFact: The Philippines drinks more gin than any other country on earth, almost all of it Ginebra San Miguel — and most of that is mixed with a sachet of powdered juice costing a few pesos.

steps: Dissolve the powdered drink mix in the cold water in a pitcher.
Add the gin and stir well.
Pour over ice into tall glasses.
Serve with a calamansi wedge if you have one.

name: Weng Weng
description: Every white spirit on the shelf plus whisky, orange juice and grenadine. Named for the noise your head makes afterwards.
funFact: 'Weng weng' is Filipino for dizzy or spinning; the drink is a Boracay beach-bar institution, and most bars cap the order at two per person.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add all five spirits.
Top with orange juice and stir.
Pour the grenadine down the inside of the glass so it sinks to the bottom.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Mad Dog
description: Vodka, raspberry syrup and Tabasco layered into one shot. Sweet, then red, then suddenly very hot. Polish student legend.
funFact: 'Wściekły pies' is a staple of Polish student bars, where the layering matters: the syrup sinks, the Tabasco floats, and the burn arrives a beat after the sweetness.

steps: Pour the raspberry syrup into the bottom of a shot glass.
Layer the vodka carefully over it with a barspoon.
Dash the Tabasco on top so it sits on the surface.
Drink in one — sipping it is a mistake people only make once.

name: Tatanka
description: Bison grass vodka and cloudy apple juice. Tastes like apple pie and freshly cut hay, which is a stranger compliment than it sounds.
funFact: Also called a Szarlotka, after the Polish apple cake. Żubrówka is flavoured with a blade of bison grass from the Białowieża Forest, and each bottle traditionally contains one.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the Żubrówka.
Top with cold cloudy apple juice.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice and a light dusting of cinnamon.

name: Nikita
description: Beer, pineapple, white wine and vanilla ice cream, blended. It should be a disaster. Madeira has been proving otherwise since the eighties.
funFact: Named after the Elton John song 'Nikita', which was in the charts when a Câmara de Lobos bar owner first blended it in the mid-1980s.

steps: Put the pineapple, ice cream and white wine into a blender.
Add the beer last, to control the foam.
Blend briefly — just enough to combine, or it will overflow.
Pour into a tall glass and serve with a spoon and a straw.

name: Poncha
description: Madeiran cane spirit muddled with honey and lemon using a wooden 'caralhinho'. Sweet, sharp and much stronger than it lets on.
funFact: The stirring tool — a ridged wooden stick called a caralhinho — is specific to Madeira, and the fishermen's original version was drunk as a cold remedy before going out in the morning.

steps: Put the honey and lemon juice into a small tumbler or a jug.
Work them together with a wooden stick or muddler until the honey fully dissolves.
Add the aguardente and the orange juice if using.
Stir vigorously until frothy and serve at room temperature, without ice.

name: Porto Tónico
description: White port and tonic over ice with mint. Portugal's answer to the Gin and Tonic, and arguably the better summer drink.
funFact: Port houses pushed it hard in the 2010s to sell white port, which had been the least-loved category in the Douro — it worked so well it is now the default aperitif in Porto.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the chilled white port.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once gently and garnish with a mint sprig and an orange slice.

name: Bilí
description: Vieques in a bottle: pitorro steeped for months with quenepas, cinnamon and sugar until the moonshine turns sweet, fruity and deceptively smooth.
funFact: Bilí is a Vieques speciality made with quenepas (Spanish limes) and is traditionally buried or hidden to age — families open bottles at Christmas that were sealed the previous summer.

steps: Put the peeled quenepas, cinnamon, sugar and vanilla into a large sealable jar.
Cover with the pitorro and seal tightly.
Store somewhere dark and cool for at least two months, turning the jar occasionally.
Strain into bottles, leaving the fruit behind.
Serve chilled in small measures.

name: Chichaíto
description: Two ingredients, no mercy: pitorro and anisette, shaken with ice and served cold enough to hide how strong it is.
funFact: A staple of Puerto Rican Christmas parrandas, where it is carried house to house in a bottle kept in the freezer — the sugar content stops it from freezing solid.

steps: Combine the pitorro and anisette in a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds to chill and slightly dilute.
Strain into chilled shot glasses.
Serve immediately, ice cold.

name: Coco Loco
description: Served in the coconut it was made from: rum, coconut cream and whatever tropical juice is closest to hand, blended into holiday shorthand.
funFact: The 'loco' is usually the pour — beach vendors from Luquillo to Loíza free-pour three spirits into the same coconut and stop when it looks about right.

steps: Cut the top off a young coconut and pour the water into a blender.
Add the rums, coconut cream, pineapple juice, lime and crushed ice.
Blend until smooth and slushy.
Pour back into the coconut shell and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Pineapple wedge and a paper umbrella

name: Țuică Fiartă
description: Plum brandy heated with sugar and peppercorns until it steams. Romanian winter, taken standing outside in it.
funFact: The sugar is caramelised in the pan before the țuică goes in, which is what gives it the amber colour; the peppercorns are traditional and genuinely change the finish.

steps: Melt the sugar in a small pan over low heat until it just caramelises.
Add the peppercorns and cinnamon and stir for a few seconds.
Pour in the țuică carefully — it will spit — and warm it through without boiling.
Serve hot in small heatproof glasses.

name: Sbiten
description: Honey, spices and herbs simmered together and spiked — Russia's hot drink of choice for four centuries before tea arrived and took over.
funFact: Sbiten was street food in imperial Russia, sold from insulated copper samovar-like urns carried on the back; it was displaced almost entirely by tea in the nineteenth century.

steps: Bring the water and honey to a simmer, skimming any foam that rises.
Add the ginger, cinnamon, cloves and mint and simmer for 15 minutes.
Strain out the solids.
Stir in the wine or vodka off the heat if you want it alcoholic.
Serve very hot in mugs.

name: Yorsh
description: Vodka poured into beer. Named after a spiny river fish, and about as gentle as one.
funFact: The name comes from the ruffe, a small bristly fish — Russian drinkers use it as a warning label, since the mix is notorious for arriving all at once.

steps: Pour the beer into a mug, leaving room at the top.
Add the vodka directly to the beer.
Stir once, or drop the shot glass in whole for the theatrical version.
Drink promptly.

name: Bambus
description: Red wine and cola, half and half, over ice. Beloved across the Balkans and defended fiercely by everyone who drinks it.
funFact: The Balkan bambus predates Spain's kalimotxo in local memory by decades, and the two regions have never agreed on who got there first.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the red wine.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and add a lemon slice if you want it sharper.

name: Tatratea Hot
description: Slovakia's herbal tea liqueur, served hot with honey and lemon. Comes in strengths from 22% to 72%, colour-coded by how serious you are.
funFact: The bottles are numbered by ABV — 32, 42, 52, 62, 72 — and the 72% 'Outlaw' edition exists mostly so that people can say they have had it.

steps: Put the honey and lemon slice in a warmed glass mug.
Add the hot water and stir until the honey dissolves.
Pour in the Tatratea and stir once.
Serve hot, with the lemon left in.

name: Dom Pedro
description: Vanilla ice cream blended with whisky or Amarula until it pours. On every South African dessert menu, and ordered by adults without embarrassment.
funFact: It appears on South African menus far more often than it does anywhere else on earth, and ordering one 'with Kahlúa' rather than whisky is a legitimate regional variation.

steps: Let the ice cream soften for a few minutes so it blends smoothly.
Put the ice cream, spirit and cream in a blender.
Blend briefly — you want it thick and pourable, not liquid.
Pour into a wine glass and dust with grated chocolate or nutmeg.
Serve with both a spoon and a straw.

name: Klippies en Coke
description: Klipdrift brandy and Coke, poured heavy. South Africa drinks more brandy-and-cola per head than almost anywhere, and this is why.
funFact: South African brandy is legally required to be pot-still aged at least three years for the premium grades — a rigour largely wasted on a drink that is then filled to the top with cola.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the brandy.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and add a lemon wedge if you like.

name: Springbokkie
description: Green over cream, in the colours of the national rugby jersey: crème de menthe under a float of Amarula. Poured in vast quantities on match day.
funFact: Amarula is made from the fruit of the marula tree, which elephants are famously — and mostly apocryphally — said to get drunk on after eating the fallen fruit.

steps: Pour the crème de menthe into a shot glass.
Float the Amarula over the back of a barspoon so it sits in a clean layer.
Serve immediately, before the layers start to bleed.
Drink in one.

name: Makgeolli
description: Unfiltered rice brew, milky and lightly fizzing, poured from the bottle into a shallow bowl. Korea's oldest drink and its most farmhouse.
funFact: Nuruk — a wild-yeast and mould starter cake — does the work that malting does for beer, breaking down the rice starch; makgeolli is traditionally drunk after farm work, and increasingly after rain, by tradition.

steps: Steam the rice and cool it to room temperature.
Mix the rice with the crumbled nuruk and the water in a clean crock.
Cover with cloth and ferment at room temperature for about a week, stirring daily.
Strain through cloth, pressing lightly — makgeolli is meant to stay cloudy.
Refrigerate, and shake the bottle before pouring into shallow bowls.

name: Somaek
description: Soju dropped into beer, in a ratio people argue about seriously. Korea's most-poured mixed drink, and the engine of the company dinner.
glassware: Beer glass and a soju shot glass
funFact: The golden ratio is contested — three parts beer to one soju is the common baseline, and there are Korean drinking games devoted entirely to pouring it correctly.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass, leaving room at the top.
Add the soju — either poured in or dropped in the shot glass whole.
Cover the top with your palm and tap the glass once on the table to mix it.
Drink promptly, while it is still fizzing.

name: Yogurt Soju
description: Soju, Yakult and lemon-lime soda. Tastes like a children's drink, disappears like one, and is not one.
funFact: Yakult has been sold in Korea since 1971 and is delivered door to door by the 'Yakult ajumma'; the cocktail is the reason Korean convenience stores stock it next to the soju.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the soju and the Yakult.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and serve immediately — it separates if it sits.

name: Agua de Valencia
description: Cava, orange juice, gin and vodka in a jug. Tastes like a Mimosa, behaves like something else entirely.
funFact: Invented at Café Madrid in Valencia in 1959, when a group of Basque regulars kept ordering 'Agua de Bilbao' — the house sparkling wine — and the barman offered them a Valencian alternative made with local oranges.

steps: Stir the sugar into the orange juice in a large jug until dissolved.
Add the gin and vodka and stir again.
Top with cold cava and stir once, gently.
Serve immediately in wine glasses over a little ice.
Make it in front of people — half the drink is the theatre of the jug.

name: Leche de Pantera
description: 'Panther's milk': gin or rum, condensed milk and cinnamon, shaken cold. Spanish Legion issue, now a Madrid dive-bar staple.
funFact: The recipe is traditionally attributed to the Spanish Legion, whose founder Millán-Astray is said to have served it to recruits — the modern Madrid version usually swaps the original brandy for gin.

steps: Add the gin, condensed milk, milk and cinnamon to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds until thick and cold.
Strain into a chilled tumbler.
Dust with more cinnamon and serve very cold.

name: Queimada
description: Orujo set alight in a clay bowl with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel while somebody reads a spell over it. Galicia does not do this ironically.
funFact: The conxuro — the incantation read while it burns — invokes the meigas, Galician witches, and asks them to leave. The ritual is old-looking but was largely written in the 1950s.

steps: Pour the orujo into a wide clay bowl and add most of the sugar, the coffee beans and the lemon peel.
Put a ladleful of orujo and the remaining sugar into a separate ladle and set it alight.
Lower the burning ladle into the bowl to ignite the whole surface.
Stir with the ladle, lifting burning liquid and pouring it back, for several minutes until the flame turns low and blue.
Cover to extinguish, then serve hot in small clay cups.

name: Rebujito
description: Manzanilla sherry lengthened with lemon-lime soda over crushed ice — the drink that keeps Seville upright through a week of Feria.
funFact: It is drunk by the jug at the Feria de Abril in Seville and the Feria del Caballo in Jerez, where the sherry comes from — and where sherry purists have made their peace with it.

steps: Fill a tall glass with crushed ice.
Pour in the cold manzanilla.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and add a mint sprig if you like.
Drink fast — it dies as the ice melts.

name: Sol y Sombra
description: 'Sun and shade': brandy and anís in equal parts, no ice. A Spanish breakfast that predates any conversation about moderation.
funFact: The name comes from the bullring, where seats are priced by whether they sit in sun or shade; the drink mixes the dark brandy and the clear anís the same way.

steps: Pour the brandy and the anís into a small tumbler.
Stir once to combine.
Serve at room temperature, without ice.
Traditionally taken standing at the bar, with coffee.

name: Vermut
description: Red vermouth on ice with a splash of soda, an olive and a slice of orange. Sunday noon in Barcelona has a drink and this is it.
funFact: 'Fer el vermut' — to do the vermouth — is a whole social occasion in Catalonia, held late on Sunday morning, and the best bars still draw their vermouth from the barrel.

steps: Fill a tumbler with ice.
Pour in the cold red vermouth.
Add a short splash of soda.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice and a skewered olive.
Serve with crisps and tinned seafood, if you are doing it properly.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a green olive

name: Arrack and Ginger Beer
description: Ceylon coconut arrack with ginger beer and lime — the island's standing highball, and better than it has any right to be.
funFact: Ceylon arrack is distilled from fermented coconut flower sap, tapped by climbers who move between palm crowns on ropes — a job with its own hereditary caste of specialists.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the arrack and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Glögg
description: Nordic mulled wine with raisins and blanched almonds waiting at the bottom of the cup — you drink it, then eat it with a spoon.
glassware: Small mug or glass with a handle
funFact: Cardamom is the marker that separates Nordic glögg from German Glühwein, and the spoon is not optional — the raisins and almonds are considered part of the serving.

steps: Warm the wine with the sugar, spices and orange peel to about 70°C and hold for 30 minutes; do not boil.
Strain out the whole spices.
Put a spoonful of raisins and almonds into the bottom of each mug.
Add the aquavit to the pot off the heat, then ladle over the raisins and almonds.
Serve hot with a small spoon.
recipe.garnish: Raisins and slivered almonds in the cup

name: Grogg
description: Swedish shorthand for spirit plus mixer, poured strong: whisky or vodka with soda or cola, and no further ceremony.
funFact: The Swedish 'grogg' descends from British naval grog — watered rum named after Admiral Vernon's grogram coat — but travelled north and lost the rum along the way.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the spirit.
Top with cold soda water or cola.
Stir once and serve, with a lemon wedge if using soda.

name: Kafi Fertig
description: Coffee with schnapps, served in a stemmed glass so you can see the colour. Swiss farmhouse fuel with a colour code all its own.
funFact: In parts of central Switzerland the strength is judged by colour: it should be dark enough that a coin dropped in the glass disappears, and no darker.

steps: Put the sugar in a small stemmed glass.
Pour in the hot coffee and stir until dissolved.
Add the schnapps and stir once more.
Serve hot, in the glass, never in a cup.

name: Boba Cocktail
description: Milk tea, rum and tapioca pearls in a shaker. Taipei's bars took the island's most famous export and put a wide straw in it.
glassware: Tall glass with a wide straw
funFact: Bubble tea was invented in Taichung in the 1980s; Taipei's cocktail bars started spiking it in the 2010s, and the brown-sugar version is now a fixture across East Asian bar menus.

steps: Cook the tapioca pearls and toss them in a little brown sugar syrup while still warm.
Spoon the pearls into the bottom of a tall glass.
Shake the rum, cooled tea, milk and remaining syrup hard with ice.
Strain over the pearls and add fresh ice.
Serve with a wide boba straw.
recipe.garnish: Brown sugar syrup streaked down the glass

name: Konyagi and Tonic
