description: Tanzania's own clear spirit with tonic and lime — light, faintly sweet, and poured on every Dar es Salaam terrace at sunset.
funFact: Konyagi occupies an odd legal space — it is bottled at 35% and labelled as a spirit rather than a gin, though it drinks like a light, sweetened one.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the Konyagi and lime juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Thai Bucket
description: Thai rum, Red Bull and cola in a child's sand bucket with several straws. Structurally a punch, spiritually a warning.
funFact: Thai Red Bull — Krating Daeng — is uncarbonated, sweeter and more heavily caffeinated than the export version, which is a meaningful part of why the buckets have the reputation they do.

steps: Fill a small plastic bucket with ice.
Pour in the half-bottle of Sangsom.
Add the bottle of Thai Red Bull.
Top with cola and stir with a straw.
Share it — the bucket is designed for four straws, not one.

name: Sorrel
description: Christmas red: hibiscus calyces steeped with clove, ginger and orange peel, sweetened and cut with rum. Tart, spiced and unmistakably festive.
funFact: The sorrel plant is a hibiscus relative that fruits right at Christmas across the Caribbean, which is precisely why the drink became a December tradition from Trinidad to Jamaica.

steps: Put the sorrel, ginger, cloves and orange peel in a large heatproof jug.
Pour over the boiling water, cover, and leave to steep for at least 12 hours.
Strain out the solids and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Add the rum to taste and refrigerate.
Serve very cold over ice.

name: Boukha and Orange
description: Tunisian fig brandy over ice with fresh orange juice — dry, faintly floral, and the standard way to serve boukha long.
funFact: Boukha has been distilled from Mediterranean figs in Tunisia since the nineteenth century; unlike most fruit brandies it carries no added sugar, which is why it drinks surprisingly dry.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the boukha.
Top with fresh orange juice.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice.

name: Aslan Sütü
description: 'Lion's milk': rakı and cold water in equal parts, which turns it milky white. Sipped slowly over a long table of meze, never rushed.
funFact: The order matters: rakı first, then water, then ice — adding ice before water shocks the anise oils and leaves the drink cloudy in the wrong way. Turks call the milky effect the louche, and drinking it fast is considered poor form.

steps: Pour the rakı into a tall narrow glass, filling it about a third.
Add cold water in roughly equal measure and watch it turn opaque white.
Only now drop in one or two ice cubes.
Sip slowly alongside white cheese, melon and meze — rakı is a meal-length drink.
recipe.garnish: None — the meze is the garnish

name: Waragi and Tonic
description: Uganda's juniper-flavoured banana spirit, lengthened with tonic and lime. Sharper and drier than the gin it is usually compared to.
funFact: The name comes from 'war gin', from the colonial era; commercial Uganda Waragi is distilled from bananas or cassava and then flavoured with juniper, which makes it gin-adjacent rather than gin.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the waragi and lime juice.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Horilka z Pertsem
description: Ukrainian vodka steeped with chilli and honey. Sweet at the front, hot at the back, drunk cold with something salted.
funFact: It is traditionally taken with salo — cured pork fat — on dark bread, a pairing that sounds unlikely and works because the fat blunts the burn.

steps: Put the chillies and peppercorns into a bottle of horilka.
Add the honey and shake until it dissolves.
Leave to infuse for three to seven days, tasting as you go — chillies work fast.
Strain out the solids once it is hot enough for you.
Serve ice cold in shot glasses.

name: Angel Face
description: Equal parts gin, apricot brandy and calvados. Three spirits, no citrus, and a name that undersells it considerably.
funFact: It appears in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book with no story attached — one of many equal-parts drinks from that era that survive on balance alone.

steps: Add all three spirits to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an apple slice or a lemon twist.

name: Atholl Brose
description: Oatmeal steeped in water, strained, then stirred with honey, cream and whisky. A Highland recipe old enough to have won a battle.
funFact: Legend holds that the Earl of Atholl put down a Highland rebellion in 1475 by filling his enemy's well with the mixture and capturing him while he was drinking it.

steps: Soak the oatmeal in the water for at least six hours, then strain through muslin, pressing to extract the creamy liquid.
Discard the oats and stir the honey into the oat liquid until dissolved.
Whisk in the whisky.
Fold in the lightly whipped cream just before serving.
Serve chilled in small glasses; it keeps a couple of days in the fridge.

name: Black Velvet
description: Stout and champagne, poured half and half so the black sits under the gold. Invented for a funeral and never quite shook the mood.
funFact: Created at Brooks's Club in London in 1861 after Prince Albert's death, when the steward decided even the champagne should be in mourning.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the stout and the champagne well.
Pour the stout into a tall glass and let the head settle.
Pour the champagne slowly over the back of a spoon to layer it on top.
Serve immediately, while the two are still separate.

name: Buck's Fizz
description: Two parts champagne to one part orange juice — the older, stronger, more London answer to the Mimosa, and the two have been arguing ever since.
funFact: Created at the Buck's Club in Mayfair in 1921 by barman Malachy McGarry, three years before the Mimosa appeared at the Ritz Paris — the difference is the ratio, and Londoners will tell you so.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the champagne and the orange juice thoroughly.
Pour the orange juice into a flute first.
Top slowly with champagne, tilting the glass to preserve the bubbles.
Do not stir — the pour mixes it.

name: John Collins
description: The Tom Collins made with whiskey instead of gin — lemon, sugar, soda, tall and cold. The original of the family, depending who you ask.
funFact: John Collins was the head waiter at Limmer's Hotel in London in the early 1800s; the gin version took his colleague's name, and the two have been confused with each other ever since.

steps: Shake the whiskey, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Paradise
description: Gin, apricot brandy and orange juice. Simple, apricot-forward and one of the few Savoy-era drinks that needs no adjustment at all.
funFact: Apricot brandy in these recipes means an apricot liqueur, not a distilled eau-de-vie — a distinction that ruins the drink for anyone who buys the wrong bottle.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

name: Pink Gin
description: Navy strength gin stained pink with Angostura and nothing else. Two ingredients, no ice, no apology.
funFact: Angostura was issued to Royal Navy officers as a stomach remedy; mixing it into the gin ration was the medicinal excuse that turned into an institution, and Plymouth Gin still trades on the association.

steps: Dash the Angostura into a chilled coupe and roll it around to coat the inside.
Discard any excess bitters, or leave them in for a stronger version.
Stir the gin over ice for 20 seconds, or serve it neat and cold from the freezer.
Strain into the coated coupe and serve without garnish.

name: Russian Spring Punch
description: Dick Bradsell's long, fizzing sour: vodka, crème de cassis, lemon and champagne over crushed ice. Modern London's house punch.
funFact: Bradsell — who also gave the world the Espresso Martini and the Bramble — created it in the 1980s at the Soho Brasserie, and it remains the drink London bartenders make when they want to show off without saying so.

steps: Shake the vodka, cassis, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a tall glass packed with crushed ice.
Top with champagne and stir gently once.
Add more crushed ice to cap the glass and garnish with berries and a lemon slice.
recipe.garnish: Fresh berries and a lemon slice

name: Snakebite
description: Lager and cider, half and half, with a shot of blackcurrant if you want it purple. The most-refused drink in British pubs.
funFact: Many British pubs refuse to serve it, citing an urban myth about the mix being unusually intoxicating — the real reason is that it is cheap, strong and popular with students.

steps: Pour the cider into a pint glass first.
Add the lager slowly at an angle to keep the foam down.
Add a dash of blackcurrant cordial if making a Snakebite and Black.
Do not stir.

name: Snowball
description: Advocaat and lemonade with a squeeze of lime — a yellow, foamy relic of the British Christmas drinks trolley that refuses to die.
funFact: Advocaat is Dutch, but the Snowball is entirely British — a 1960s Christmas fixture that has been ironically revived so many times it is now simply back.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the advocaat and lime cordial.
Top with lemonade and stir briskly until the drink foams pale yellow.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry and, if you are committing to it, a slice of orange.

name: Treacle
description: An Old Fashioned with a float of apple juice on top. Bradsell again, and one of the few modern riffs the classicists never argued with.
funFact: Bradsell built it at the Player in Soho as a rum Old Fashioned, then floated cloudy apple juice over the top — the apple reads as freshness on the nose and disappears entirely by the second sip.

steps: Stir the rum, sugar syrup and bitters over ice until chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Float the apple juice gently over the top so it sits as a distinct layer.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Whisky Mac
description: Scotch and green ginger wine, in equal measure, no ice. The drink Scotland reaches for when the weather turns properly hostile.
funFact: Named for Colonel Hector Macdonald, and traditionally made with Stone's Ginger Wine — a British fortified ginger wine that has been made since 1740 and exists almost solely for this purpose.

steps: Pour the Scotch and the ginger wine into a small tumbler.
Stir briefly to combine.
Serve at room temperature — ice is considered a mistake.
Drink beside something warm.

name: White Lady
description: Gin, triple sec and lemon, shaken with egg white to a dense pale foam. The Sidecar's gin cousin, and quietly one of the best.
funFact: Harry MacElhone first made it with crème de menthe in 1919, then rebuilt it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929 — the second version is the one that survived.

steps: Dry-shake all the ingredients without ice for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before garnishing with a lemon twist.

name: Wibble
description: Gin, sloe gin, grapefruit and lemon — pink, brambly and named for what it does to your legs, not your speech.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it at The Player and said the name came from the fact that 'it makes you wibble, not wobble' — sloe gin was deeply unfashionable at the time and the drink helped rescue it.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Alaska
description: Gin and yellow Chartreuse, stirred cold. Two ingredients, and the Chartreuse does exactly as much work as you would expect.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book insists that 'so far as can be ascertained this delectable potion is NOT the staple diet of the Esquimaux' — which is roughly all anyone knows about the name.

steps: Combine the gin, Chartreuse and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Between the Sheets
description: A Sidecar with rum added — cognac, rum, triple sec and lemon. Prohibition-era, and it does not pretend to be gentle.
funFact: The name is usually credited to Harry MacElhone at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, though the drink appears in American sources around the same time — it is a Sidecar with the volume turned up.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and discard.

name: Bijou
description: 'Jewel': gin, green Chartreuse and sweet vermouth — diamond, emerald and ruby, in equal parts, as the name intends.
funFact: Harry Johnson's 1900 recipe explains the name directly: the gin is the diamond, the Chartreuse the emerald and the vermouth the ruby — three jewels in one glass.

steps: Combine everything in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry and a lemon twist.

name: Blue Blazer
description: Burning whisky poured between two mugs in a long arc of fire. Jerry Thomas's showpiece, and still the most dangerous thing on any menu.
funFact: Thomas performed it at the El Dorado in gold-rush San Francisco with silver mugs he had made specially; he advised practising with cold water first, which remains excellent advice.

ingredients.item: Two heatproof metal mugs with handles

steps: Warm both metal mugs. Put the whisky in one and the boiling water in the other.
Clear the area of anything flammable, then set the whisky alight.
Pour the burning whisky into the second mug, then back again, in a long steady stream — four or five passes.
Cover to extinguish the flame, stir in the sugar, and pour into a heatproof glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist. Practise with cold water before you ever light it.

name: Boilermaker
description: A shot of whiskey and a beer. Drop the shot in, or drink them side by side — the argument is older than most bars.
glassware: Beer glass and a shot glass
funFact: The name comes from the industrial workers who drank them after shifts; purists insist the shot is drunk beside the beer, not dropped into it — dropping it makes a Depth Charge.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass and let the head settle.
Pour the whiskey into a separate shot glass.
Either drink the shot and chase it with the beer, or drop the shot glass in whole.
Do not overthink it.

name: Bronx
description: Gin, both vermouths and orange juice — a Perfect Martini with juice in it. Once the third most-ordered cocktail in America.
funFact: Created at the Waldorf-Astoria around 1906 and named after the Bronx Zoo; barman Johnnie Solon said he was inspired by the strange animals people claimed to see after drinking.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

name: Brooklyn
description: The Manhattan's overlooked sibling: rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and Amer Picon. Drier, more bitter, and far harder to find.
funFact: It languished for a century largely because Amer Picon was reformulated and became unavailable in the US — the modern revival relies on substitutes like Amaro CioCiaro or Bigallet China-China.

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.

name: Cable Car
description: A spiced-rum Sidecar with a cinnamon-sugar rim, invented at the top of a San Francisco hotel and served by the thousand.
funFact: Tony Abou-Ganim built it in 1996 for the Starlight Room on the 21st floor of the Sir Francis Drake Hotel, and it became one of the few 1990s hotel-bar drinks to survive the cocktail revival with its reputation intact.

steps: Rim a coupe with lemon and cinnamon sugar, then chill it.
Shake the rum, curaçao, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Double-strain into the rimmed coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
recipe.garnish: Orange twist on a cinnamon-sugar rim

name: Casino
description: Old Tom gin, maraschino, orange bitters and lemon. Sharp, floral and considerably drier than the ingredient list suggests.
funFact: Maraschino is distilled from whole Marasca cherries — stones, stems and all — which is why it tastes nutty and dry rather than like the syrup in a jar of cocktail cherries.

ingredients.item: Old Tom or London dry gin

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry and a lemon twist.

name: Eggnog
description: Eggs, cream, sugar and spirit, whisked thick and dusted with nutmeg. Every American December, and better if you make it months early.
funFact: Aged eggnog is a real practice — the alcohol sterilises the mixture, and batches left in the fridge for a year develop a smooth, almost cheese-like complexity. Food scientists have tested this and it holds up.

steps: Whisk the egg yolks with the sugar until pale and thick.
Slowly whisk in the milk and cream.
Whisk in the bourbon and rum — add the spirit gradually or the eggs will seize.
Refrigerate for at least a day; a month is better, a year is better still.
Serve cold in small cups with plenty of grated nutmeg.

name: French Connection
description: Cognac and amaretto, equal parts, over ice. Two ingredients, no dilution to speak of, and a name borrowed from a car chase.
funFact: Named after the 1971 film; it belongs to a family of two-ingredient duos — Godfather with Scotch, Godmother with vodka, French Connection with cognac — that were the whole of 1970s bartending in some hotels.

steps: Put a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Pour over the cognac and the amaretto.
Stir gently for 10 seconds.
Serve with no garnish — or a lemon twist if the amaretto is very sweet.

name: Godfather
description: Scotch and amaretto over a big cube. The smoke and the marzipan should fight, and instead they get on.
funFact: Legend attaches it to Marlon Brando and the 1972 film, which is almost certainly marketing — but Disaronno has never had any reason to correct the record.

steps: Put a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Add the Scotch and the amaretto.
Stir gently for 10 seconds to chill without over-diluting.
Serve with an orange twist if you want to lift it.

name: Golden Dream
description: Galliano, triple sec, orange juice and cream, shaken to a pale gold froth. Unapologetically of its decade.
funFact: Galliano's tall bottle was designed to stand out on a back bar and is named after an Italian hero of the Abyssinian war; the 1970s put it in almost everything, including this.

steps: Add all four ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds — the cream needs the work.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish, or dust with nutmeg.

name: Greenpoint
description: Rye, yellow Chartreuse and sweet vermouth — the Brooklyn neighbourhood series' best entry, and the one that stuck.
funFact: Milk & Honey's bartenders named a series of drinks after Brooklyn neighbourhoods — Red Hook, Greenpoint, Bensonhurst, Carroll Gardens — all built as Manhattan variations, all riffing on the near-lost Brooklyn cocktail.

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.

name: Horse's Neck
description: Bourbon and ginger ale with a lemon peel spiralled around the inside of the glass. The peel is the whole point of the name.
funFact: It began in the 1890s as an alcohol-free drink — just ginger ale and the lemon spiral. The bourbon was added later, and the version with it was for a while distinguished as a 'Horse's Neck with a kick'.

steps: Peel a lemon in one continuous spiral and hang it inside a highball glass with one end over the rim.
Fill the glass carefully with ice, holding the spiral in place against the side.
Add the bourbon and the bitters.
Top with cold ginger ale and stir once.

name: Hot Buttered Rum
description: Dark rum, spiced butter batter and boiling water. Colonial American, and the butter is not a novelty — it is the whole texture.
funFact: Colonial New England imported molasses from the Caribbean to distil its own rum, which is why a butter-and-spice rum drink became a northeastern winter tradition rather than a tropical one.

steps: Cream the softened butter with the brown sugar, spices and vanilla to make a batter.
Put a heaped spoonful of the batter in a warmed heatproof mug.
Add the rum and stir until the batter starts to melt.
Top with boiling water and stir until fully combined and glossy.
Grate nutmeg over the top.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a cinnamon stick

name: Illegal
description: Mezcal and rum with lime, falernum and agave — smoke and clove in a sour that hits harder than it reads.
funFact: It joined the IBA list in the 2020 revision, one of the first official cocktails built on mezcal — a category that barely existed outside Mexico twenty years earlier.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe, or serve over a large cube.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Jasmine
description: Gin, Campari, Cointreau and lemon — a bitter, grapefruit-pink sour that tastes far more complicated than its four ingredients.
funFact: Paul Harrington created it at a Berkeley bar in the 1990s and named it after a regular; there is no grapefruit in it, which is the drink's best trick.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Lava Flow
description: A frozen Piña Colada poured over blended strawberry so the red bleeds up through the white. Hawaii's most photographed drink.
funFact: The strawberry goes in the glass first and the colada is poured down the middle — the eruption effect only works if you pour into the centre, not down the side.

steps: Blend the strawberries with a splash of the pineapple juice until smooth, then pour into the bottom of a hurricane glass.
Rinse the blender and add the rums, coconut cream, remaining pineapple juice, banana and ice.
Blend until thick and smooth.
Pour slowly into the centre of the glass so the strawberry rises up the sides.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.

name: Little Italy
description: A Manhattan with Cynar in place of some of the vermouth. Artichoke bitterness against rye, which sounds wrong and lands beautifully.
funFact: Audrey Saunders created it at Pegu Club, and it did more than almost any other drink to make Cynar — a bitter liqueur made from artichokes — a standard American back-bar bottle.

steps: Combine the rye, vermouth and Cynar in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with brandied cherries.

name: Pisco Punch
description: Pisco, pineapple gum syrup and lemon — the drink that made gold-rush San Francisco famous, with a recipe its inventor took to the grave.
funFact: Duncan Nicol served it at the Bank Exchange saloon and refused to give up the recipe; when Prohibition closed the bar in 1920 the original formula was genuinely lost, and every modern version is a reconstruction.

steps: Shake the pisco, pineapple gum syrup, lemon juice and water with ice.
Strain into a chilled punch cup or coupe.
Garnish with a chunk of fresh pineapple.
Make a second one — the original was famous for tasting far weaker than it was.

name: Remember the Maine
description: Rye, sweet vermouth, cherry brandy and absinthe. Charles H. Baker recorded it in Havana during a revolution and told you to stir it clockwise.
funFact: Baker's original note instructs the reader to 'stir this one with a long spoon; and mind you, always in a clockwise direction' — the kind of instruction that tells you more about Baker than the drink.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Stir the rye, vermouth and Cherry Heering over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.

name: Revolver
description: Bourbon, coffee liqueur and orange bitters with a flamed orange peel. A Manhattan that drinks its coffee black.
funFact: Jon Santer created it at Bruno's in San Francisco in the early 2000s; the flamed orange peel is not decoration — the caramelised oils are what tie the coffee to the bourbon.

steps: Stir the bourbon, coffee liqueur and bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Hold a wide strip of orange peel over the glass, warm it briefly with a flame, then squeeze it through the flame to flare the oils.
Drop the peel into the drink.

name: Rob Roy
description: A Manhattan built on Scotch. The smoke changes everything, and the drink has been quietly better than its reputation for 130 years.
funFact: Created at the Waldorf Hotel in 1894 and named after an operetta about the Scottish outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor that had just opened a few blocks away.

steps: Combine the Scotch, vermouth and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry, or a lemon twist for a drier read.

name: Salty Dog
description: A Greyhound with a salted rim. The salt does not make it salty — it makes the grapefruit taste less bitter, which is the whole trick.
funFact: Salt suppresses the bitterness receptors on the tongue, which is why a salted rim makes grapefruit juice read as sweeter — the same principle behind salting a Margarita.

steps: Rim a highball glass with a grapefruit wedge and coarse salt.
Fill the glass with ice.
Pour in the spirit.
Top with fresh grapefruit juice and stir once.
Garnish with a grapefruit wedge.
recipe.garnish: Grapefruit wedge on a salted rim

name: Siesta
description: A Hemingway Daiquiri rebuilt on tequila, with Campari instead of maraschino. Grapefruit, lime and bitterness in balance.
funFact: Katie Stipe created it at Flatiron Lounge in 2006, and it became one of the first modern cocktails to convince American bartenders that Campari belonged with tequila.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.

name: Southside
description: Gin, lime, sugar and mint, shaken hard. A Mojito without the soda, or a Daiquiri with mint — either way it disappears fast.
funFact: Two stories compete: that it comes from Chicago's South Side during Prohibition, where rough gin needed mint to hide it, and that it comes from the 21 Club in New York. The New York version has better records.

steps: Put the mint leaves in the shaker and add the lime juice and syrup.
Press the mint gently with a muddler — bruise it, do not tear it.
Add the gin and ice, then shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a fresh mint leaf on top.

name: Stinger
description: Cognac and white crème de menthe, shaken hard. A nightcap so clean it was once considered acceptable at any hour.
funFact: It was the drink of the American upper class in the early twentieth century — Reginald Vanderbilt is credited with popularising it, and it appears in enough novels to count as a character trait.

steps: Add the cognac and crème de menthe to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds — the Stinger is traditionally shaken, not stirred.
Strain into a chilled coupe, or over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig if serving over ice.

name: Stone Fence
description: Rum or whiskey topped with hard cider. Ethan Allen's men reportedly drank it before taking Fort Ticonderoga, which explains a great deal.
funFact: It is one of the oldest recorded American mixed drinks, predating the word 'cocktail' — colonial New England had cider and rum in abundance and very little else to mix.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum or whiskey and the bitters.
Top with cold hard cider.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice.

name: Tom and Jerry
description: A hot eggnog batter spiked with rum and brandy, topped with boiling milk. American Christmas before eggnog took over the marketing.
funFact: Jerry Thomas claimed to have invented it, which is doubtful — but he popularised it so thoroughly that dedicated Tom and Jerry mug sets were sold across America for a century.

steps: Beat the egg whites to stiff peaks, then beat the yolks separately with the sugar and spices.
Fold the yolk mixture into the whites to make a thick batter — this keeps for days in the fridge.
Put two heaped tablespoons of batter in a warmed mug.
Add the rum and brandy and stir to loosen.
Top with hot milk, stir until foamy, and grate nutmeg over the top.

name: Tuxedo
description: A Martini with maraschino and absinthe. Dry, faintly nutty and named for the New York enclave that also named the dinner jacket.
funFact: The Tuxedo Club in Tuxedo Park gave its name to both the jacket and the drink; the cocktail is essentially a Martinez cousin that never became as famous as either.

ingredients.item: Old Tom or London dry gin

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry and a lemon twist.

name: Twelve Mile Limit
description: Rum, rye, brandy, lemon and grenadine — three spirits in one glass, named for the line where Prohibition stopped applying.
funFact: The twelve-mile limit was the boundary of US jurisdiction after 1924 — beyond it sat 'Rum Row', a floating line of ships selling legally to anyone who sailed out far enough.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Widow's Kiss
description: Calvados, Bénédictine and yellow Chartreuse with Angostura. Autumnal, herbal and considerably heavier than its delicate name suggests.
funFact: It first appears in George Kappeler's 1895 'Modern American Drinks', from the Holland House Hotel in New York — a rare nineteenth-century cocktail with no base spirit dilution at all.

steps: Combine all the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 to 30 seconds — this one needs the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry or an apple slice.

name: Medio y Medio
description: Half sparkling wine, half sweet white — Uruguay's national aperitif, poured at the Mercado del Puerto beside a plate of grilled meat.
funFact: The Roldós stall in Montevideo's Mercado del Puerto has been mixing it since 1886 and bottles its own; the ratio is exactly what the name says, and nobody there will negotiate.

steps: Chill both wines thoroughly.
Pour the sweet white wine into a wine glass first.
Top with the sparkling wine, poured slowly down the side to preserve the bubbles.
Serve immediately, without ice.

name: Guarapita
description: Rum or aguardiente loaded with passionfruit and sugar, mixed in a jug and served from a plastic bottle at the beach. Deceptively fruity.
funFact: Guarapita is Venezuelan beach and street-party currency, usually sold in recycled water bottles — the fruit hides the proof so effectively that it is known as 'the liar'.

steps: Stir the sugar into the passionfruit and orange juice until fully dissolved.
Add the rum and mix well.
Chill for at least two hours.
Serve very cold over ice, and warn people.

name: Ponche Crema
description: Venezuela's Christmas cream: eggs, milk, sugar and rum cooked into a custard-thick liqueur that coats the glass and the season.
funFact: Eliodoro González P. commercialised it in 1900 and the brand still dominates December in Venezuela, but home-made versions with a heavier rum hand remain the point of pride.

steps: Whisk the egg yolks with the condensed milk over a very low heat until slightly thickened; do not let it scramble.
Remove from the heat and whisk in the evaporated milk and vanilla.
Cool completely to room temperature.
Stir in the rum, then bottle and refrigerate overnight.
Serve chilled with nutmeg grated over the top.

name: Rượu Rắn
description: Rice wine with a snake in the bottle. Sold as a tonic, drunk as a dare, and genuinely traditional across northern Vietnam.
funFact: The ethanol denatures the venom, which is why the practice is not as dangerous as it looks — though the bottles are still confiscated at most international borders.

steps: Clean and prepare the snake thoroughly — this step is traditionally done by a specialist.
Place it in a large sealed glass jar with the herbs and ginseng.
Cover completely with rice wine and seal airtight.
Leave to infuse for several months to a year.
Serve in very small cups, at room temperature.

name: Adonis
description: Sherry and sweet vermouth with orange bitters — a low-proof aperitif named after a Broadway musical that ran for over 500 nights in 1884.
funFact: Adonis was the first musical in Broadway history to run more than 500 performances, and the Waldorf's bartender named the drink to catch its publicity.

steps: Combine everything in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 seconds — this is low-proof, so watch the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top.

name: Chrysanthemum
description: Dry vermouth, Bénédictine and a whisper of absinthe. No base spirit at all, and far more interesting than that sounds.
funFact: It appears in Hugo Ensslin's 1916 'Recipes for Mixed Drinks', one of the last American cocktail books published before Prohibition shut the genre down.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and discard.

name: Diplomat
description: Two vermouths and a spoon of maraschino. A vermouth cocktail from the era when ordering one was completely unremarkable.
funFact: Before Prohibition, vermouth-only cocktails were standard afternoon drinking in American hotels — the category vanished so completely that it had to be rediscovered a century later.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry and a lemon twist.
Serve as an aperitif before dinner.

name: Coronation
description: Sherry, dry vermouth and maraschino — created for the coronation of Edward VII and served at the Knickerbocker.
funFact: Edward VII's 1902 coronation was postponed at two days' notice for an emergency appendectomy, but the cocktails named for it went ahead regardless.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve well chilled.

name: Turf Cocktail
description: Gin and dry vermouth with maraschino and absinthe — a Martinez cousin from the racetrack era, drier and sharper than the Tuxedo.
funFact: The Turf, the Tuxedo and the Martinez are essentially the same drink with the dial turned differently, and nineteenth-century bar books rarely agreed on which was which.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an olive or a lemon twist.
Serve very cold.

name: Income Tax
description: A Bronx with bitters added — gin, both vermouths and orange juice, named for the tax that arrived in 1913 and never left.
funFact: The American federal income tax became permanent in 1913, and the cocktail named after it appeared almost immediately — bartenders have always found a drink in bad news.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Bobby Burns
description: A Rob Roy with Bénédictine in place of the bitters — honeyed herbs against Scotch, named for the poet with an extra B.
funFact: Every bar book spells it differently — Bobby Burns, Bobbie Burns, Robert Burns — and the Savoy insists it is 'one of the very best whisky cocktails'.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Affinity
description: A perfect Rob Roy: Scotch with both vermouths and Angostura, balanced between sweet and dry rather than committing to either.
funFact: 'Perfect' in cocktail language never means excellent — it means split evenly between sweet and dry vermouth, a convention that confuses nearly everyone who orders one.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry.
Serve very cold.

name: Old Pal
description: A Boulevardier stripped dry: rye, dry vermouth and Campari in equal parts. Leaner, more bitter and considerably more bracing.
funFact: Harry MacElhone recorded it at his Paris bar alongside the Boulevardier, crediting it to a sports writer who called everyone 'old pal'.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top.
Serve without garnish beyond the twist.

name: Scofflaw
description: Rye, dry vermouth, lemon and grenadine — named for the word Americans invented in 1924 to describe people who drank anyway.
funFact: 'Scofflaw' was the winning entry in a 1924 Boston competition to coin a word for a Prohibition lawbreaker; Harry's Bar in Paris had a cocktail named after it within weeks.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Diamondback
description: Rye, applejack and yellow Chartreuse in equal measure. Described by one writer as a drink that will 'put hair on your chest' — accurately.
funFact: It comes from the Diamondback Lounge in Baltimore's Lord Baltimore Hotel, and at equal parts with no dilution from citrus it is one of the stiffest classics still in circulation.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish is traditional.
Serve very cold and sip slowly.

name: De La Louisiane
description: New Orleans' other great rye drink: rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe, from a restaurant that served it as the house cocktail.
funFact: Restaurant de la Louisiane on Iberville Street served it as its signature; it is essentially a Vieux Carré with the cognac removed and the Bénédictine turned up.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with three brandied cherries.
Serve cold.

name: Fancy Free
description: Bourbon with maraschino standing in for sugar, and two kinds of bitters. An Old Fashioned that went to finishing school.
funFact: Maraschino here does the sweetening job that sugar does in an Old Fashioned, which is why the drink tastes richer without actually being sweeter.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve immediately.

name: Improved Whiskey Cocktail
description: The Old Fashioned with maraschino and absinthe added — 'improved' was a genuine nineteenth-century menu category, not a boast.
funFact: Jerry Thomas listed 'improved' versions of several cocktails in 1876, meaning ones upgraded with maraschino and absinthe — the word described a recipe family, not an opinion.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve immediately.

name: Morning Glory Fizz
description: Scotch, absinthe, lemon and egg white under soda — a Victorian hangover cure that took the previous night's absinthe as the remedy.
funFact: Victorian bar manuals recommended it explicitly as a morning restorative, on the reasoning that a little of what hurt you was the cure — advice modern medicine does not endorse.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled highball glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam.
Serve without garnish.

name: Sloe Gin Fizz
description: Sloe gin, lemon and soda over ice — pink, tart and gentle, and the reason most Americans have heard of sloe gin at all.
funFact: Sloe gin is not gin but a liqueur made by steeping blackthorn sloes in gin and sugar — traditionally picked after the first frost, which softens the fruit.

steps: Shake the sloe gin, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Chicago Fizz
description: Rum and ruby port shaken with lemon and egg white. Darker and richer than a fizz has any right to be.
funFact: The fizz family once ran to dozens of named variations — silver with egg white, golden with yolk, royal with the whole egg — of which only a handful survive on menus.

steps: Dry-shake everything but the soda for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled highball with no ice.
Top gently with soda water.
Serve immediately.

name: Whiskey Smash
description: Bourbon, lemon and mint pounded together over crushed ice — a julep that took a lemon along.
funFact: Jerry Thomas defined the smash in 1862 as 'a julep on a small plan', and the form barely changed in the 160 years since.

steps: Muddle the lemon quarters with the syrup in a shaker.
Add the mint and press gently — do not shred it.
Add the bourbon and ice, then shake hard for 10 seconds.
Double-strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint bouquet.

name: Brandy Flip
description: Brandy, a whole egg and sugar, shaken to a custardy foam and dusted with nutmeg. The oldest cocktail template still in use.
funFact: Flips originally involved plunging a red-hot iron 'flip dog' into a mug of spiked ale to make it froth — the egg version is the domesticated descendant.

steps: Dry-shake the brandy, egg and syrup without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled wine glass.
Grate fresh nutmeg generously over the top.

name: Coffee Cocktail
description: Port, cognac and a whole egg. Contains no coffee at all — it was named for looking like one.
funFact: Jerry Thomas named it for its appearance rather than its contents, and then had to explain in print that it contained no coffee whatsoever.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for 15 seconds more.
Double-strain into a small wine glass.
Grate nutmeg over the surface.

name: Bourbon Milk Punch
description: Bourbon, milk, sugar and vanilla over ice with nutmeg. New Orleans brunch, and a genuine hangover institution.
funFact: Along with the Ramos Gin Fizz and the Sazerac, it is one of the three drinks New Orleans considers acceptable before noon.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds until frothy.
Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg generously over the top.

name: Presbyterian
description: Whiskey with ginger ale and soda in equal measure — the highball for people who find straight ginger ale too sweet.
funFact: The split of ginger ale and soda is the whole idea: the ginger carries flavour while the soda cuts the sugar, which is why the drink outlived the whiskey-and-ginger.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the whiskey.
Top with equal parts ginger ale and soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon twist.

name: Mamie Taylor
description: Scotch, lime and ginger beer — the 1899 hit that the Moscow Mule copied wholesale fifty years later with vodka.
funFact: Named for a Broadway singer, it was a national craze in 1900; the Moscow Mule is structurally the same drink and got all the credit.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the Scotch and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Nevada
description: Rum with grapefruit and lime over sugar and bitters — a Cuban-era sour that deserved better than obscurity.
funFact: It appears in Havana bar books of the 1930s alongside the Daiquiri and Mary Pickford, part of a whole grapefruit-and-rum family that never travelled.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a grapefruit twist.
Serve immediately.

name: Hotel Nacional
description: Rum, apricot, pineapple and lime from Havana's grandest hotel — tropical without tipping into a tiki drink.
funFact: The Hotel Nacional opened in 1930 and hosted everyone from Churchill to the mafia summit that inspired The Godfather Part II; its bar produced this alongside the Mary Pickford.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a thin apricot or pineapple slice.
Serve cold.

name: Air Mail
description: Rum, honey and lime topped with champagne — a Daiquiri that took flight, named for the airmail service of the 1930s.
funFact: It appears in a 1949 Bacardi promotional booklet, though the name dates it to the era when airmail stamps were exotic enough to name a drink after.

steps: Shake the rum, honey syrup and lime juice hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled flute or coupe.
Top slowly with champagne.
Garnish with a mint sprig.

name: Gibson
description: A Martini garnished with a pickled onion instead of an olive. That single swap changes the whole drink, which is the point.
funFact: The onion is not decoration — its vinegar and sweetness measurably change the finish, which is why Gibson drinkers are so specific about it.

steps: Stir the gin and vermouth over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a thoroughly chilled coupe.
Drop in two cocktail onions on a pick.
Serve immediately, very cold.

name: Dirty Martini
description: A Martini with olive brine stirred in. Divisive by design, and the most-ordered Martini variation in America.
funFact: Franklin Roosevelt is often credited with popularising it — he mixed Martinis at the White House and was reportedly heavy-handed with the olive juice.

steps: Stir the gin, vermouth and olive brine over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with three olives on a pick.
Serve very cold.

name: Black Manhattan
description: A Manhattan with amaro in place of the sweet vermouth — darker, more bitter and noticeably more serious.
funFact: Todd Smith created it at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco around 2005, and it did more than any other drink to put Averna on American back bars.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Bensonhurst
description: Rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and Cynar — the driest of the Brooklyn neighbourhood series and the most bitter.
funFact: Chad Solomon created it at Milk & Honey as part of the Brooklyn-variation family that also produced the Red Hook and the Greenpoint.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish is traditional.
Serve very cold.

name: Rosita
description: A tequila Negroni with both vermouths — reposado against Campari, from Gary Regan's 1991 bartender's bible.
funFact: Gary Regan printed it in 'The Bartender's Bible' in 1991, years before anyone else was seriously mixing tequila into stirred aperitif drinks.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Kingston Negroni
description: A Negroni built on Jamaican overproof rum. The funk of the rum against Campari's bitterness is the whole argument, and it works.
funFact: Joaquín Simó created it at Death & Co, using Smith & Cross — a high-ester Jamaican rum whose banana-and-overripe-fruit character survives even Campari.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve immediately.

name: Mezcal Negroni
description: Smoke where the juniper was. Mezcal turns the Negroni savoury and campfire-scented without touching its structure.
funFact: The Negroni's equal-parts structure is unusually robust — swapping the gin for mezcal, rum, whiskey or sherry all produce drinks that still work, which is why the variations are endless.

steps: Stir all three over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Express an orange twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve immediately.

name: Jet Pilot
description: Three rums, falernum, cinnamon and grapefruit with a drop of absinthe — a Zombie descendant built to be even harder to reverse-engineer.
funFact: Tiki bars deliberately obscured their recipes — Don the Beachcomber numbered his mixes and had staff work from coded bottles so nobody could copy them, including his own bartenders.

steps: Add every ingredient to a blender with a cup of crushed ice.
Flash-blend for about five seconds — do not liquefy it.
Pour unstrained into a double rocks glass.
Top with more crushed ice to fill.
Garnish with a mint sprig.

name: Test Pilot
description: Don the Beachcomber's rum-and-falernum formula with Cointreau and Angostura. Complex, dry and considerably stronger than it tastes.
funFact: Also called the Missionary's Downfall in some bars, though that is properly a different drink — tiki recipe names were reused and misattributed constantly.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug or coupe.
Add crushed ice to fill if needed.
Garnish with a cherry and a mint sprig.

name: Doctor Funk
description: Rum, absinthe, lemon and grenadine over soda — named for a real doctor who practised in Samoa and prescribed something similar.
funFact: Dr Bernard Funk was a German physician in Samoa who treated Robert Louis Stevenson; his absinthe-and-lemonade remedy became a South Pacific drink long before tiki bars adopted it.

steps: Shake everything except the soda with ice.
Pour into a highball glass packed with crushed ice.
Top with soda water.
Stir gently once with a swizzle stick.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a lime wheel.

name: Cobra's Fang
description: Demerara rum with falernum, orange, lime and a lash of absinthe. Spiced, bitter-edged and one of the sharper Beachcomber formulas.
funFact: Falernum, a Barbadian lime-clove-almond syrup, is the single most tiki ingredient there is — it appears in more Beachcomber recipes than any spirit except rum.

steps: Shake all ingredients with crushed ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug.
Top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel and mint.
Serve with a straw.

name: Missionary's Downfall
description: Blended with fresh mint, peach and pineapple — bright green, herbaceous and the least brown drink in the tiki canon.
funFact: Most tiki drinks are variations on rum, citrus and spice; this one is essentially a frozen mint julep with fruit, and it stands out on any tiki menu for that reason.

steps: Put the mint, pineapple and lime juice in a blender.
Add the rum, peach brandy and honey syrup.
Add crushed ice and blend until smooth and pale green.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a mint sprig.

name: Nui Nui
description: Gold rum with vanilla, cinnamon and allspice over orange and lime. The spice cabinet of tiki in one glass.
funFact: Beachcomber's spice syrups were mixed in advance and labelled only with numbers — 'Don's Spices #2' is allspice and vanilla, and the code was cracked decades later by tiki archaeologists.

steps: Shake all ingredients with crushed ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Garnish with an orange twist and a cinnamon stick.
Serve with a straw.

name: Pearl Diver
description: Three rums whipped with a butter-and-spice 'gardenia mix' — the only classic cocktail that calls for butter as a core ingredient.
funFact: The gardenia mix — butter, honey, cinnamon and allspice creamed together — is what makes it work; it emulsifies into the drink and gives a richness nothing else achieves.

steps: Make the gardenia mix by creaming softened butter with honey, cinnamon and allspice.
Add a spoonful to a blender with the rums, juices and crushed ice.
Flash-blend for five seconds until emulsified.
Pour into a tall glass and top with crushed ice.
Garnish with a mint sprig.

name: Royal Hawaiian
description: Gin, pineapple, lemon and orgeat from the pink hotel on Waikiki — the rare tiki-era drink built on gin rather than rum.
funFact: The Royal Hawaiian hotel opened in 1927 and is still called the Pink Palace of the Pacific; its bar predates the mainland tiki craze by a decade.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge.
Serve immediately.

name: Halekulani
description: Gin, lemon, orange and grenadine with bitters — the house drink of a Waikiki hotel, sharper and less sweet than its neighbours.
funFact: The Halekulani's House Without a Key bar has served it since the 1930s under a century-old kiawe tree that still stands on the terrace.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe or over fresh ice.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Beachcomber
description: A Daiquiri with triple sec and maraschino — the drink Don the Beachcomber named himself after, and simpler than anything else he made.
funFact: Ernest Gantt legally changed his name to Donn Beach after the bar became famous — the man took his identity from the restaurant rather than the other way round.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve immediately.

name: Chief Lapu Lapu
description: A rum punch scaled up and named for the Filipino chief who killed Magellan. Served in a hollowed pineapple where possible.
funFact: Lapulapu defeated Magellan at the Battle of Mactan in 1521 and is a national hero in the Philippines, which makes his appearance on a Los Angeles tiki menu somewhat unexpected.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a hollowed pineapple or a large tiki mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Garnish extravagantly with fruit and mint.
Serve with long straws, ideally shared.

name: Shrunken Skull
description: Two rums, lime and grenadine over crushed ice in a skull mug. Short, tart and considerably less complicated than its neighbours.
funFact: Tiki mug collecting is now a serious market, and vintage skull mugs from mid-century Los Angeles bars change hands for hundreds of dollars.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a skull mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve with a straw.

name: Port Light
description: Bourbon, passionfruit, lemon and honey shaken with egg white — a tiki drink built on whiskey, which almost none of them are.
funFact: Its bourbon base makes it an outlier in a category defined by rum, and it is one of the few tiki drinks that works as well in winter as in summer.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for 15 seconds more.
Pour into a hurricane glass over crushed ice.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.
Serve with a straw.

name: Blue Hawaiian
description: A Piña Colada turned blue with curaçao. Distinct from the Blue Hawaii, which has vodka and no coconut — a difference nobody enforces.
funFact: Harry Yee, at the Hilton Hawaiian Village, created the original Blue Hawaii in 1957 at the request of a blue-curaçao sales representative — the drink existed to sell an ingredient.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with ice.
Blend until smooth and pale blue.
Pour into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.
Serve with a straw and a paper umbrella.

name: Chi Chi
description: A Piña Colada made with vodka instead of rum. Cleaner, less funky, and the version ordered by people who say they dislike rum.
funFact: The swap is the entire recipe — everything else matches a Piña Colada — and it exists mostly because vodka outsold rum in the 1970s American market.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with ice.
Blend until completely smooth.
Pour into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and cherry.
Serve with a straw.

name: Bahama Breeze
description: Coconut rum, banana and pineapple with a dark rum float — the resort blender drink refined into something with actual structure.
funFact: The dark rum float is the difference between a fruit smoothie and a cocktail — it hits the nose first and reframes everything underneath it.

steps: Shake the coconut rum, banana liqueur, pineapple and lime with ice.
Strain into a hurricane glass over fresh ice.
Float the dark rum over the back of a spoon.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge.
Serve with a straw.

name: Rum Barrel
description: A multi-rum punch served in a barrel-shaped mug, closer to a scaled-up Zombie than to anything restrained.
funFact: Barrel mugs, skull mugs and hollowed pineapples were part of the same commercial logic — the vessel was the marketing, and customers frequently stole them.

steps: Combine everything in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a barrel mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Garnish with mint and a cherry.

name: Aku Aku
description: Light rum blended with peach, mint and pineapple — pale, fresh and named for Thor Heyerdahl's book about Easter Island.
funFact: Heyerdahl's 'Aku-Aku' was a 1957 bestseller about Easter Island, and tiki bars borrowed Polynesian book titles as freely as they borrowed everything else.

steps: Put the mint in a blender with the lime juice and press briefly.
Add the rum, peach liqueur, pineapple juice and syrup.
Add crushed ice and flash-blend for five seconds.
Pour into a tiki mug.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a pineapple wedge.

name: Sidewinder's Fang
description: A large, spice-heavy rum and citrus punch, traditionally served with a coil of orange peel arranged to look like a snake.
funFact: The garnish is the name: a long spiral of orange peel draped over the rim, which the bar staff cut in one continuous piece as a small display of knife work.

steps: Shake everything but the soda with crushed ice.
Pour unstrained into a large tiki mug.
Top with soda and more crushed ice.
Cut a long spiral of orange peel and drape it over the rim.
Serve with a straw.

name: Molokai Mule
description: Rum, ginger, orange and lime — the tiki answer to a Moscow Mule, spiced rather than sharp.
funFact: Ginger runs through tiki from falernum to Doctor Funk; the mule format simply gives it the lead instead of a supporting role.

steps: Shake the rum, ginger syrup and juices with ice.
Pour into a mug packed with crushed ice.
Top with soda water.
Stir once with a swizzle stick.
Garnish with candied ginger and a lime wheel.

name: Puka Punch
description: Four rums, honey, passionfruit and grapefruit, served long over crushed ice. One of the heaviest pours in the canon.
funFact: The Tiki-Ti bar in Los Angeles has served it since 1961, and the staff ring a bell and shout when one is ordered — a ritual that has outlasted most of the tiki era.

steps: Shake everything except the overproof rum with crushed ice.
Pour unstrained into a large tiki mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Float the overproof rum over the top.
Garnish with mint and a cherry.

name: Tahitian Rum Punch
description: Rhum with lime, grenadine and tropical juice, poured long — the French Polynesian take on a punch, lighter than its American imitations.
funFact: Tahiti gave tiki bars their aesthetic vocabulary and almost none of their recipes — the actual drinking culture of French Polynesia runs to rhum, beer and fruit juice.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Pour into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Stir once to bring the grenadine through.
Garnish with a lime wheel and a flower if you have one.
Serve with a straw.

name: Hukilau
description: Rum with passionfruit, lime and a dry curaçao — named for the communal net-fishing that ends with everyone eating on the beach.
funFact: A hukilau is a Hawaiian group fishing method where the whole village hauls a single net; the song about it was a mainland hit in 1948 and the drink followed the song.

steps: Shake all ingredients with crushed ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug.
Top with crushed ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel and mint.
Serve with a straw.

name: Vicious Virgin
description: Two rums, falernum, curaçao and lime — a short, dry Beachcomber formula with none of the fruit-juice padding of later tiki.
funFact: The early Beachcomber drinks were markedly drier and stronger than the tiki of the 1960s; the sweetening happened later, as the format spread to restaurants that wanted volume.

steps: Shake all ingredients with crushed ice for 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a small tiki mug or coupe.
Add crushed ice to fill.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve immediately.

name: Shark's Tooth
description: Demerara rum with lemon, grenadine and soda — a long, red, deceptively simple drink from the same kitchen as the Zombie.
funFact: Donn Beach built dozens of recipes from the same handful of syrups; the difference between many of his drinks is a quarter-ounce of one ingredient, which is exactly what made them hard to copy.

steps: Shake everything except the soda with ice.
Pour into a tall glass packed with crushed ice.
Top with soda water.
Stir once with a swizzle stick.
Garnish with a lime wheel and a cherry.

name: Cradle of Life
description: Rum, lime, honey and a cinnamon-spiced syrup with a whole egg — one of very few tiki drinks built on an egg.
funFact: Tiki almost never used eggs, which makes this an outlier — the egg gives it a texture closer to a flip than to a punch.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dust with grated cinnamon.
Serve immediately.

name: Slippery Nipple
description: Sambuca under Irish cream, layered so the two stay separate until you drink them. Named with the subtlety of its era.
funFact: The layers hold because Irish cream is less dense than sambuca; add the grenadine last and it sinks through both to sit at the bottom as a red dot.

steps: Pour the sambuca into a shot glass.
Float the Irish cream over the back of a barspoon so it sits cleanly on top.
Drop two drops of grenadine through the centre — they should sink.
Serve immediately, before the layers bleed.

name: Duck Fart
description: Kahlúa, Irish cream and whisky in three layers. Alaska's contribution to the shooter canon, and the name is not explained.
funFact: It was invented at the Peanut Farm bar in Anchorage in the 1980s, and Alaskans defend both the drink and its name with more energy than either strictly warrants.

steps: Pour the Kahlúa into the bottom of a shot glass.
Float the Irish cream over a barspoon to make the middle layer.
Float the whisky on top the same way.
Serve immediately and drink in one.

name: Alabama Slammer
description: Southern Comfort, amaretto and sloe gin with orange juice — a shot in some bars, a tall drink in others, sweet in both.
funFact: It spread through American college bars in the 1970s and is usually associated with the University of Alabama, though no one has ever produced evidence for that.

steps: Shake all ingredients briefly with ice.
Strain into a shot glass, or into a tall glass over ice for the long version.
Add a squeeze of lemon if serving long.
Serve cold.

name: Red Headed Slut
description: Jägermeister, peach schnapps and cranberry — herbal and fruity at once, and far more drinkable than its reputation.
funFact: Jägermeister contains 56 botanicals and was formulated in 1934 as a digestif for hunters; its American career as a party shot would have baffled its inventor.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass or a small rocks glass.
Serve cold, immediately.
For a longer version, pour over ice and top with more cranberry.

name: Woo Woo
description: Vodka, peach schnapps and cranberry. A Sex on the Beach with the orange juice removed, and better for it.
funFact: It belongs to a whole 1980s family built on peach schnapps, which the American market had barely heard of before 1985 and then could not get enough of.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass, or over ice in a highball for a long version.
Garnish with a lime wedge if serving long.
Serve cold.

name: Purple Hooter
description: Vodka, raspberry liqueur and lime — bright purple, sharp and gone in one.
funFact: Chambord is made in the Loire from black raspberries and honey to a recipe claiming descent from a seventeenth-century royal liqueur — a grand pedigree for a bar shot.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 8 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled shot glass.
Serve immediately.
A lime wedge on the side is optional.

name: Surfer on Acid
description: Jägermeister, coconut rum and pineapple. Sounds alarming and tastes, unexpectedly, like a tropical dessert.
funFact: The coconut and pineapple mask Jägermeister's bitterness almost completely, which is why people who insist they hate Jäger reliably finish this one.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass or small rocks glass.
Serve cold.
Scale it up over ice for a longer drink.

name: Scooby Snack
description: Melon liqueur, coconut rum, pineapple and cream, shaken to a pale green froth. A dessert disguised as a shot.
funFact: Midori was launched in the US in 1978 at Studio 54, and the whole family of green shots that followed exists because of that one marketing party.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 10 seconds.
Double-strain into a shot glass.
It should be pale green and foamy on top.
Serve immediately.

name: Liquid Marijuana
description: Blue curaçao and melon liqueur with coconut rum and pineapple, turning an improbable green. Named for the colour, nothing else.
funFact: Blue curaçao plus yellow pineapple juice makes green — the same colour trick behind half the novelty drinks invented between 1975 and 1995.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 8 seconds.
Strain into a shot glass or over ice in a rocks glass.
The colour should be a clear green.
Serve immediately.

name: Three Wise Men
description: Jack Daniel's, Jim Beam and Johnnie Walker in equal measure, neat. No mixer, no ceremony, no mercy.
funFact: Variations swap in Jose Cuervo to make the Four Horsemen, or add Jägermeister for the Five Wise Men — the joke scales in exactly one direction.

steps: Pour all three whiskies into a shot glass.
Do not stir, chill or dilute — the point is that it is undignified.
Serve at room temperature.
Drink in one.

name: Prairie Fire
description: Tequila and Tabasco. Two ingredients, one of which is hot sauce, and no attempt at balance.
funFact: It belongs to the dare category of shots rather than the drinking category, and the capsaicin genuinely does mask the tequila — which is the only reason it works at all.

steps: Pour the tequila into a shot glass.
Add the Tabasco directly on top.
Do not stir.
Drink in one, and have something cold ready.

name: Cement Mixer
description: Irish cream held in the mouth, then lime juice added. It curdles on your tongue. That is the entire drink.
funFact: The curdling is real chemistry: lime juice drops the pH below the point where casein proteins stay suspended, and they clump instantly — the same reaction that makes cheese.

steps: Pour the Irish cream into a shot glass and the lime juice into a second.
Take the Irish cream into your mouth but do not swallow.
Add the lime juice and hold both for a few seconds.
Swallow, and accept the consequences.

name: Chartreuse Bomb
description: A shot of green Chartreuse dropped into a glass of cider or beer. Bartender currency, and traded as such.
funFact: Green Chartreuse is still made by Carthusian monks to a recipe held by two of them at a time; supply shortages since 2021 have made bartenders noticeably less willing to bomb it.

steps: Pour the cider into a small glass, leaving room.
Fill a shot glass with green Chartreuse.
Drop the shot glass into the cider.
Drink immediately, before it dilutes.

name: Lemon Drop Martini
description: The Lemon Drop scaled up into a coupe with a sugared rim — sharper and more grown-up than the shot it came from.
funFact: Norman Jay Hobday created the original at Henry Africa's in San Francisco in the 1970s, a bar widely credited with inventing the fern-bar format.

steps: Rim a chilled coupe with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the vodka, triple sec, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Double-strain into the rimmed coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
recipe.garnish: Lemon twist on a sugared rim

name: Blue Kamikaze
description: A Kamikaze with blue curaçao standing in for the triple sec. Same drink, different colour, considerably more popular.
funFact: Blue curaçao and triple sec are the same liqueur with food colouring added, which means the Blue Kamikaze is chemically a Kamikaze that photographs better.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 8 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled shot glass.
Serve immediately.
Scale up into a coupe for a full-size version.

name: Tokyo Tea
description: A Long Island Iced Tea with melon liqueur in place of the cola. Green, enormous and exactly as strong as its parent.
funFact: The Long Island family is defined by five white spirits plus a modifier: cola makes the original, cranberry the Long Beach, blue curaçao the Blue Motorcycle, and melon this one.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add all the spirits, the melon liqueur and the lemon juice.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once from the bottom.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Long Beach Iced Tea
description: The Long Island with cranberry instead of cola. Pink rather than brown, and it fools people just as effectively.
funFact: The whole Long Island format exists to look like iced tea, which is why the original uses cola — the cranberry version abandons the disguise entirely and keeps the strength.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the five spirits and the lemon juice.
Top with cranberry juice.
Stir once from the bottom up.
Garnish with a lemon wedge.

name: Adios Motherfucker
description: The Long Island turned blue: five spirits, blue curaçao and lemonade. Also sold politely as an AMF.
funFact: Most bars list it as 'AMF' on the menu to avoid printing the full name, which has done nothing at all to stop customers ordering it by the full name.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the four spirits, blue curaçao and sour mix.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once to bring the colour through.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.

name: Irish Car Bomb
description: Irish cream and whiskey dropped into stout. Drink it fast — the cream curdles within seconds, and the name is genuinely unwelcome in Ireland.
funFact: The name references the Troubles and is considered offensive across Ireland; many bars now list it as an Irish Slammer, and asking for it by the original name in Dublin will not go well.

steps: Pour the stout into a pint glass and let the head settle.
Layer the Irish cream and whiskey in a shot glass.
Drop the shot into the stout.
Drink immediately — the cream curdles in about ten seconds.

name: Boilermaker's Daughter
description: A half of bitter with a shot of whisky poured in rather than beside — the gentler British reading of the boilermaker.
funFact: British pubs traditionally poured the whisky into the beer rather than serving them separately, which is the opposite of the American convention and produces a noticeably different drink.

steps: Pour the ale into a half-pint glass.
Add the whisky directly to the beer.
Stir once, gently.
Drink at cellar temperature.

name: Sake Bomb
description: A cup of sake balanced on chopsticks over a beer, knocked in by pounding the table. Loud, communal and not remotely traditional.
funFact: Despite the presentation it is an American invention, not a Japanese one — sake and beer are rarely combined in Japan, and the table-pounding would be startling in Tokyo.

steps: Pour the beer into a pint glass, leaving room at the top.
Rest two chopsticks across the rim, parallel.
Balance a cup of sake on the chopsticks.
Pound the table until the sake falls in, then drink immediately.

name: Flaming Sambuca
description: Sambuca set alight with three coffee beans floating in it — one each for health, happiness and prosperity.
funFact: The three beans are called 'con la mosca' — with the fly — and the number matters: an even number is considered unlucky across much of Italy.

steps: Pour the sambuca into a heatproof glass and drop in three coffee beans.
Light the surface carefully and let it burn for a few seconds to toast the beans.
Extinguish by covering the glass — never blow on it.
Let the glass cool before touching it, then drink and chew the beans.

name: Gin Alexander
description: The original Alexander, made with gin rather than brandy — juniper against chocolate and cream, and stranger than the version that replaced it.
funFact: The gin version came first and the brandy version took the name; most bars now serve a Brandy Alexander if you order an Alexander, which reverses the history exactly.

steps: Shake all three hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate fresh nutmeg over the surface.
Serve immediately, before it separates.

name: Golden Cadillac
description: Galliano, white crème de cacao and cream — pale gold, vanilla-scented, and named for a car parked outside the bar that invented it.
funFact: Poor Red's Bar-B-Q in California claims it, named for a customer's gold Cadillac; the same bar's Golden Cadillac sales once made it one of the largest single accounts for Galliano in America.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish, or with a light dusting of nutmeg.
Drink while cold and still emulsified.

name: Pink Squirrel
description: Crème de noyaux, white crème de cacao and cream. Pale pink, almond-scented, and a Wisconsin supper-club fixture.
funFact: Crème de noyaux is made from apricot and peach kernels rather than almonds, and the Pink Squirrel is essentially the only drink keeping the category commercially alive.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve immediately.
In Wisconsin it is often blended with ice cream instead of shaken.

name: Pink Lady
description: Gin, applejack, lemon and grenadine shaken with egg white. Dismissed for decades as a ladies' drink, and considerably tougher than that suggests.
funFact: Its reputation as a soft drink is entirely a marketing artefact of the 1950s — the original is gin and applejack with a whole egg white, which is not a gentle formula.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry.

name: Colorado Bulldog
description: A White Russian topped with cola. The cream and the cola should fight; somehow they broker a truce.
funFact: Adding cola to a cream drink risks curdling if the cola goes in first — pour it last and gently, and the fat stays suspended.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka, coffee liqueur and cream.
Stir gently to combine.
Top slowly with cola, poured down the side of the glass.
Do not stir again.

name: Godmother
description: Vodka and amaretto over a large cube. The Godfather's cleaner sibling, with the Scotch swapped out.
funFact: The 1970s duo format — one spirit, one liqueur, one big cube — produced the Godfather, Godmother, French Connection and Rusty Nail, and all four are still on menus.

steps: Put a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Add the vodka and amaretto.
Stir gently for 10 seconds.
Serve with no garnish, or a lemon twist if it reads too sweet.

name: Toasted Almond
description: Amaretto, coffee liqueur and cream. A dessert drink that tastes exactly like its name and makes no apology for it.
funFact: Add vodka and it becomes a Roasted Toasted Almond; the 1970s cream-drink family expanded by adding a spirit and lengthening the name.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 12 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Dust with grated nutmeg.
Serve cold.

name: Freddy Fudpucker
description: A Harvey Wallbanger built on tequila instead of vodka — orange juice with a Galliano float, and a name from the same school.
funFact: It is a straight substitution on the Wallbanger, and both drinks exist mainly because Galliano's importer spent the 1970s pushing bars to float it on things.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the tequila and top with orange juice.
Stir once to combine.
Float the Galliano over the back of a spoon.
Garnish with an orange slice.

name: Bay Breeze
description: Vodka, cranberry and pineapple. The Sea Breeze with pineapple in place of the grapefruit, and gentler for it.
funFact: The whole breeze family is vodka plus cranberry plus one other juice — grapefruit makes a Sea Breeze, pineapple a Bay Breeze, and orange a Madras.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka and cranberry juice.
Top with pineapple juice.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Madras
description: Vodka, cranberry and orange juice over ice. Named for the fabric, not the city, and the least demanding drink in any bar.
funFact: The name comes from madras plaid, whose overlapping red and orange stripes the layered juices were thought to resemble before they are stirred together.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka and cranberry juice.
Float the orange juice on top without stirring.
Serve with a straw and let the drinker mix it.

name: Angel's Tip
description: Crème de cacao under a float of cream, with a cherry suspended from a pick across the rim. A pousse-café for people in a hurry.
funFact: It belongs to the pousse-café tradition of layered after-dinner drinks, a genre that largely died because it takes a steady hand and nobody has time.

steps: Pour the crème de cacao into a pony glass.
Float the cream carefully over the back of a barspoon.
Spear a cherry on a cocktail pick and rest it across the rim.
Serve immediately without stirring.

name: Velvet Hammer
description: Triple sec, crème de cacao and cream — a smoother, orange-scented cousin of the Alexander family.
funFact: Recipes differ wildly — some versions use vodka, some Tia Maria, some Cointreau — which is common for drinks that spread through hotel bars rather than books.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve immediately.
Dust with cocoa if you like.

name: Bitter Giuseppe
description: Cynar, sweet vermouth, lemon and orange bitters. Almost entirely bitter, served on the rocks, and a genuine test of your palate.
funFact: Stephen Cole created it at The Violet Hour in Chicago, and it is one of very few cocktails where the amaro is the base spirit rather than the modifier.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve as a digestif rather than an aperitif.

name: Art of Choke
