components.detail: White, élevé sous bois and vieux all produced

composition.process: Three distilleries on one small island, each with a distinctly different house style.

name: Mezcal Espadín
description: Made from Agave angustifolia, the cultivated workhorse behind around ninety per cent of all mezcal. Matures in six to eight years, which is fast for agave, and is the baseline against which every wild varietal is judged.
funFact: Espadín is the same species as the blue Weber used for tequila is closely related to, and it is the only agave farmed at real scale for mezcal.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, in a wide shallow glass, sipped rather than shot. Orange slices with sal de gusano are the traditional accompaniment in Oaxaca. Never chill it.

composition.summary: Cultivated Espadín agave pit-roasted, crushed and twice pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave angustifolia (Espadín), 6–8 years to maturity

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, tahona-crushed, copper or clay pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually joven, unaged

composition.process: Earth-pit roasting over hot stones is where all the smoke comes from — nothing is added.

name: Mezcal Tepeztate
description: From a wild agave that grows sideways out of cliff faces and takes up to twenty-five years to mature. Herbaceous, vegetal and unlike anything else — one of the most distinctive spirits made anywhere.
funFact: Tepeztate can take a quarter of a century to flower, which means a bottle drunk today comes from a plant that started growing before the mezcal boom existed.

serve.how: Neat and unhurried, in small sips. The vegetal, almost savoury profile confounds people expecting smoke and sweetness. It is a spirit to sit with rather than to introduce anyone to the category with.

composition.summary: Wild Tepeztate agave pit-roasted and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave marmorata, wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, small pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Maturation times this long make sustainable harvesting a genuine and unresolved problem.

name: Mezcal Madrecuixe
description: A wild agave with a long narrow trunk rather than a round heart, giving a mineral, almost saline mezcal. Twelve to fifteen years to maturity and harvested from the hillsides rather than farmed.
funFact: Madrecuixe is one of several karwinskii agaves whose long trunks look more like small trees than the rosette shape most people picture.

serve.how: Neat, small sips, at room temperature. The mineral quality is the signature and comes through most clearly on an empty palate — taste it before richer mezcals, not after.

composition.summary: Wild Madrecuixe agave roasted and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave karwinskii (Madrecuixe), wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: The trunk holds less sugar than a round piña, so yields are low and prices high.

name: Mezcal Arroqueño
description: A huge wild agave, sometimes over two metres across, taking fifteen to twenty-five years to mature. Sweet, earthy and full-bodied, with a richness the smaller agaves cannot reach.
funFact: Arroqueño is an ancestor of Espadín and one of the largest agaves used for mezcal, with single plants weighing hundreds of kilos.

serve.how: Neat and slowly. Its size means one plant yields a lot of spirit, but the decades to maturity keep it rare. Richer and sweeter than the karwinskii agaves, so serve it later in a tasting.

composition.summary: Wild Arroqueño agave roasted, crushed and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave americana var. oaxacensis, wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, tahona-crushed, pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: As a genetic parent of Espadín it shows the sweetness that cultivation selected for.

name: Mezcal Cuishe
description: Another long-trunked karwinskii agave, giving a mezcal that is dry, herbal and faintly medicinal. Around twelve years to maturity and almost entirely wild-harvested.
funFact: The karwinskii family — cuishe, madrecuixe, barril, tobasiche — are all closely related and locals distinguish them by trunk length and where on the hillside they grow.

serve.how: Neat, small pours. Drier and more austere than Espadín, and it makes an excellent bridge between the cultivated and wild styles for someone working through a flight.

composition.summary: Wild Cuishe agave pit-roasted and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave karwinskii (Cuishe), wild-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, crushed, copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Producers often distil the different karwinskii varieties separately purely to show the differences.

name: Mezcal Ensamble
description: Made by roasting and fermenting several agave varieties together, rather than blending finished spirits. A deliberate composition, and often how a producer uses a small wild harvest that could not fill a batch alone.
funFact: An ensamble differs from a blend: the agaves are combined before roasting, so they ferment and distil as one rather than being married afterwards.

serve.how: Neat, at room temperature. Ensambles are often more complex than any single varietal in them, and they are usually the best value in a producer's range because wild agave goes further.

composition.summary: Several agave species roasted, fermented and distilled together.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Two or more agave species, typically Espadín plus wild varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Combined before roasting, then distilled as one batch

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Combining before roasting rather than after distilling is what makes it an ensamble and not a blend.

name: Destilado de Agave
description: Agave spirit made outside the mezcal denomination — from the wrong state, the wrong paperwork or an unapproved method. Often identical in quality and sometimes better, but legally forbidden the name.
funFact: Several Mexican states with centuries of agave distilling — including Jalisco outside the tequila zone — fall outside the mezcal DO entirely, so their spirits cannot be called mezcal.

serve.how: Neat, as you would any mezcal. The label tells you about regulation rather than quality, and some of the most interesting agave spirits in Mexico sit in this category by geography alone.

composition.summary: Agave roasted, fermented and distilled outside the DO's boundaries.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Any agave species, cultivated or wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional pit-roast and pot still, usually

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Typically unaged

composition.process: The category exists because denominations of origin draw lines on maps, not around traditions.

name: Flavoured Pink Gin
description: Gin sweetened and coloured with red fruit — strawberry, raspberry, rhubarb — which took over British gin shelves in the late 2010s. Legally often not gin at all but a gin-based spirit drink, because of the sugar.
funFact: EU rules cap sweetening in anything sold as gin, so most pink gins are legally classed as gin-based spirit drinks rather than gin.

serve.glass: Chilled coupe for the classic, copa for the modern
serve.how: With tonic and ice, or with sparkling wine. It is sweet enough that a dry tonic and a wedge of lemon rather than more fruit keeps it in balance. Not to be confused with the naval Pink Gin, which is a cocktail of gin and Angostura and tastes nothing like this.

composition.summary: Gin sweetened and flavoured with red fruit after distillation.

components.label: Base
components.detail: London Dry or contemporary gin

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Strawberry, raspberry, redcurrant or rhubarb, plus sugar

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Fruit infused after distillation, not redistilled

composition.process: Sugar above 0.1g per litre disqualifies it from the plain gin designation in the EU.

name: Cream Gin
description: A Victorian curiosity revived by modern bartenders: gin redistilled with dairy cream, which leaves the texture and the sweetness behind but not the fat. Silky, faintly lactic, and entirely clear.
funFact: Nineteenth-century gin palaces sold it from casks, and the recipe was reconstructed in the 2000s from a Victorian bartending manual.

serve.how: In a Martini variant or a Ramos-style fizz, where the texture does work no other gin can. It is clear in the glass, so the mouthfeel takes people by surprise.

composition.summary: Gin redistilled with dairy cream so texture carries but fat does not.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Juniper-forward gin

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Fresh dairy cream, redistilled

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Cream added to the still and the spirit redistilled off it

composition.process: Distilling off the cream captures lactones and sugars while leaving fat and solids in the pot.

name: Gin de Mahón
description: Menorca's protected gin, distilled in wood-fired copper stills from wine alcohol rather than grain — a legacy of the British occupation of the island in the eighteenth century.
funFact: The British held Menorca for most of the 1700s and the Royal Navy's demand for gin outlived the occupation by three centuries.

serve.how: As a pomada — gin with cloudy lemonade over ice, which is the island's summer drink and served by the jug at the Sant Joan festival. Neat it is softer and rounder than a grain-based gin.

composition.summary: Wine alcohol redistilled with juniper over a wood fire.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Distilled wine alcohol, not grain

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper dominant, with a short supporting list

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills over wood fires

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak vats

composition.process: A wine base gives a rounder, slightly fruitier body than neutral grain spirit.

name: Jonge Jenever
description: The young style, capped at 15% malt wine, developed in the 1950s when grain was scarce and drinkers wanted something lighter. Closer to a soft vodka with a whisper of juniper than to gin.
funFact: Young and old here refer to the recipe rather than to ageing — a jonge jenever can be older in cask than an oude one.

serve.glass: Small tulip, filled to the brim
serve.how: From the freezer, poured until it domes over the rim, first sip taken with hands behind the back. A blonde lager alongside makes it a kopstootje — a headbutt.

composition.summary: Neutral grain spirit with a small proportion of malt wine and juniper.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit, max 15% malt wine

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, used sparingly

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column-distilled base, botanicals redistilled

composition.process: Wartime grain shortages drove the style, and Dutch taste never went back.

name: Oude Jenever
description: The old style, requiring at least 15% malt wine and often carrying far more. Maltier, rounder and closer to what gin tasted like in the seventeenth century before the English stripped the grain out of it.
funFact: English soldiers fighting in the Low Countries brought the habit home, and the phrase Dutch courage dates from those campaigns.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Holland Gin cocktail from a pre-Prohibition book — those recipes were written for this, not for London Dry, and taste entirely different when made correctly.

composition.summary: Malt wine and neutral spirit blended with juniper, often cask-rested.

components.label: Base
components.detail: At least 15% malt wine from rye, corn and malted barley

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, sometimes with caraway and aniseed

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot-distilled malt wine plus redistilled botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Frequently oak-rested

composition.process: The malt wine is the flavour; juniper is seasoning rather than the point.

name: Mediterranean Gin
description: A Spanish-led style built on olive, rosemary, thyme and citrus rather than a juniper spine, and served in enormous balloon glasses packed with ice. It changed how the whole world serves gin and tonic.
funFact: The oversized copa de balón came from Basque chefs, who reasoned that a wider bowl and more ice kept the drink colder and released more aroma.

serve.glass: Copa de balón, filled with ice
serve.how: Fill the glass with ice, add gin, then tonic poured down a bar spoon. Garnish to match the botanicals — rosemary, a strip of grapefruit, a green olive. Not lime, which fights the herbs.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with Mediterranean botanicals and softer juniper.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Arbequina olive, rosemary, thyme, basil, citrus peel, juniper

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with separate botanical distillates blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Pulling juniper back to make room for herbs is what defines the style and irritates traditionalists.

name: German Gin
description: Germany's gin scene grew out of its fruit-brandy tradition, so the base spirit is often grape or fruit rather than grain. Black Forest botanicals — spruce, lavender, angelica — dominate.
funFact: Monkey 47 takes its name from 47 botanicals and 47% ABV, and was inspired by a Black Forest recipe left by a British RAF officer after the war.

serve.how: With a light tonic and a garnish that echoes the forest — a spruce tip, a slice of apple, or lingonberries. Heavy Mediterranean tonics bury the delicate lavender and spruce entirely.

composition.summary: Grain or fruit spirit redistilled with Black Forest botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain, or a molasses and fruit blend

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, spruce, lavender, lingonberry, angelica, bramble leaf

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot stills, often fruit-brandy equipment

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some rested in earthenware

composition.process: A fruit-distilling heritage means German gin makers think about maceration times differently than grain distillers.

name: French Gin
description: Frequently built on a grape base rather than grain, which gives a softer, rounder body. Distillers borrow from perfumery and from wine, using floral botanicals and sometimes finishing in wine casks.
funFact: Grape-based gin is legal and increasingly common — the EU sets no restriction on the source of the neutral alcohol, only on the juniper.

serve.how: With a neutral tonic and a strip of lemon or a sprig of thyme. The grape base makes it unusually good in a Martini, where its softness reads as texture rather than weakness.

composition.summary: Grape or grain spirit redistilled with floral botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape spirit, often from Cognac or the Loire

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, rose, iris root, citrus blossom, cubeb

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, sometimes vapour infusion

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Occasionally wine-cask finished

composition.process: Grape spirit carries more body than grain, so French gin often needs less sweetening to taste round.

name: Nordic Gin
description: Built on foraged Scandinavian botanicals — dill, caraway, lingonberry, sea buckthorn, birch — and sometimes on aquavit's spice palette. Clean, herbal and unmistakably northern.
funFact: Juniper grows wild across all of Scandinavia and has flavoured Nordic food and drink for centuries, long before anyone there made gin.

serve.how: With a dry tonic and a sprig of dill or a few lingonberries. The caraway note means it also works in a Martini for anyone who likes aquavit — it sits halfway between the two categories.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with foraged Nordic botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, dill, caraway, lingonberry, sea buckthorn, birch, meadowsweet

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour baskets

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: Wild-foraged botanicals mean batches shift with the season, which producers treat as a feature.

name: Mexican Gin
description: Gin distilled with Mexican botanicals — damiana, cempasúchil marigold, avocado leaf, guava — and often on a base of agave or cane spirit rather than grain. A young category with a distinct accent.
funFact: Cempasúchil, the marigold used on Day of the Dead altars, appears in several Mexican gins and gives a distinctly resinous, floral note.

serve.how: With tonic and a slice of grapefruit or a sprig of epazote. The agave-based versions carry a vegetal edge that makes them excellent in a Negroni against a bitter amaro.

composition.summary: Agave, cane or grain spirit redistilled with Mexican botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Agave, cane or neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, damiana, cempasúchil, avocado leaf, guava, lime

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Unaged

composition.process: An agave base is what marks the most distinctive Mexican gins out from imports.

name: Bathtub Gin
description: Compound gin — botanicals steeped in finished spirit rather than redistilled — which is how gin was made illicitly during Prohibition and legitimately for centuries before. Cloudier, softer and fuller than a distilled gin.
funFact: The name comes from the story that Prohibition-era producers topped their bottles with water from a bathtub tap, being too tall to fit under a sink.

serve.how: With tonic and orange rather than lime — the cold-compounding leaves a rounder, spicier gin that suits a warmer garnish. It also makes an unusually rich Negroni.

composition.summary: Botanicals steeped directly in finished spirit and filtered, not redistilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, orange peel, coriander, cassia, cardamom, clove

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Cold compounding — infusion only

composition.process: Infusing rather than redistilling carries colour and oils that a still would leave behind.

name: Damson Gin
description: Damsons steeped in gin with sugar, the darker and tarter cousin of sloe gin. An English hedgerow tradition made at home each autumn and drunk the following winter.
funFact: Damsons were once grown in vast numbers in Westmorland for dyeing cloth as much as for eating, and the surviving orchards now supply gin makers.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or topped with sparkling wine. Tarter than sloe gin and less almond-driven, and it makes an excellent substitute in a Sloe Gin Fizz for anyone who finds sloe too sweet.

composition.summary: Damsons steeped in gin with sugar for several months.

components.label: Base
components.detail: London Dry gin

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Damsons, sugar; stones often left in

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, not redistilled

composition.process: Stones left in the steep supply the almond note, exactly as in sloe gin.

name: Rye Vodka
description: The Polish classic, distilled from rye and left with more character than the wheat and potato styles. Peppery, faintly spicy and sweeter on the finish than most drinkers expect vodka to be.
funFact: Rye was the grain of choice across Poland long before wheat, because it tolerates the poor sandy soils that wheat will not grow in.

serve.how: Cold rather than frozen — freezer temperatures mute exactly the peppery character that makes rye vodka worth choosing. With food, in small measures, alongside herring or salo.

composition.summary: Rye fermented and rectified, then cut with water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Polish rye

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column rectification, though not to full neutrality in good examples

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Stopping rectification slightly short is what leaves the grain character in the glass.

name: Wheat Vodka
description: The lightest and sweetest of the grain vodkas, and the base for most premium Western brands. Soft, faintly aniseed and easy — which is exactly why it dominates the market.
funFact: Wheat's high starch and low protein make it the most efficient grain for producing neutral spirit, which is as much of the reason for its dominance as taste.

serve.glass: Chilled shot glass, or Martini glass
serve.how: From the freezer, neat, or as the base of a Martini where its softness lets vermouth show. It is the least assertive vodka style, which makes it the safest in any mixed drink.

composition.summary: Winter wheat fermented and heavily rectified.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Winter wheat

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Multiple column rectification

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Charcoal filtration after distillation removes what little congener content survives.

name: Grape Vodka
description: Distilled from wine grapes rather than grain, which produces a vodka with noticeable floral and stone-fruit character. Naturally gluten-free, and a French speciality built on the country's wine surplus.
funFact: France produces more wine than it drinks, and distilling the surplus is a centuries-old solution that vodka gave a new market to.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Martini where the fruit character is a genuine asset. It is silkier than grain vodka and worth trying beside one to see how much the base material survives rectification.

composition.summary: Wine grapes fermented and rectified into neutral spirit.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Wine grapes, often Ugni Blanc or Colombard

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column rectification

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Even at high rectification a trace of the grape's terpenes carries into the finished spirit.

name: Whey Vodka
description: Distilled from the whey left over from cheesemaking, fermenting its lactose into alcohol. A genuinely circular use of a waste stream, and produced seriously in New Zealand and Ireland.
funFact: Cheese whey was for decades a disposal problem for dairies; fermenting its lactose turned a pollutant into a premium spirit.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Martini. It carries a faint creaminess that survives rectification, which makes it noticeably rounder than grain vodka in a stirred drink.

composition.summary: Cheese whey fermented on its lactose and rectified.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Whey from cheddar or similar cheesemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column rectification

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Lactose needs specific yeast strains to ferment, which is the technical hurdle the category had to clear.

name: Khrenovukha
description: Vodka infused with horseradish, honey and sometimes lemon, and one of Russia's most enduring household infusions. Sharp, hot and genuinely sinus-clearing, drunk with heavy food in winter.
funFact: Peter the Great is credited with decreeing that vodka be infused with horseradish, though the story is repeated far more often than it is sourced.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer, in one, with fatty food. The cold blunts the horseradish just enough to make it possible; at room temperature it is close to unpleasant.

composition.summary: Vodka infused with fresh horseradish root and honey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain vodka

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Fresh horseradish root, honey, sometimes lemon and mustard seed

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused for days, then strained

composition.process: Steeping time is critical — left too long the horseradish turns bitter and overwhelming.

name: Wiśniówka
description: Polish cherry-infused vodka, made at home each summer by steeping sour cherries with sugar. Deep red, sweet-tart, and one of the most widely made nalewki in the country.
funFact: The steeped cherries are eaten afterwards and are, by that point, considerably more alcoholic than the drink itself.

serve.how: At cellar temperature after a meal, with a couple of the steeped cherries in the glass. Polish households open the summer's batch at Christmas, which is when it is at its best.

composition.summary: Sour cherries macerated in vodka with sugar for months.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rye or wheat vodka

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sour cherries, sugar; some stones left in

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated only

composition.process: Cracked stones supply the almond note that separates a good wiśniówka from cherry syrup.

name: Citron Vodka
description: Lemon-flavoured vodka, launched in 1988 and responsible almost single-handedly for the Cosmopolitan and the Lemon Drop. The flavoured-vodka boom of the 1990s started here.
funFact: Absolut Citron's launch is generally credited with kicking off the flavoured vodka category, which grew to hundreds of variants within a decade.

serve.how: In a Cosmopolitan or a Lemon Drop, both of which were built around it. Neat from the freezer it is sharper and cleaner than the sugary flavoured vodkas that followed it.

composition.summary: Grain vodka flavoured with citrus peel distillate.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Winter wheat vodka

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Lemon and lime peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Citrus distillate blended in after rectification

composition.process: Better versions use a peel distillate rather than an essence, and the difference is obvious neat.

name: Swedish Vodka
description: Made from winter wheat grown on the plains around Åhus and distilled continuously rather than in batches. Soft, faintly grainy and the template most premium Western vodka followed.
funFact: Absolut is distilled entirely in one small Swedish town, using wheat grown within a short radius and water from a local well — a level of concentration unusual at that scale.

serve.glass: Chilled shot glass or Martini glass
serve.how: Freezer cold and neat with food, in the Swedish snaps tradition, or as a clean Martini base. Its softness makes it forgiving in almost any mixed drink.

composition.summary: Winter wheat continuously distilled and cut with local water.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Åhus winter wheat

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Continuous rectification

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Continuous rather than batch distillation is what gives the consistency the brand was built on.

name: Birch Sap Vodka
description: Made using birch sap, tapped from trees for a few weeks each spring as the ground thaws. Faintly sweet and mineral, and a Baltic and Nordic tradition older than vodka itself.
funFact: Birch sap runs for only two or three weeks a year, and a mature tree yields just a few litres a day before the leaves open and the flow stops.

serve.how: Cold and neat in a small glass. The sap character is delicate, so it is wasted in a mixed drink — this is one to taste beside a plain grain vodka to see what the sap actually does.

composition.summary: Grain spirit cut or fermented with spring-tapped birch sap.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain spirit, with birch sap in place of water or in the ferment

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column rectification

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: The harvest window is fixed by the thaw, so annual production is capped by nature rather than demand.

name: Quinoa Vodka
description: Distilled from Andean quinoa, a seed rather than a grain, giving a naturally gluten-free spirit with a distinctly nutty character. A modern South American answer to the premium vodka market.
funFact: Quinoa must be washed thoroughly before use because its natural saponin coating is bitter and soapy — a step that matters as much for distilling as for cooking.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or in a Martini where the nuttiness gives more to work with than grain vodka does. It also stands up well in a savoury cocktail.

composition.summary: Andean quinoa fermented and rectified into vodka.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Royal quinoa from the Bolivian altiplano

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column rectification

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Saponins must be washed off before fermentation or they carry a bitterness right through the process.

name: Feng-Aroma Baijiu
description: The phoenix aroma from Shaanxi, sitting between the light and strong styles. Fermented in earthen pits that are rebuilt annually rather than aged for centuries, then rested in wicker baskets sealed with wax.
funFact: Xifeng's storage vessels are woven baskets lined with pig's blood and beeswax, a method that imparts a specific flavour no other baijiu has.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. It is a good bridge for anyone who finds strong-aroma too pungent and light-aroma too plain.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in annually rebuilt earth pits, then basket-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with barley and pea qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Wax-sealed wicker baskets rather than earthenware jars

composition.process: Rebuilding the pits each year is the opposite of the strong-aroma approach and deliberately so.

name: Sesame-Aroma Baijiu
description: The chi aroma from Shandong, created in the 1950s and the newest of the recognised baijiu categories. Smells distinctly of toasted sesame, which is unusual enough that it earned its own classification.
funFact: It was identified as a distinct aroma category only in 1957, making it the youngest of the major baijiu styles by several centuries.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food. The sesame note is genuinely reminiscent of the oil, and it pairs remarkably well with northern Chinese dishes that already use it.

composition.summary: Sorghum, wheat and bran fermented in brick-lined pits.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with wheat, bran and barley qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, in brick and mud pits

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The sesame note comes from the fermentation, not from any sesame — none is used.

name: Mixed-Aroma Baijiu
description: The jian aroma, deliberately combining techniques from the sauce, strong and light styles in one spirit. A twentieth-century innovation that treats the classical categories as a palette rather than a set of rules.
funFact: Baijiu aroma categories are formally defined by Chinese national standards, and adding a new one requires state recognition.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with a meal. It is the most approachable style for a newcomer, because no single characteristic dominates the way sauce-aroma umami or strong-aroma funk does.

composition.summary: Techniques from several aroma families combined in one production process.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with mixed grains

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended methods drawn from sauce, strong and light aroma production

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: Deliberate hybridisation rather than regional tradition, which makes it unusual in a conservative category.

name: Medicinal-Aroma Baijiu
description: The yao aroma from Guizhou, fermented with over a hundred medicinal herbs worked into the qu starter. Herbal, bitter-edged and closer to a tonic than the other baijiu styles.
funFact: Dongjiu's qu starter incorporates more than a hundred Chinese medicinal herbs, which is why the category is named for medicine rather than for a flavour.

serve.how: Room temperature, small cups, with food. The herbal bitterness makes it the baijiu most likely to appeal to an amaro drinker, and the least likely to appeal to a whisky one.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented with a herb-laden qu in stone pits.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, rice, and qu containing 100+ herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation in stone-lined pits

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware

composition.process: The herbs go into the starter culture rather than being infused afterwards, so they drive fermentation as well as flavour.

name: Soba Shochu
description: Buckwheat shochu, first made in Miyazaki in 1973 and now a category of its own. Lighter and more delicate than barley or sweet potato, with the faint nuttiness of soba noodles.
funFact: Buckwheat is not a grain but a seed related to rhubarb, which is why soba shochu is naturally gluten-free.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with cold water
serve.how: On the rocks or mizuwari with cold water. It is among the gentlest shochu styles, which makes it a good introduction, and it is exceptional alongside actual soba noodles.

composition.summary: Buckwheat fermented with koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Buckwheat

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or buckwheat koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, often vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Vacuum distillation at low pressure preserves the delicate nutty character heat would strip.

name: Kasutori Shochu
description: Distilled from sake lees — the pressed rice solids left after sake is made — rather than from fresh grain. A genuine circular product, and unmistakably sake-scented.
funFact: Sake lees, kasu, are also used to pickle vegetables and marinate fish, so distilling them is one of several traditional uses for what is technically a by-product.

serve.how: Cool and neat, or on the rocks. It smells strikingly of sake, which surprises people expecting a neutral spirit, and it is superb with the same food sake suits.

composition.summary: Sake lees fermented further and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sake kasu — pressed lees from sake production

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually rested briefly

composition.process: Lees still carry rice starch and yeast, so they ferment again readily before distilling.

name: Goma Shochu
description: Sesame shochu, a rare Japanese style in which roasted sesame seeds are fermented alongside rice. Deeply nutty and aromatic, and produced by only a handful of distillers.
funFact: Sesame is expensive and low-yielding as a fermentable, which is why the style has never grown beyond a few producers.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with hot water
serve.how: On the rocks, or oyuwari with hot water, which lifts the sesame aroma dramatically. It is one of the few shochu styles that genuinely improves with heat.

composition.summary: Roasted sesame seeds fermented with rice and koji, then distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sesame seeds with rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

composition.process: Roasting the seeds before fermentation is what develops the aroma the style is built on.

name: Awamori Kusu
description: Awamori aged at least three years in earthenware, traditionally by topping older jars from younger ones. Some family kusu is said to have been maintained for over a century before the war destroyed most of it.
funFact: Almost all of Okinawa's pre-war kusu was destroyed in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, so genuinely ancient stock effectively no longer exists.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.how: Neat at room temperature in a small cup, or on the rocks. Okinawans traditionally cut it with water and let it sit overnight before serving, which softens it noticeably.

composition.summary: Awamori aged three years or more in clay pots by fractional topping.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Long-grain Thai rice with black koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware; traditional systems run far longer

composition.process: Clay is slightly porous, so the spirit oxidises slowly in a way glass or steel would not allow.

name: Sato
description: Thai glutinous rice spirit from the northeast, made with a traditional starter cake and distilled at village scale. The rural counterpart to commercial lao khao, and central to Isan hospitality.
funFact: Home production was illegal in Thailand for most of the twentieth century and was only partially liberalised in the 2000s, driving a revival of village distilling.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, shared, with food. In Isan it appears at every festival and family gathering, and refusing the first glass is difficult to do gracefully.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a look pang starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Glutinous rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Look pang — a yeast and mould starter cake

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Village pot stills

composition.process: The same fermented base drunk unfiltered and undistilled is also called sato, which causes confusion.

name: Rượu Nếp
description: Northern Vietnamese sticky rice spirit, distilled from the fermented glutinous rice that is also eaten as a dish in its own right. Sweeter and rounder than the southern rượu đế.
funFact: The fermented rice itself is eaten at the Tết Đoan Ngọ festival, traditionally on an empty stomach and first thing in the morning.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, poured for others and drunk together. Northern Vietnamese households make it for Tết and it appears at weddings and ancestor ceremonies year-round.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a herb-laden starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Northern glutinous rice varieties

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Men rượu starter, often containing herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, usually single

composition.process: Sticky rice ferments sweeter than ordinary rice, which carries into the distillate.

name: Aguardiente Antioqueño
description: Colombia's national spirit: anise-flavoured cane alcohol, produced under state monopoly with each department bottling its own brand. Fiercely regional — Antioqueños and Caleños will argue about it at length.
funFact: Colombian departments hold the production monopoly, so each has its own aguardiente brand and defending yours is a matter of regional identity.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in small glasses, shared from the bottle over a long evening. Colombians drink it with food and music rather than as a shot, and the sin azúcar versions are drier and increasingly preferred.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit flavoured with anise and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Colombian sugarcane alcohol

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Aniseed, plus sugar in the standard versions

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column-distilled, then flavoured

composition.process: Departmental monopolies date to the colonial era and still fund regional budgets.

name: Absinthe Verte
description: The green style, coloured naturally by steeping herbs in the finished spirit so chlorophyll bleeds in. That colour fades to amber with age, which is how a genuine old bottle is recognised.
funFact: Naturally coloured absinthe turns amber over years as the chlorophyll degrades — a bottle described as feuille morte, dead leaf, is old rather than spoiled.

serve.glass: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
serve.how: Three to five parts iced water dripped slowly over a sugar cube on a slotted spoon. The louche should build gradually. No flames — burning the sugar is a 1990s invention that scorches the herbs.

composition.summary: Wormwood, anise and fennel distilled, then steeped with herbs for colour.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral or wine-based spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel; petite wormwood and hyssop for colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then a second cold steep for natural colour

composition.process: Artificially coloured absinthe stays green forever, which is the giveaway.

name: Absinthe Blanche
description: The clear style, bottled straight off the still with no colouring step. Swiss in origin, where clandestine producers kept it colourless through the ban so it could pass as something innocent.
funFact: Swiss bootleggers kept it clear precisely because a colourless bottle was easier to explain to the authorities than a vivid green one — the style outlived the reason for it.

serve.how: Iced water dripped slowly, three to five parts to one. Blanche louches to a bright opalescent white rather than a cloudy green, and it tends to be cleaner and more herbal than verte.

composition.summary: Wormwood and anise distilled and bottled without a colouring steep.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled once with botanicals; no second steep

composition.process: Skipping the colouring step also skips the extra herb tannin, which is why blanche often tastes brighter.

name: Dill Aquavit
description: The Danish and Swedish variation in which dill leads rather than caraway. Fresher and greener than the classic style, and built for the summer table rather than the winter one.
funFact: Scandinavian aquavit must legally take its dominant flavour from caraway or dill — those two, and no others, define the category in EU law.

serve.how: From the freezer, in small measures, with food rather than before it. Dill aquavit belongs with crayfish and new potatoes in a way the caraway styles do not — it is a summer spirit.

composition.summary: Grain or potato spirit redistilled with dill as the lead botanical.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grain or potato neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dill leading, with fennel, coriander and citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: Dill's aromatics are fragile, so it goes in later and gentler than caraway would.

name: Taffel Akvavit
description: The classic Danish table aquavit, clear and caraway-forward, unaged and bottled at 45%. What Danes mean when they say akvavit without qualifying it further.
funFact: Taffel means table, and the name marks it as the everyday version rather than an aged or special bottling.

serve.how: Freezer cold, in small measures, with the meal. Danish tradition is a beer alongside and a toast before each glass, with eye contact — skipping the eye contact is the part visitors get wrong.

composition.summary: Grain spirit redistilled with caraway and citrus, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Caraway dominant, plus citrus peel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Redistilled with botanicals

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

composition.process: Bottling unaged and clear is what distinguishes it from the oak-rested Norwegian styles.

name: Kruidenbitter
description: The Dutch herbal bitter category, of which Beerenburg is the most famous example. Juniper spirit steeped with gentian, bay and laurel, drunk cold and largely by people who grew up with it.
funFact: Amsterdam spice merchants sold the herb blends over the counter so drinkers could steep their own jenever at home, which is how the category began.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass. Dutch and Frisian drinkers take it before or after food rather than with it, and often alongside a beer.

composition.summary: Jenever or neutral spirit steeped with a fixed herb blend.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Jenever or grain spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, bay, laurel, juniper berry, and a dozen more

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated rather than redistilled

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation keeps the herbs green and raw rather than polished.

name: Horincă
description: The Maramureș variant of Romanian fruit brandy, double or triple distilled to a considerably higher strength than țuică. Made from plums or apples in the far north, and a matter of local pride.
funFact: Names shift by region across Romania — țuică in the south, horincă in Maramureș, pălincă in Transylvania, jinars in parts of the west — for broadly the same tradition.

serve.how: Room temperature, neat, in small glasses, offered on arrival. Northern Romanian households serve it warmed with honey and pepper in winter, which is called a fiartă.

composition.summary: Plums or apples fermented and distilled two or three times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plums, apples or pears from Maramureș orchards

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double or triple distillation in copper

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes rested in mulberry or oak

composition.process: The extra distillation is what separates it from țuică, and locals consider the strength a point of honour.

name: Medovina Rakija
description: Honey-fermented rakija from the Balkans — distinct from medovača, which is rakija sweetened with honey after the fact. Here the honey is fermented and distilled, which is a different drink entirely.
funFact: Fermenting honey is the basis of mead, the oldest known alcoholic drink, so distilling it produces something closer to a mead brandy than to a fruit rakija.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small pour after a meal. It is rounder and more floral than fruit rakija, and worth tasting beside a medovača to see the difference between fermenting honey and adding it.

composition.summary: Honey fermented into mead and then distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Honey, fermented with water

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, usually twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes oak-rested

composition.process: Honey ferments slowly and needs nutrient additions, which is why honey distillates are rare everywhere.

name: Macallan 12 Sherry Oak
description: Sherry Cask Single Malt from Scotland. Speyside; matured in seasoned Oloroso casks.
funFact: Macallan 12 Sherry Oak: Speyside; matured in seasoned Oloroso casks

serve.how: Neat, with water added sparingly. Sherry casks carry a lot of tannin, so heavy dilution turns them drying rather than sweeter. Oloroso gives nuts and spice; PX gives raisin and syrup.

composition.summary: Malt whisky matured in ex-sherry European or American oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-oloroso, ex-Pedro Ximénez or ex-fino casks

composition.process: European oak gives more tannin and spice; American oak seasoned with sherry is softer and sweeter.

name: Macallan 18 Sherry Oak
description: Sherry Cask Single Malt from Scotland.
funFact: One of 8 Sherry Cask Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

name: Glenfiddich 12
description: Speyside Single Malt from Scotland. The world's best-selling single malt.
funFact: Glenfiddich 12: The world's best-selling single malt

serve.how: Serve a neat dram in a Glencairn at cellar temperature and nose it patiently — apple, honey, and vanilla should rise in sequence, with sherried fruit on richer bottlings. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate; Speyside's elegance is about balance rather than punch. A few drops of water can unfold extra orchard fruit, but many Speysides are perfect exactly as poured.

composition.summary: All-malt Scotch from a single distillery in the River Spey valley.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Malted barley, typically unpeated

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot stills, twice, at one of roughly fifty distilleries

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak; sherry casks are a regional signature

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Typically 40–46% ABV

composition.process: Tall stills and generous sherry-cask maturation build the honeyed, orchard-fruit house style.

serve.how: Serve a neat dram in a Glencairn at cellar temperature and nose it patiently — apple, honey, and vanilla should rise in sequence, with sherried fruit on richer bottlings. Sip slowly and let it coat the palate; Speyside's elegance is about balance rather than punch. A few drops of water can unfold extra orchard fruit, but many Speysides are perfect exactly as poured.

name: Ardbeg 10
description: Islay Single Malt from Scotland. Heavily peated Islay.
funFact: Ardbeg 10: Heavily peated Islay

serve.how: Pour a dram neat into a Glencairn and let it breathe for several minutes — peat smoke dominates a fresh pour and settles into iodine, brine, and tar complexity with air. Sip in small doses and exhale slowly through your nose to get the full bonfire effect. A few drops of water famously cracks Islay malts open, trading some smoke for surprising sweetness underneath; ice just puts the fire out.
pair: oysters (even with a drop of whisky in the shell)

serve.how: Pour a dram neat into a Glencairn and let it breathe for several minutes — peat smoke dominates a fresh pour and settles into iodine, brine, and tar complexity with air. Sip in small doses and exhale slowly through your nose to get the full bonfire effect. A few drops of water famously cracks Islay malts open, trading some smoke for surprising sweetness underneath; ice just puts the fire out.
pair: oysters (even with a drop of whisky in the shell)

name: Glenmorangie Original 10
description: Highland Single Malt from Scotland.
funFact: One of 19 Highland Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve a dram at cool room temperature in a Glencairn, swirl gently, and nose for heather and dried fruit before the first sip. Because the Highlands span so many styles, taste it on its own terms — some pours lean floral and honeyed, others muscular with a wisp of smoke. A teaspoon of water is the classic move if the malt feels closed; add it gradually and re-nose each time.

serve.how: Pour a dram into a Glencairn and let it rest five full minutes — Campbeltown's oily, briny character rewards patience. serve.how: This is the most flexible Scotch on the shelf: sip it neat in a rocks glass at cellar temperature, add a single cube, or stretch it into a highball with chilled soda — all three are legitimate. name: Knob Creek Single Barrel
description: Single Barrel Bourbon from USA.
funFact: One of 4 Single Barrel Bourbon bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat into a Glencairn and taste attentively, because this exact flavor exists only in this one barrel's run: note the dark caramel, cherry, and oak, and jot down the barrel number if the label carries one. Add a few drops of water on higher-proof picks to spread the fruit out. Comparing two different barrels of the same label side by side is one of bourbon's great home games.

name: Basil Hayden
description: High-Rye Bourbon from USA.
funFact: One of 2 High-Rye Bourbon bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour neat into a rocks glass and taste for the tug-of-war that defines the style: bourbon's caramel sweetness up front, then a cinnamon-and-pepper rye snap on the back half. A single large cube softens the spice without erasing it. This is also the ideal Old Fashioned bourbon, since the rye kick stands up to sugar and bitters.

name: Jim Beam White Label
description: Bourbon from USA.
funFact: One of 11 Bourbon bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour two fingers into a rocks glass and try it neat first, nosing for caramel, vanilla, and charred oak before the first sip. Let each sip rest on the tongue a beat so the corn sweetness spreads before the oak spice arrives. One large cube slowly opens it up on a warm evening, and if you would rather go long, bourbon and ginger ale is a forgiving classic.

name: Wild Turkey Rare Breed
description: Cask Strength Bourbon from USA.
funFact: One of 5 Cask Strength Bourbon bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp, with water on standby
serve.how: Pour a smaller-than-usual measure into a Glencairn and approach in stages: nose gently from a distance first, since 60%-plus alcohol will singe an eager nostril. Take a tiny first sip to calibrate, then add water a few drops at a time, tasting between additions until the burnt sugar and dark cherry bloom out of the heat. Finding each barrel's ideal dilution point is the whole sport.

name: Russell's Reserve 10
description: Small Batch Bourbon from USA.
funFact: One of 6 Small Batch Bourbon bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour into a rocks glass neat or over one big cube; small batch is blended for balance, so it rarely needs taming. Nose for vanilla and toasted nuts, then sip for the caramel mid-palate and gentle oak-spice finish that the blender worked to make consistent. It is the reliable house pour: great neat, great in an Old Fashioned, never a wasted dram.

name: Balcones Texas Single Malt

funFact: One of 5 American Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a standard dram into a Glencairn, swirl gently, and nose in short sniffs with your mouth slightly open to catch malt, chocolate, and orchard fruit. Sip neat first, then add a few drops of water to unlock the toasted-oak depths; many American single malts run above 43% and open beautifully. Compare it mentally to Scotch, the malt DNA is the same but the New World oak speaks louder.

serve.how: Honor the highball: fill a tall glass to the brim with clear ice, pour one part whisky, stir a few times to chill, then gently add three to four parts cold soda and stir once. The delicate honey, incense, and orchard-fruit notes stay vivid through the dilution — precision drinking for a precise spirit. Better bottles equally reward a quiet neat pour in a Glencairn at room temperature; either way, restraint is the flavor.

funFact: One of 12 Japanese Whisky bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Honor the highball: fill a tall glass to the brim with clear ice, pour one part whisky, stir a few times to chill, then gently add three to four parts cold soda and stir once. The delicate honey, incense, and orchard-fruit notes stay vivid through the dilution — precision drinking for a precise spirit. Better bottles equally reward a quiet neat pour in a Glencairn at room temperature; either way, restraint is the flavor.

name: Amrut Fusion
description: Indian Single Malt from India.
funFact: One of 4 Indian Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve a dram in a Glencairn at cool room temperature and expect ripeness beyond its years — tropical heat matured this malt at a sprint. Nose for mango-adjacent tropical fruit and barley sugar, then sip and follow the spice into toasted oak. Bottlings often run 46-50%, so keep water handy and add a few drops if the jammy fruit feels buried under heat.

name: Kavalan Classic
description: Taiwanese Single Malt from Taiwan.
funFact: One of 3 Taiwanese Single Malt bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour a dram into a Glencairn at cellar temperature and nose it slowly — the mango and sherried-fruit perfume is the calling card of subtropical aging. Sip and let it linger; the vanilla and polished oak arrive fast and rich because the Taiwanese climate compresses decades of maturation into a few years. Cask-strength releases can top 55%, so add water drop by drop until the fruit basket fully opens.

name: Tanqueray London Dry
description: London Dry Gin from England.
funFact: One of 14 London Dry Gin bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: London dry is at its best ice-cold and bracing: stir it into a martini with dry vermouth over plenty of ice, strain into a chilled coupe, and finish with a lemon twist expressed over the surface. For a simpler serve, build a gin and tonic over abundant ice with a wedge of lime. Either way, nose before sipping and let the piney juniper hit first, then hunt for the citrus peel and coriander backbone that follow.

name: Sipsmith V.J.O.P.
description: Navy Strength Gin from England.
funFact: One of 2 Navy Strength Gin bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: At 57%+, this gin rewards cold and dilution: stash the bottle in the freezer, then pour a small measure into a chilled coupe, or stir it into a martini where the extra proof keeps the juniper vivid through the ice. If sipping it straight, add a few drops of water and let it sit a minute before nosing. Notice how the pepper-and-heat edge recedes as it opens, leaving intense juniper and bright citrus oils.

name: Hayman's Old Tom
description: Old Tom Gin from England.
funFact: One of 3 Old Tom Gin bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Chill the bottle well and pour a couple of ounces into a cold coupe — Old Tom's light sweetness makes it far more sippable neat than a London dry. For the full history lesson, build it into a Tom Collins or a Martinez, the drinks it was revived to complete. Taste for the rounded, honeyed edge that softens the juniper; that gentle sweetness is the whole point of the style.

name: Hendrick's
description: Contemporary Gin from Scotland. Cucumber and rose.
funFact: Hendrick's: Cucumber and rose

serve.how: Build a Spanish-style gin tonic: fill a large copa glass to the top with ice, pour in two ounces of well-chilled gin, add a quality tonic slowly down a bar spoon, and garnish to match the botanicals — cucumber for fresh styles, rose petals or grapefruit for floral and citrus-led ones. The big bowl traps the aromatics, so nose the glass before each sip. Taste for what leads: in these modern gins the juniper steps back and the signature botanical should shine.

name: Bols Genever
description: Genever from Netherlands.
funFact: The only Genever bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: 38-45°F, well chilled (oude styles closer to cellar temp)
serve.how: Do it the Dutch way: fill a small tulip glass to the very brim with chilled genever, leave it on the bar, and bend down for the first sip hands-free — the ritual is called the 'kopstootje' when paired with a beer chaser. Sip slowly and notice how the malty, bready base makes it read halfway between whisky and gin. Richer oude and barrel-aged genevers deserve slightly warmer service so the honeyed malt can open up.

name: Reyka
description: Grain Vodka from Iceland.
funFact: One of 13 Grain Vodka bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Store the bottle in the freezer and pour small measures into chilled shot glasses — the cold thickens the texture to a silky, almost viscous pour. Sip rather than slam it, and pay attention to the finish: good grain vodka shows faint cream, white pepper, and mineral notes instead of burn. Serve it alongside salty little bites, Eastern European style, refilling glasses in rounds.
pair: caviar or salted roe on blini

name: Bacardí Carta Blanca
description: White Rum from Cuba.

serve.how: Serve it cold — straight from the freezer door or over fresh ice in a rocks glass — since chill sharpens its clean sugarcane snap. description: Gold Rum from Cuba.

name: Appleton Estate Signature
description: Jamaican Pot Still Rum from Jamaica.
funFact: One of 7 Jamaican Pot Still Rum bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour it neat in a rocks glass and give it a good nose before sipping — the famous 'hogo' of overripe banana and pineapple is the whole show. Let it sit on your tongue a beat longer than you would other rums so the ester funk unfolds into allspice on the finish. High-proof bottlings welcome a big cube or a teaspoon of water, which softens the heat and amplifies the fruit.

name: Wray & Nephew Overproof
description: Overproof Rum from Jamaica.
funFact: One of 2 Overproof Rum bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: At 57%+ this is not a neat-pour spirit for most people — serve a small measure over one large cube, or better yet lengthen it into a highball with plenty of ice in its natural habitat, a tiki mug. If you do taste it neat, take tiny sips and let the ripe banana and burnt sugar punch through the heat; a splash of water reveals surprising fruit. Keep it well away from open flames unless you actually intend the theatrical float.

serve.how: Serve it in a rocks glass over one big cube, which slowly opens the molasses and coffee notes as it melts. name: Rhum Clément VSOP
description: Rhum Agricole from Martinique.
funFact: One of 4 Rhum Agricole bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Drink it the Martinique way: a short pour in a rocks glass at room temperature, ideally as a Ti' Punch — a squeeze of lime disc and a small spoon of cane syrup stirred right in the glass. Neat, swirl gently and breathe in the fresh-cut-grass and green-olive aromas that molasses rums never show. Skip heavy ice on aged expressions; the vegetal character is delicate and fades when over-chilled.

name: Clairin Sajous
description: Clairin from Haiti.
funFact: One of 2 Clairin bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or one large cube
serve.how: Pour a modest ounce and a half neat into a rocks glass and let it sit for a minute — wild-ferment cane spirits open up dramatically with a little air. Sip slowly and hunt for the olive-brine savoriness underneath the fresh cane and tropical fruit; every bottling is different, so taste it blind before deciding whether it needs a cube. If the proof runs hot (many are 50%+), a single large cube or a few drops of water tames the fire without muting the funk.

name: Cruzan Single Barrel

name: Pusser's Gunpowder Proof
description: Overproof Rum from British Virgin Islands.
funFact: One of 2 Overproof Rum bottlings catalogued here.

If you do taste it neat, take tiny sips and let the ripe banana and burnt sugar punch through the heat; a splash of water reveals surprising fruit. Keep it well away from open flames unless you actually intend the theatrical float.

name: Captain Morgan Spiced
description: Spiced Rum from Jamaica.
funFact: One of 4 Spiced Rum bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Spiced rum is happiest long and cold: fill a highball with ice, pour two ounces, and top with cola or ginger beer plus a lime wedge. The vanilla and cinnamon are built to mingle with a mixer rather than stand alone, though a chilled neat pour works as an easy after-dinner nip. Notice how the clove and caramel bloom on the finish once the initial sweetness fades.

name: Ypióca Ouro
description: Cachaça from Brazil.
funFact: One of 5 Cachaça bottlings catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp, neat (unaged) or one cube (aged)
serve.how: Sip artisanal unaged cachaça neat at room temperature in a rocks or small tulip glass, nosing for the fresh-cane, grass, and green-banana brightness that column rum lacks; barrel-aged expressions take a single cube well. And of course, muddle lime and sugar in a rocks glass, add ice and a generous pour, and you have Brazil's caipirinha — the drink this spirit was destined for. Notice how the vegetal cane character stays lively even under citrus.

funFact: The only Batavia Arrack bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Taste it first neat at room temperature in a small glass or punch cup, taking short sniffs to map its smoky, funky, black-tea strangeness — it is unlike any rum you know. Then honor its history: build a classic punch with lemon, sugar, water, and tea, where its 48-50% funk blooms into dried-fruit richness. A little goes a long way as a seasoning spirit, even a quarter ounce transforming an otherwise ordinary cocktail.

name: Pitorro Casero
description: Pitorro from Puerto Rico.
funFact: The only Pitorro bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Serve traditional clear pitorro in a small shot glass at cellar temperature, sipping slowly and respectfully — at 40-60% it demands small draws, revealing raw sugarcane and a green funky edge. Fruit-cured 'pitorro curao,' steeped with tropical fruit for months, is best lightly chilled so the infusion stays bright. Around the holidays, do as Puerto Rican families do and fold it into homemade coquito, or toast with it straight at the Christmas table.

Take small sips and look for white pepper, citrus, and green herbs riding over the sweet agave core. A slight chill crisps it up in summer, but avoid heavy icing, which mutes the vegetal brightness.

No ice, no citrus, no mixing: at this rarity you are tasting a plant that took a decade to grow in a mountain canyon.

Room temperature keeps those delicate herbal notes alive.

description: Armagnac from France.

serve.how: Pour a modest ounce and a half into a snifter or small tulip and give it ten patient minutes to breathe — older Armagnacs unfold dramatically with air. Sip in small draws with no ice and no water at first; this is a fireside spirit meant to be interrogated over an hour.

name: Torres 10
description: Brandy de Jerez from Spain.
funFact: One of 4 Brandy de Jerez bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Pour into a snifter at room temperature and let it rest a few minutes before nosing — the sherry-cask perfume of raisin and fig needs a moment to assemble. Swirl gently and sip slowly, chasing the nutty oloroso richness through to the toffee finish. Its softer 36-40% strength makes it an easy neat sipper after dinner; ice is forgivable on a hot Andalusian-style afternoon but mutes the sherry character.

name: Nardini Grappa

serve.how: Serve a small pour — an ounce or so — in a narrow tulip glass, slightly cool for young grappa and closer to room temperature for barrel-aged riservas. Sip in small amounts as a digestivo after dinner, or tip a splash into your espresso for a classic caffè corretto.

serve.how: Hungarians insist pálinka be served around 60-65°F, never ice-cold — chilling smothers the pure apricot and orchard-fruit aromatics that are the whole point. Traditionally it opens a meal as much as it closes one, always accompanied by a toast: egészségedre.

serve.how: Pour one part pastis into a tall or small tumbler and top with about five parts very cold water — the drink blooms milky yellow on contact. Sip unhurried, aperitif-style, noticing star anise and licorice mellowing into gentle sweet herbs; it should taste like a Marseille terrace at golden hour.

Sip it alongside food rather than alone, letting small sips reset your palate between bites of mezze; notice the grape sweetness underneath the licorice.

description: Light-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Light-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food, or lightly chilled if it is your first baijiu. Its cleaner profile also makes it the style most usable in cocktails, where it behaves a little like a funky gin.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in stone jars with barley and pea qu.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, with a barley and pea qu starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, two fermentations

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware, typically shorter than other styles

composition.process: Stone jars keep the ferment isolated from soil microbes, which is why the style stays clean.

name: Erguotou Red Star
description: Erguotou from China.
glassware: Small cup or straight from the bottle
funFact: The only Erguotou bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature, in small cups, with street food. It is a working drink and treated as one; nobody in Beijing contemplates their erguotou. It also mixes surprisingly well with sour or citrus flavours.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented and distilled, with only the middle cut kept.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state distillation, middle fraction only

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimal

composition.process: Discarding the head and tail of the run is exactly what the name describes, and why it is cleaner than its price suggests.

name: Kinmen Kaoliang
description: Kaoliang from Taiwan.
funFact: The only Kaoliang bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. At 58% it is not a sipping spirit; Taiwanese custom is to drain the cup on a toast and refill.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented with wheat qu and solid-state distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum grown on Kinmen

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Stored in granite tunnels cut into the island

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 38–63%, with 58% the signature

composition.process: The granite tunnels hold a stable cool temperature year-round, which is why they are still used.

name: Xifeng
description: Feng-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Feng-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. It is a good bridge for anyone who finds strong-aroma too pungent and light-aroma too plain.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in annually rebuilt earth pits, then basket-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with barley and pea qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state fermentation and distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Wax-sealed wicker baskets rather than earthenware jars

composition.process: Rebuilding the pits each year is the opposite of the strong-aroma approach and deliberately so.

name: Jinmailang Sesame
description: Sesame-Aroma Baijiu from China.
funFact: The only Sesame-Aroma Baijiu bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food. The sesame note is genuinely reminiscent of the oil, and it pairs remarkably well with northern Chinese dishes that already use it.

composition.summary: Sorghum, wheat and bran fermented in brick-lined pits.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with wheat, bran and barley qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, in brick and mud pits

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Earthenware jars

composition.process: The sesame note comes from the fermentation, not from any sesame — none is used.

name: Iichiko
description: Mugi Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Mugi Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with cold water
serve.how: On the rocks, or mizuwari with cold water at about one to one. Barrel-aged versions drink comfortably neat and are often mistaken for a light whisky in a blind pour.

composition.summary: Barley fermented with barley koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Barley

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Barley or rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, often under vacuum for a lighter result

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Vacuum distillation lowers the boiling point and produces a markedly cleaner, fruitier spirit.

name: Kurokirishima
description: Imo Shochu from Japan.
funFact: One of 2 Imo Shochu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%, sometimes 20%

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

name: Satsuma Shiranami
description: Imo Shochu from Japan.
funFact: One of 2 Imo Shochu bottlings catalogued here.

serve.glass: Tumbler, or a ceramic kurojoka for warming
serve.how: Oyuwari — cut with hot water, hot water poured first — opens the aroma and is the traditional Kagoshima serve. On the rocks in summer. Never chilled to the point of numbness; the earthiness is the point.

composition.summary: Sweet potato fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Kogane sengan and other Kagoshima sweet potatoes

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice or barley koji, black or white

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%, sometimes 20%

composition.process: Black koji, revived from Okinawan awamori production, gives a richer and sweeter result than white.

name: Takara Jun
description: Kome Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Kome Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp, warm or on the rocks
serve.glass: Wine glass, or warmed in a choku
serve.how: Warmed gently in winter, on the rocks in summer, or neat at room temperature. Kuma shochu is traditionally pre-mixed with water and warmed in a ceramic flask overnight before serving.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation, atmospheric or vacuum

components.label: Strength
components.detail: Usually 25%

composition.process: Both the base and the koji are rice, which is why it sits so close to sake on the palate.

name: Lento Kokuto
description: Kokuto Shochu from Japan.
funFact: The only Kokuto Shochu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with water
serve.how: On the rocks, or with cold water. Despite the base it is not sweet, since the sugar ferments out entirely. It sits somewhere between a light rum and a shochu, which is exactly what it is.

composition.summary: Brown sugar fermented with rice koji and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Amami kokuto, unrefined brown sugar

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Rice koji, which is legally required

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

composition.process: The rice koji requirement is what keeps it classified as shochu rather than as rum.

name: Zuisen Awamori
description: Awamori Kusu from Japan.
funFact: The only Awamori Kusu bottling catalogued here.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.how: Neat at room temperature in a small cup, or on the rocks. Okinawans traditionally cut it with water and let it sit overnight before serving, which softens it noticeably.

composition.summary: Awamori aged three years or more in clay pots by fractional topping.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Long-grain Thai rice with black koji

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware; traditional systems run far longer

composition.process: Clay is slightly porous, so the spirit oxidises slowly in a way glass or steel would not allow.

name: Jinro Chamisul
description: Andong Soju from South Korea. The world's best-selling spirit by volume.
funFact: Jinro Chamisul: The world's best-selling spirit by volume

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with nuruk and distilled in a traditional soju gori.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nuruk, a Korean wild-culture starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in an earthenware soju gori

composition.process: Nuruk carries a wilder mix of moulds and yeasts than Japanese koji, which gives a more rustic result.

name: Chum Churum
description: Andong Soju from South Korea.
funFact: One of 3 Andong Soju bottlings catalogued here.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small cup, poured for others rather than yourself, which is fixed Korean etiquette. It is strong and clean, and deserves to be sipped rather than shot.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with nuruk and distilled in a traditional soju gori.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rice

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Nuruk, a Korean wild-culture starter

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in an earthenware soju gori

composition.process: Nuruk carries a wilder mix of moulds and yeasts than Japanese koji, which gives a more rustic result.

name: Korn Berentzen
description: Korn from Germany.
funFact: The only Korn bottling catalogued here.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a tiny glass, drunk in one go with a beer to follow. In the north it is called Herrengedeck when paired with a pilsner. Ageing it in oak makes something closer to a light whisky, but that is no longer Korn.

composition.summary: Rye, wheat, barley or oats distilled to a modest strength with nothing added.

components.label: Base
